title: Due To Unforeseen Circumstances
subtitle: Who Gave This Guy a Mic?
body:
## COLD OPEN
A drummer blows up a kit live on TV. A band plays a song called "Break Stuff" to a quarter million angry people, and they take it as instructions. And a man bites the head off a bat. On purpose. Sort of.
Each one of these nights ended, at least figuratively, with a guy in a suit taping a sign to a door that said "Due to unforeseen circumstances," and it shut everything down.
They were not unforeseen. Somebody saw every one of them coming.
## TODAY
So that's what this podcast is about. The crazy stories that happened in the music industry.
So without further ado: I'm Duck, and this is Defacing the Music.
[THEME SONG, hard stop]
Episode zero. Due To Unforeseen Circumstances. Or, Who Gave This Guy a Mic?

## WHO I AM
All right. So like I said, I'm Duck. Quick intro about me.
I've been playing guitar for thirty two years, and I've been in the scene for pretty much all of those years. I've heard a lot of stories.
I'm not an expert. But I've stood on enough stages and played with enough bands to see some people make some really bad decisions that were fucking awesome.
I've met enough guys that were like, "I used to be a roadie for Foghat in the '80s, and here's a story that happened." And it's usually bullshit. But that's fine.
[FILL: who Duck is, in his words. Anything else you want people to know about you.]

## WHAT THIS IS
There are a lot of good stories out there in the music industry. You've heard a lot of them. I'm gonna talk about those ones.
There's a lot you haven't heard. I'm gonna try to talk about those, too.
But the biggest thing is, I'm gonna try to bring in details you might not know and might not have heard, to bring something new to it.
Every episode is one story, roughly fifteen minutes long, about a real night where a band, a promoter, a label, or a crowd took a bad idea all the way to the end.

## THE RULES
It's all real. That's the point.
If there's anything in these stories that everybody just repeats and nobody can prove, I'm gonna tell you that's just how the legend goes. That way you're not having to decipher what's bullshit and what's not. I'm gonna do that for you.
When real people get hurt, I'll let you know that it was real, because that's not funny. Usually.
And then we're gonna talk about that guy. Because at every one of these, there's that guy. The one where you go, "That guy fucked it up for everybody."
And that guy is usually awesome. And that's kind of what makes this whole show work.
So that's gonna be a thing. Every episode, somewhere in the story, there's a guy. I'll point out the suspects as we go. And at the end, I'm gonna name him. That Guy. The one person we're blaming for all of it.
And sometimes it's not one guy. Sometimes it's a whole office full of guys. I'll tell you when it is.

## WHAT'S COMING
Here's some of what's coming.
A drummer who packed his bass drum with about ten times the flash powder he was supposed to, on live network TV, and singed his guitarist's hair off.
A band that got asked to calm down a quarter million people at Woodstock '99, and played "Break Stuff" instead.
Ozzy and the bat. Plus the meeting a year earlier, with a dove, that explains a lot.
The night in 1976 when Jerry Lee Lewis drove up to the gates of Graceland at three in the morning, drunk, with a loaded gun, demanding to see Elvis.
[Pause.]
Elvis was home. He did not come down.
And a baseball promotion right here in Chicago. Disco Demolition Night, in 1979. They blew up a crate of disco records in center field at Comiskey Park between games of a doubleheader, the crowd rushed the field, and the White Sox had to forfeit the second game.

## OUT
So that's pretty much it. That's what this show is gonna be about.
If you have ideas about stuff you want to hear, comment or send a message, and we'll see if we can get to it.
[RIFF: defacingthemusic.com, Guest List, socials. Or use this:]
You can get on the Guest List at defacingthemusic.com to find out when new episodes drop.
That's about it for episode zero.
I'm Duck. Due to unforeseen circumstances, I'll see you next week.

title: Due To Excessive Flash Powder
subtitle: Who Gave The Who Explosives?
body:
## COLD OPEN
[CLIP: Cold open: The Who blow up a Sunday night comedy show]
September 1967. CBS Television City, Los Angeles. The set of a nice Sunday night comedy show.
Tommy Smothers strolls over to a British rock band with a big friendly smile and asks them a few easy questions. Where are you from. What's your name.
The band is not really meeting him halfway.
Behind them sits a bass drum with something extra packed inside it.
And Tommy is holding an acoustic guitar. That part, believe it or not, was in the plan.
## TODAY
Today: a drummer, a bass drum, way too much flash powder, a guitarist with noticeably less hair than he started the day with, and a TV host who loses his own guitar on his own show.
Also, the biggest band in this story was opening for Herman's Hermits. We'll get to that. It's important to me that we get to that.
And somewhere in this story, there's a guy. There always is. Keep an eye out for him.
I'm Duck, and due to excessive flash powder, this is Defacing the Music.
[THEME SONG, hard stop]
Episode [NUMBER]. Who Gave The Who Explosives?

## THE OPENING ACT
[CLIP: The Who opening for Herman's Hermits]
Okay. Before we get anywhere near a bass drum, you need to know where The Who were in the summer of 1967.
In England, they're a big deal. In America, they're touring, and they are not the headliner. They are the opening act.
For who?
[Pause.]
Herman's Hermits.
Line these two bands up next to each other for a second, because I don't think the answer lands until you do.
The Who. "My Generation." "I hope I die before I get old." A guitar player who windmills his arm and then smashes the guitar into the amp until it's in pieces. A drummer who kicks the whole kit off the riser every night like it owes him money.
Herman's Hermits. "Mrs. Brown, You've Got a Lovely Daughter." "I'm Henery the Eighth, I Am." Peter Noone, who looked like he would help your grandma with her groceries and then ask if she needed anything else.
That's a tour. Somebody booked that. Somebody sat at a desk and went, "Yeah. Same night. Same stage. This makes sense."
[FILL: I didn't believe it either, so I went and checked. It's real. The Who spent a chunk of summer 1967 warming up crowds for Herman's Hermits.]
So picture the crowd. You're twelve. You're in Ohio. Your mom drove you three hours in a station wagon with no air conditioning so you could see Peter Noone smile in your general direction. You have a sign. You made the sign.
And before Peter comes out, four guys from London walk on stage and murder their equipment in front of you. Feedback. Smoke. A guitar in splinters. Your mom has her hand over your eyes.
And then they leave, and a nice young man comes out and sings about Mrs. Brown's daughter like none of that just happened.
[RIFF: opening for a band the crowd didn't come for. Or use this:]
Every musician has played that show. The one where you can see the whole room looking past you at the door. But most of us didn't do it by setting our gear on fire in front of children.
Anyway. That's where The Who are in the summer of 1967. Big in England. Kind of a weird rumor in America. And in the middle of that tour, somebody books them on national television.

## WHO IS KEITH MOON
[CLIP: Keith Moon, hotel toilet bomber]
Before we get to the TV show, I have to tell you about Keith Moon. Because "drummer" doesn't cover it. "Drummer" is the job title on paper. The actual job was something closer to "weather event."
Keith Moon is the guy who walked into a five star hotel room and started thinking about how to get it down to one star. Not in a mean way. In a curious way. Like a scientist.
His favorite thing was blowing up toilets. With cherry bombs, and later with stronger stuff. And I want to be clear, that is not one of those legends I'm going to put an asterisk on. That was a documented hobby. Hotel chains knew his name the way your mailman knows which house has the dog.
[FILL: Think about the hotel manager who has to call the front office. "Hi, yes, it's the toilet again. No, a different one. No, the same guy."]
And here's my favorite Keith Moon story from this exact tour, and this one does go in the "the story goes" pile, so hold it loosely.
August 1967. Flint, Michigan. A Holiday Inn. Keith is turning twenty one. Actually twenty one, born August 23rd, 1946. I checked, because with Keith you have to check.
There's a party. There's a cake. The cake does not survive. There's a cake fight, there's a fire extinguisher situation, and the legend says that by the end of the night a car ended up at the bottom of the hotel pool.
Did a car end up in the pool? Nobody's ever proven it. People have gone looking. People have argued about it for fifty years.
Did The Who get a very large bill from that Holiday Inn? Yes. That part's real.
[RIFF: the car in the pool. Is it better if it's true or better if it's not? Your call. Or use this:]
If it's fake, somebody made up a story so good that people have spent fifty years looking for a car at the bottom of a pool in Flint, Michigan. Most true things don't get that kind of attention.
So that's our guy. Twenty one, as of that week. Loves explosions. Recently banned from a Holiday Inn, allegedly. And now CBS is going to put him on national television with a pyrotechnic in his bass drum.
What could possibly.

## THE SMOTHERS BROTHERS
Quick thing for anybody under fifty, because I had to look some of this up too.
The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour was a Sunday night variety show on CBS. Tom and Dick Smothers. Brothers. Folk singers who did comedy. Tommy played the dumb one, Dick played the straight man, and the bit was mostly Tommy losing an argument with his brother. "Mom always liked you best." That was their line.
And on paper that sounds like the safest show on television. Two guys in matching sweaters doing folk songs.
But they were actually the cool show. They booked rock bands. They got in fights with CBS about politics and the war almost every week. Network censors basically had a desk with their name on it.
And here's the decision nobody talks about. The show asked for the smashing. Pete Townshend said it in a VH1 interview years later: the Smothers Brothers had a pretty radical show for the time, and they bravely asked the band if they'd destroy their instruments. So The Who didn't sneak this onto CBS. CBS sent them an invitation.
And one thing I got wrong in the pilot, so let me fix it here. This wasn't live. They taped it on a Friday, September 15th, 1967, at CBS in Los Angeles, and it aired that Sunday night.
[Pause.]
Which is somehow worse. Because that means CBS had two full days with the tape. Two days to watch a drum kit explode and a guitar player come out of the smoke with his hair on fire. And somebody at CBS watched it, and thought about it, and said, "Yeah. Sunday. Family hour. Send it."
[FILL: So, to recap the booking: a network that's already nervous about this show lets it bring on the band that destroys its own equipment for a living. And then says, "Can you make the ending bigger?"]

## THE SETUP
The Who come on to do two songs. "I Can See for Miles," which was brand new, and is going to become their biggest American hit. And "My Generation," which is the one where they wreck everything.
And for TV, the wrecking has to be bigger. It's a stage show, but now it's a stage show on a screen the size of a toaster. So the plan is a small explosive charge in Keith's bass drum. A flash. A pop. A little puff of smoke. Great television. Everybody goes home.
Now here's where the story gets murky, and I'm going to be straight with you about it, because nobody agrees on exactly what happened.
Start with the part almost nobody tells. The show's producer, a guy named Allan Blye, said years later that in rehearsal the charge was a powder puff. A little poof. Not good enough for television. So he asked for a bigger effect. And the band, it turns out, had already told their own guy the same thing.
[FILL: So that's two different people asking for more boom, and neither one of them knows the other one asked. That's not a plan. That's a group text with no group.]
And then there's Keith.
The most common version: Keith pays off a stagehand to load extra flash powder. Some versions say the crew loaded the normal amount, and Keith added more on top when nobody was watching. One account says it ended up being around ten times what it should've been.
[FILL: Ten times. Not "a little extra." Not "a splash more." Ten times. That's not a recipe adjustment, that's a different recipe.]
And I keep thinking about the stagehand. Because in every version of this, there's a guy. There's a crew guy holding a can of flash powder, and a twenty one year old Englishman with a reputation for blowing up toilets walks up and goes, "Mate. A bit more."
And the guy says yes.
[RIFF: the stagehand. What's in his head. What does he tell his wife that night. "How was work?" "Well." Or use this:]
He gets home that night, his wife asks how work was, and he just says, "Well." And then he doesn't say anything else for about an hour.
There's always a guy. We're gonna find the guy. We're not gonna find the guy. Nobody knows his name. But he's out there. In spirit.

## THE BOOM
Okay. So. They play "I Can See for Miles," it's great, nobody's on fire yet.
Then Tommy Smothers comes out and does a little interview with them. And you can watch this, it's on YouTube, and it's honestly one of the best things on the internet. Tommy's being friendly, asking names, making small talk, and the band is not really meeting him halfway. Tommy is doing his best.
[FILL: Watch Tommy in that clip. He has no idea. He's the guy in a horror movie saying "I'll be right back."]
Then they go into "My Generation." And it's building, and building, and Pete starts smashing his guitar, and Keith kicks over the drums, and then somebody hits the charge.
And it is not a pop.
[Pause.]
It is a bomb. On a soundstage. There's a wall of smoke where the drums used to be, and when the footage clears, the heads and hoops are blown clean off the bass drum.
The blast reportedly took out one of the cameras and the studio's monitors too. So for a second, the people running the show couldn't even see the thing that just happened on their show.
Roger Daltrey was out front with the microphone, minding his own business. Years later he told Ultimate Classic Rock, "It blew me flat on my face." The singer. Not even near the drums.
And then there's John Entwistle. The bass player. Go find the clip and watch him, not Pete, not Keith. Smoke everywhere, the drummer's yelling, the singer's on the floor, and Entwistle, in a nice suit, just kind of glances back over his shoulder. Barely flinches. Like a guy at a bus stop who heard a car backfire. That's the most British thing that's ever happened on American television.
[FILL: Every band has an Entwistle. The guy who's seen too much. You could set the stage on fire and he'd ask if we're still doing the second set.]
The way it usually gets told, the blast throws Keith right off his drum riser. What every account agrees on is that he took shrapnel in his arm. Some versions say it was a piece of his own cymbal. You can hear him yelling on the tape. Pete Townshend is standing right in front of the bass drum when it goes, and it singes his hair. Pete comes out of the smoke looking like a cartoon. Like he lost a fight with a cigar. His own words for it, from that VH1 interview: "It set my hair alight."
[RIFF: describe Pete's face in the clip. Then tell people to go watch it after the episode. Or use this:]
He looks like a guy who leaned over a grill to check the burgers and the grill had opinions. Go watch it after this. Watch his face, not the drums.
And here's the part that's not funny, and I'll say it once. Pete has said for years that this night is part of why his hearing has been bad ever since. He's lived with tinnitus most of his life.
To be fair to Keith, and I can't believe I'm being fair to Keith, Pete also stood in front of the loudest amplifiers on Earth for sixty years. So it's not all one night. But Pete has pointed at this one. He remembers which night it was.

## THE GUITAR
[CLIP: Pete takes Tommy Smothers' guitar]
Now. My favorite part. And this is on tape, so no asterisk.
The smoke is still clearing. Pete's hair is still smoking. The drummer is bleeding. The audience doesn't know if this is the bit or a real emergency.
And Tommy Smothers walks back out. With an acoustic guitar. Smiling. Because the show must go on.
[Pause.]
Pete takes the guitar out of his hands. And smashes it on the floor.
[FILL: Not angry. Not a fight. Just, "Oh, I'll take that." Like a waiter clearing a plate.]
And Tommy just kind of stands there. Holding the air where his guitar was. On his own show. In front of the whole country.
Now here's the part I didn't know until I went digging. The guitar was the bit. Tommy said it himself, decades later, in an oral history of the show: the whole thing was supposed to end with Pete smashing his guitar. That was the plan. The comedy button on the segment.
The bomb was not the plan. Tommy said there was shrapnel everywhere, and he honestly thought there were going to be dead bodies. And because he's walking out there looking around in a panic, everybody watching figured it couldn't be part of the act. He called it a real, authentic moment. Which is a very polite way of saying, "I thought I was going to die on my own show and then a guy took my guitar."
[RIFF: Tommy's face. The rehearsed bit happening on schedule inside an unrehearsed disaster. Or use this:]
That's the best part. Tommy still does the bit. The building just blew up, he's got no idea if his guest drummer is alive, and he hands over the guitar right on cue anyway. That's a professional. If a guy smashed my guitar at a gig, there'd be a second show after the first one, out in the parking lot.
I think about that a lot. A guy built an entire career on being the nice brother who loses arguments, and then he loses his guitar to a British art student covered in soot. That's the most Tommy Smothers thing that could have possibly happened.

## THE LEGEND
One more piece of this, and this one gets the biggest asterisk of the episode.
The story goes that Bette Davis was backstage that night, waiting to go on. Bette Davis. Old Hollywood royalty. All About Eve. And when the bass drum went off, she was so shaken up that she fainted. Into the arms of Mickey Rooney.
[Pause.]
Is that true? Here's what I can tell you. Bette Davis and Mickey Rooney really were on the show that week. So the casting is right.
But Dick Smothers, the straight-man brother, said he was standing in the wings next to Bette Davis, watching, when it went off. And his take on the fainting rumor was basically: are you kidding? He said Bette Davis could see an atom bomb go off and wouldn't faint. He didn't even know if she blinked. And Tommy has denied the fainting story too.
[FILL: Some people think Keith Moon himself pumped up the fainting part when he told the story later. Which, if you've been paying attention, is the least surprising sentence in this episode.]
So the two guys whose show it was, one of them standing right next to her, say no. That's about as debunked as a legend gets.
But I'm telling it anyway, because somebody made up "Bette Davis faints into Mickey Rooney," and that person deserves something. An award. A plaque.
[RIFF: picture it. Smoke, a bleeding drummer, and Bette Davis going down like a folding chair into Mickey Rooney. Or use this:]
Smoke everywhere, a drummer bleeding, a guitar player with his hair on fire, and one of the greatest actresses who ever lived folding up like a lawn chair. Into Mickey Rooney. It's made up, and it's still the best thing in this whole episode.

## THE FALLOUT
So what happened to everybody?
Keith Moon got bandaged up and went right back to being Keith Moon for another eleven years. If anything, the explosion was great for business. It's one of the most famous clips in rock and roll.
Pete Townshend got a story he's told for over fifty years, and ears that still ring.
"I Can See for Miles" became The Who's biggest hit single in America. So, in a way, the explosion worked. Two months later nobody was asking who opened for Herman's Hermits.
[FILL: Herman's Hermits, meanwhile. Wonderful band. Lovely people. Did not explode on television. And nobody's making a podcast about them.]
And the Smothers Brothers? CBS canceled the show in 1969. Not because of The Who. They had a long fight with the network over politics and censorship, and the network finally just pulled the plug. But I'd like to think somebody at CBS had a folder, and the drum kit was in it.

## THAT GUY
[CLIP: That Guy verdict]
Okay. Time to name him. That Guy.
The suspects.
Suspect one: Keith Moon. Twenty one that very summer. Known toilet bomber. The man who, in most versions of this story, walked up to the crew and asked for more.
Suspect two: the stagehand. The guy holding the can of flash powder, who looked at Keith Moon, a man with a documented history of exploding plumbing, and said yes.
Suspect three: CBS. And the Smothers Brothers. Who booked the band that destroys its own gear every night, asked them to destroy it on their show, and then their own producer asked for a bigger bang.
[Pause.]
And the verdict.
Honestly? It's the stagehand. I know nobody knows his name. I know the stories don't agree on exactly what he did. But Keith Moon asking for more explosives is not news. That's just Keith being Keith. That's weather. The stagehand was the one person in the building whose whole job was to say no. And he didn't.
[THAT GUY STING]
[RIFF: your verdict. Do you let Keith off the hook? Or use this:]
Keith's still guilty. Keith's always guilty. But you don't blame the tornado. You blame the guy who said, "Yeah, park the trailers right there."
And, because the rule is "that guy is usually awesome": somewhere out there, there's a retired stagehand who has been telling this story at barbecues for fifty years. And every single time, he's the hero.

## OUT
So that's it. One drummer. One bass drum. Way too much flash powder. A stagehand who said yes. And a man who walked out to do a bit and lost his guitar.
And the lesson, if there is one: when the guy who blows up hotel toilets for fun asks for a little more, the answer is no. Write it down. Put it on the wall.
[RIFF: one last thought. What it says about 1967 that this was Sunday night family viewing. Or use this:]
This was Sunday night family viewing. Grandma's on the couch. Somebody's eating a TV dinner off a tray. And a drum kit explodes. And nobody at CBS thought, maybe not this one.
Next time, another one. Another band, another night, another guy.
[RIFF: defacingthemusic.com, Guest List, subscribe, socials. Keep it short. Or use this:]
Get on the Guest List at defacingthemusic.com. No flash powder. We checked.
I'm Duck. Due to unforeseen circumstances, I'll see you next time.

title: Due To Not Giving Peace a Chance
subtitle: Who Asked Fred Durst to Be a Therapist?
body:
## COLD OPEN
[CLIP: Cold open: let's do that again]
Summer, 1999. An old Air Force base in upstate New York on the government's toxic waste list.
A four dollar pretzel.
A plywood wall, twelve feet high, around the whole party.
A guy in a red cap with a microphone and some strong opinions about Alanis Morissette.
And a peace group with a box of candles and the very best of intentions.
Thirty years after the nicest party in American history, somebody said: let's do that again.

## TODAY
Today: the original Woodstock, the sequel nobody asked for, four dollar water on a concrete runway, and the single worst song choice for a specific moment in the history of recorded music. Maybe two of those.
Somewhere in this story there's a guy. A lot of people think they already know who it is. I've got a couple other names for you.
I'm Duck, and due to not giving peace a chance, this is Defacing the Music.
[THEME SONG, hard stop]
Episode [NUMBER]. Who Asked Fred Durst to Be a Therapist?
So, the name. "Give Peace a Chance." John Lennon and Yoko Ono recorded it in June 1969, in bed, in a hotel room in Montreal. They were doing one of their bed-ins, where they stayed in bed for a week for world peace and invited the press over. It came out that July, one month before the original Woodstock. And it became the anthem for that whole generation. That November, at an anti-war rally in Washington, a huge crowd sang it together, over and over. The whole chorus is one line: "All we are saying is give peace a chance."
Then they kept trying to do it again. Once in 1994, and then again in 1999, for the thirtieth anniversary. And in 1999, nobody gave peace a chance.
Now, before I get into how, I want to say one thing straight, and then I'll leave it alone.
People died at Woodstock '99, and women were sexually assaulted. That was real, and it was awful. I'm not going to make jokes about it, and I'm not going to dig into it. If you want that side of the story, the HBO and Netflix documentaries cover it. This one's about everything else that went wrong.
Okay.

## THE ORIGINAL
To understand how bad the sequel was, you have to understand how weirdly nice the first one was.
August 1969. A dairy farm in Bethel, New York, owned by a guy named Max Yasgur. And Max is not a hippie. Max is a conservative Republican dairy farmer who rents his field to a bunch of long-haired kids anyway.
The promoters were expecting about fifty thousand people. Somewhere around four hundred thousand show up. The fences go down, and it's a free concert now.
It rains. It turns into a mud pit. The food runs out. And here's the part that makes it Woodstock instead of a disaster: it mostly works.
A commune called the Hog Farm runs the free kitchen. Their guy, Wavy Gravy, gets on the mic and tells the crowd that what they have in mind is breakfast in bed for four hundred thousand.
[FILL: A man named Wavy Gravy was in charge of breakfast for a crowd the size of a city. And it went fine. Remember that when we get to the guys in charge of breakfast in 1999.]
And the police chief in the next town over tells the New York Times these were the most courteous, considerate and well-behaved group of kids he'd been in contact with in twenty four years of police work.
[Pause.]
A cop said that. About four hundred thousand hippies in a mud pit.

## THE SEQUEL TO THE SEQUEL
So that's the legend. And when you have a legend like that, somebody's always going to look at it and think, "We could do that again."
They try it in 1994, for the twenty fifth anniversary, with one of the original guys, Michael Lang, behind it. And everything that goes wrong in 1999 is already there in '94. Big ticket prices. Corporate sponsors. Way more people than the fences can hold. Mud flying at the stage. It just didn't catch fire.
And the people running it learn exactly the wrong lesson. Not "we got lucky." They learn "it always works out."

## 1969 VERSUS 1999
Now. What did a nineteen year old in 1999 actually want to hear?
Because the culture moved. The original Woodstock poster said "3 Days of Peace and Music." The big songs were about the garden, and peace, and getting it together.
In 1999, the number one album in America, a few weeks before the festival, was Limp Bizkit's "Significant Other." It came out in June, sold somewhere around six hundred and thirty five thousand copies its first week, and knocked the Backstreet Boys off the top of the chart.
That's the mood. Boy bands on one side, guys in red caps yelling on the other, and the guys in red caps were winning.
And on that album, there's a song called "Break Stuff."
If you somehow have never heard it: it opens with Fred Durst telling you it's just one of those days. And then for about two and a half minutes he explains, in great detail and with a lot of swearing, that he is in a terrible mood and he is going to break things, and possibly your face.
That's the shift. You go from a farmer saying "God bless you" to a song that is, top to bottom, about wanting to break your stuff.
I'm not knocking it. I've been in bars where somebody puts "Break Stuff" on after midnight and you watch people with 401ks decide to start shoving each other. The song works. It does exactly what it says on the label.
And the '99 lineup was full of that energy. The festival opens Friday with James Brown. The godfather of soul. And then it's Korn, DMX, Kid Rock, Limp Bizkit, Rage Against the Machine, Metallica. A few nice acts sprinkled in, Sheryl Crow, Alanis, Jewel. But the center of gravity was guys who wanted you to jump.
And the hippies? Gone. Not one band from 1969 is on the bill. Rolling Stone counted exactly two people from the original festival: John Entwistle of The Who, playing a solo set, and the Grateful Dead's drummer, Mickey Hart, with his band Planet Drum. That's it. Two guys. Out of a whole weekend. In 1994 the hippies were outnumbered. In 1999 they were extinct.
[RIFF: the 1999 rock radio dial. Or use this:]
In 1999, rock radio sounded like a dozen guys in track pants who were all mad at their dads. And for a nineteen year old in a parking lot, that was church.

## THE PLAN
So. Michael Lang, from the original, teams up with a big New Jersey concert promoter named John Scher. Planning starts in the fall of 1998.
At first they're going to go back to the '94 site. Then they find something better. Better for them.
Griffiss Air Force Base. Rome, New York. The Air Force had pulled out in the mid nineties, so now it's a giant empty base with miles of runway.
And here's my first oddly specific detail, and you're welcome. Griffiss had been on the EPA's Superfund list, the official list of the most contaminated hazardous waste sites in the country, since 1987. They threw the peace and love party on a Superfund site.
[Pause.]
Now think about what an Air Force base actually is. It's not grass. It's tarmac. Flat concrete and asphalt built so bombers can land on it. Hardly any trees, because trees and airplanes don't get along. No shade.
The two main stages were about two miles apart. One write-up says two point three. The guy who wrote it up for Pollstar says he drove a van between them, because if you wanted to see acts on both stages, on foot, on that concrete, in that heat, you were not going to make it.
They pick late July.
And to keep the gate crashers out, because the original went free when the fences fell, they build a wall. Around the whole site. Twelve feet tall, mostly plywood. Reports say three miles of it, some say closer to six.
You know what they called it?
The Peace Wall.
[FILL: They built a twelve foot wooden wall to keep people out of a peace festival and named it the Peace Wall. That's like calling the bouncer "Hugs."]
Security is a crew called the Peace Patrol, in yellow shirts. A lot of them were basically kids themselves.
Tickets are a hundred and fifty bucks. In today's money, that's about three hundred. Pay-per-view at home is fifty nine ninety five. That's about a hundred and twenty in today's money. MTV reported the whole thing cost about thirty eight million dollars to put on.
And now the food.
Lots of people say security took their food and water at the gate. Some people say they walked right in with a case of bottled water. Depends which gate, apparently. Either way, once you're in, you're buying from the vendors.
Here's the menu, courtesy of MTV News, live from the festival. A bottle of water, four dollars. In today's money, that's about eight. For one bottle. On a runway.
[CLIP: Four dollar water, twelve dollar cheese cardboard]
And there's a vendor named Frank Cristiano who told Spin the company holding the concession contract was selling water to the vendors at seventy bucks a case. That's about a hundred and forty today. Which works out to more than three bucks a bottle before the vendor even makes a dime.
So the four dollar water isn't even the guy at the booth getting greedy. The guy at the booth is getting robbed too. It's robbery all the way down.
And then there's the pizza. A twelve inch pizza, twelve dollars. In today's money, that's about twenty four.
I'm from Chicagoland. I have had pizza worth twenty four bucks.
This was not that. This was cheese cardboard.
[RIFF: the Chicago pizza rant. Go as long as you want. Or use this:]
Real pizza has a structure. It has a philosophy. Woodstock pizza was a paper plate that somebody described cheese to. And you couldn't even fold it, because folding is a New York thing, and this was upstate, where nobody's getting fancy with cardboard.
[TALK: the most you've ever paid for the worst food at a show]

## THURSDAY TO SATURDAY
Okay. The gates open, Thursday, July 22nd. Somewhere around two hundred thousand people. Some estimates go higher.
And it's hot. Right around a hundred degrees. On blacktop, which soaks up the sun all day and throws it back in your face. By Saturday, the promoter says medical crews have treated nearly a thousand people for heat exhaustion and dehydration.
There are free water fountains. Not enough. Lines up to half an hour in the sun. So people get frustrated and start breaking the pipes to get at the water.
Now here's the Associated Press, on Saturday:
"At the original Woodstock, there were warnings about bad acid. At Woodstock '99, the admonishments are about water. Drink lots of it."
"Organizers on Saturday tried to push H2O on more than 225,000 people sweltering in 90-degree-plus temperatures during the second day of the three-day megaconcert. 'There's lots of free water here. There's water all over the site. We just have to get people to use it,' promoter John Scher said."
We just have to get people to use it. John, they're breaking the pipes open with their hands. They are using it. Aggressively.
And then the AP runs down everything that was not the big worry that weekend:
"Not crime. Not traffic. Not gatecrashers. Not the growing piles of garbage and overflowing portable toilets."
The overflowing toilets made the list of things nobody was worried about. That's going to come back.
And now you've got broken water lines, on a site that also has porta potties that aren't getting emptied fast enough and start overflowing. And it all runs downhill to the same low spots.
And people are rolling around in it. Sliding in it. Calling it mud.
It was not mud.
There were even reports of trench mouth, a gum infection with a name from World War One. At a music festival. In 1999.
Then on Saturday, Kid Rock plays. And as a big finish, he tells the crowd to throw stuff at him. He specifically adds, "But nothing that could hurt each other!" And the crowd, who has been buying four dollar water for two days, buries the stage in plastic bottles.
Now, he probably meant that as a joke about the water prices. Some people took it that way. But think about what just happened. A guy on the main stage asked a couple hundred thousand people to throw things, and they did it instantly, and it looked awesome on camera.
That's a crowd checking what it's allowed to do.
By Saturday afternoon, Spin reported kids without tickets had already split open little gaps in the Peace Wall. So the wall's already getting tested too.

## SATURDAY NIGHT
Here's Saturday on the east stage. Dave Matthews Band plays late afternoon. Around six thirty, Alanis Morissette. A nice, mellow set. People sway.
Then, a little after eight, golden hour, sun going down, the next band walks out...
[CUT TO: crazy photo of the band + the "Limp Bizkit" announcer sound bite from their album intro, the low demon carnival voice. Duck doesn't say the name.]
So picture the crowd at that exact moment. Day three. Sunburned, dehydrated, broke from the water. Standing in not-mud. Hyped up by a guy who just asked them to throw things at him and loved it. And now the band with the number one album in the country walks out.
Now here's the legend, and I'm going to tell it the way it usually gets told.
The story goes, the organizers go to Fred before the set and say, "Fred. It's getting crazy out there. They're hot, they're tired, they're pissed. We need you to go out there and settle everybody down."
Has anybody ever proven that conversation happened? No. That's the legend pile. A couple of write-ups of the set say Fred himself told the crowd that "they" wanted him to ask everybody to mellow out. If that's right, the only source we have for the request is Fred, on stage, making fun of it.
And if it did happen, it's like dropping me into a convention of people who sell crystals and healing water and expecting me not to be an asshole.
[RIFF: the crystals convention. This is your line, run with it. Or use this:]
You don't send the guy with the flamethrower to the fireworks factory and ask him to keep it down. That's not a plan. That's a dare.
Here's what's on tape.
Fred gets on the mic and says, "Don't let anybody get hurt. But I don't think you should mellow out. That's what Alanis Morissette had you motherfuckers do."
[FILL: Different write-ups have "anybody" or "nobody," and "had you" or "just had you." The point survives either way.]
He said don't let anybody get hurt. Give him that. He did say it. And then in the next breath he told them the one thing they should not do is calm down.
[TALK: if you're Fred and they ask you to calm that crowd down, what do you actually play?]

## BREAK STUFF
[CLIP: Why Break Stuff was the spark]
About two thirds of the way through the set, they play "Break Stuff."
And this is where it turns. Let me tell you why.
"Break Stuff" did not burn Woodstock down. The big fires were the next night, Sunday. Anybody who tells you Limp Bizkit played one song and the place went up in flames has the timeline wrong.
But "Break Stuff" is where this crowd went from miserable to destructive. That's the moment. Before it, you've got a hot, angry, ripped off crowd. During it, the walls start coming down.
People pull plywood off the Peace Wall, and off a lighting tower, and start surfing on it. Big sheets of plywood floating across the crowd with people standing on them. People climb the towers.
And here's how that works, because it's not complicated. One guy pulls a board off a wall. Nothing happens to him. Then another guy does it. Nobody stops him either. And then it starts looking permitted. It's like looting. Once a few people are doing it and nobody's coming, everybody figures the rules are off. It snowballs, and every new board makes the next one easier.
And the song playing while that starts is a song whose entire message is "I'm in a bad mood and I'm going to break things." You couldn't have picked a worse soundtrack for that exact moment if you'd held auditions.
So the song didn't light the fire. The song is where the crowd figured out it was allowed to start pulling the place apart.
Now this next bit is real. Near the end of the set, there are photos of Fred himself on a torn down panel of the wall, surfing the crowd.
The lead singer of the band that everybody blames for the riot rode a piece of the Peace Wall over the crowd. I had that one in the legend pile at first because it sounds made up. It isn't.
To be fair to Fred, because I said I'd try: he's said since that "Break Stuff" means start jumping and singing, not start burning the place down. "That's not what I meant." He's also said he didn't see anybody getting hurt, because when you're looking out at a sea of people from a stage twenty feet in the air, you can't see what's going on in the middle of it.
And honestly? I believe him that he didn't see it. That doesn't mean he didn't help cause it.
[TALK: the song that turns a normal bar crowd into a mosh pit, and the worst place you've seen it happen]

## SUNDAY
After Bizkit, Saturday night is Rage Against the Machine and Metallica. Not exactly a cool down.
Sunday is the last day. Some people are already heading home. Jewel plays to whoever's left, which is a sentence I never thought I'd say about this festival.
And all day Sunday, a peace group called PAX, an anti gun violence group, is handing out candles from their booth. The plan is a candlelight vigil during the Red Hot Chili Peppers' closing set, during "Under the Bridge." This is three months after Columbine. It's coming from a real, decent place.
How many candles? One report says a hundred thousand. Others just say thousands. Either way, a lot of open flames, handed out on purpose.
But think about where those candles are going. A field covered in trash and plastic bottles. A plywood wall that people already learned, the night before, comes apart with your hands. And a crowd that's been baking and getting robbed for three days.
So once the Chili Peppers are on, people start lighting things. The trash, the bottles, and then the wall. The Peace Wall feeds the fires.
Here's Rolling Stone, the next day:
"Concert goers began chucking massive amounts of trash, sleeping mats, umbrellas, whatever was nearby, onto the pyres. As the chaos escalated, audience members began scaling the speaker towers while others pushed over outhouses, one goofily exclaiming, 'Hope nobody was in there.'"
And the same article points out that just a few hours earlier, the organizers had held a press conference to pat themselves on the back for pulling it off. And then, "the whole thing went up in smoke. Literally."
A victory lap press conference. On the last day. A few hours before the last set. That's spiking the football at the two yard line, and then the stadium catches fire.
And John Scher, the promoter, actually comes out during the set to plead with people about the fires.
Then the band goes off, comes back out, and in the encore they play Jimi Hendrix's "Fire."
[CLIP: They played Fire]
Now, the order matters here, so let me get it right. The fires came first. The song came at the end. The band was reportedly asked to do a Hendrix tribute, by Hendrix's sister. The song didn't give anybody the idea. People were already burning the place down.
But you've got fires visibly burning in the crowd. And the song is "Fire." And they played it anyway.
[FILL: I didn't write that. I couldn't write that. If I pitched that, they'd tell me it was too much.]
After the music stops, it turns into a riot. One count says seventeen fires, with about a hundred police and twenty two fire trucks trying to deal with it. A dozen trailers torn apart. Vendor booths looted. ATMs broken open. Propane in the trucks catches and goes off. The way the organizers tell it, the firefighters on site wouldn't leave their station, because the crowd was too out of control. That's their version, nobody's proven it.
The Associated Press talked to people walking away from it that night. Here's Karen Thomas, twenty four, from Massachusetts:
"They're jerks. It's been great all weekend. People were cool, and now this is how people will remember Woodstock."
Karen called it. That night. Twenty seven years later, here I am, remembering it exactly like that.
And those speaker towers? A guy watched one go. Steven Rochlin was there shooting photos for a website called Enjoy the Music, and here's what he wrote the next day:
"The rioters worked extremely hard for about 10 minutes in trying to push this well designed and normally extremely stable structure over."
And once it was down, he says about four of them unhooked the speakers and carried them into the fire.
Worked extremely hard for about ten minutes. That's the hardest anybody worked all weekend, and that includes the guys running it. And then four guys stop to carefully unhook the speakers first. They had time to unhook them. Nobody was coming.
State troopers in riot gear come in and clear the field.
The peace and love festival ends with riot police.
And my favorite quote of the whole thing: an eighteen year old named Spencer Parker told the Associated Press the riot had some meaning when people were paying four dollars for a pretzel.
His exact words, from E! News, quoting the AP: "It has a little bit of meaning when you pay $4 for a pretzel."
Spencer. That's an eight dollar pretzel today. Spencer has a point.

## THE MORNING AFTER
So what do the guys in charge say?
Start with the mayor of Rome, Joe Griffo, the morning after. Here's Rolling Stone again:
"Riot would be an overstatement in my opinion right now," said Rome's mayor Joe Griffo.
And then he tells the reporters, "I believe that you people are using the word 'riot.'"
Joe. The state troopers showed up in riot gear. The word was on their equipment.
Same article: this is a mayor who, less than a day earlier, had offered to host the next Woodstock. Now he says he'd have to "reassess."
And Michael Lang:
"I don't think it was an anti-Woodstock statement," said Lang. "I think it was an anti-establishment, anti-everything, anti-anti statement. They were really tearing down their own facility."
Anti-anti. The man watched his festival burn and came up with a new word for it.
Michael Lang calls the people who did it "a few assholes." John Scher blames what MTV's headline called "deranged" fans. Years later he puts it like this: the generation was irresponsible, and they gave him and themselves the finger.
But that night, right after, here's what he told reporters, per E! News:
"It put a permanent blemish on what happened here. I think the kids made a mistake. They did not intend for this to happen."
The kids made a mistake. Says the guy who sold them the four dollar water.
And Lang, a decade later, says the images of kids dancing around the fire were more dramatic than the actual event.
[Pause.]
More dramatic than the event. The event was on fire.
Meanwhile, MTV, who's broadcasting this whole thing, pulls its people out. Carson Daly, who was hosting Total Request Live, has said his boss told the crew they could no longer guarantee their safety and it was time to go. Carson has said he thought he was going to die. The guy who counted down the top ten videos every afternoon.
[TALK: Carson Daly was basically the Ryan Seacrest of the 90s. Go.]
And Limp Bizkit? The week after the festival, "Significant Other" sold about two hundred fifty thousand copies, more than the week before. The whole country's talking about how they wrecked Woodstock, and the reaction is: more people buy the album.
[RIFF: the any publicity is good publicity bit. Or use this:]
That's the music business in one sentence. Burn down a festival, sell fifteen thousand extra records.
[TALK: an album you bought, or a band you got into, because everybody was mad at them]

## WOULD ANYBODY TRY THIS AGAIN
So did anybody learn anything? Kind of. Mostly the people who were watching.
Less than three months later, a brand new festival opens on a polo field in Indio, California. Coachella. And their ads bragged about free water fountains. Free water was the selling point. A festival advertised "we won't let you die of thirst" like it was a headliner.
And Woodstock '99 itself? HBO did a documentary. Netflix did one. Twenty five years later it's not a festival anymore, it's a genre. It's the festival you point to when you want to say how not to do it.
So would anybody try this again?
Yes. Him. In the HBO one, they ask Michael Lang if he'd ever do another festival. And he says, "If it works."
For the fiftieth anniversary, in 2019, he tries. Woodstock 50. Jay-Z, the Killers, Miley Cyrus, Santana. And it falls apart in slow motion. The money pulls out. They lose the venue. They can't get permits for the backup. So they try to move the whole thing to an amphitheater in Maryland that holds less than twenty thousand people.
Woodstock. For twenty thousand. In Maryland.
[Pause.]
About two weeks before it was supposed to start, Woodstock 50 is officially canceled.
They couldn't even get it to happen badly. After '99, the name was cursed.
[TALK: what it would take to get you to a festival called Woodstock now]

## THAT GUY
[CLIP: That Guy verdict]
Okay. Time to name him. That Guy.
Suspect one: Fred Durst. The easy answer for twenty five years. In a lot of people's heads, the face of this whole disaster is a guy in a red cap telling a crowd not to mellow out, and then playing "Break Stuff."
Suspect two: the peace group with the candles. No. They meant well, it was three months after Columbine, and nobody hands out candles expecting a riot. You don't get to be That Guy for trying to hold a vigil.
Suspect three: the promoters. Michael Lang and John Scher. The guys who picked a concrete Air Force base on the Superfund list. In July. With the stages two miles apart. Who built the walls out of plywood and named them the Peace Wall. Who let water get sold for four bucks a bottle on a hundred degree runway.
And here's the best piece of evidence. Years later, John Scher says he doesn't really have regrets about the festival. Except one. He wishes he hadn't booked so many hard rock acts on Saturday.
[Pause.]
John. You booked Saturday. You are the guy who booked Saturday.
Fred did not help. Fred did not fucking help. Fred poured gasoline on it, and then surfed on the gasoline. And honestly, Fred is kind of awesome in this story, in the That Guy way. He did the most Fred Durst thing a person could possibly do at the worst possible moment.
But Limp Bizkit didn't pick the runway. They didn't price the water. They didn't build the walls out of plywood, and they didn't put the angriest bands in America on the same stage on the same night, on day three, in the heat.
So That Guy is the promoters. Lang and Scher. And if I have to pick one, it's the guy who still thinks his mistake was the lineup.
John Scher.
[THAT GUY STING]
Because in every story there's a that guy. Don't be that guy.
[RIFF: your verdict. Do you let Fred off? Or use this:]
Fred lit a match. The promoters built the house out of matches, sold tickets to it, and charged you four bucks for the water to put it out.
[TALK: Fred or Scher? Who's your That Guy?]

## WHERE ARE THEY NOW
So where's Limp Bizkit now? Because for a long time the answer was "a punchline."
Then, in 2021, they play Lollapalooza. Here in Chicago, Grant Park. And Fred walks out and nobody recognizes him. Gray hair. A mustache. Glasses. He looks like a guy who's about to explain your 401k. And they play a new song called "Dad Vibes."
The internet loses its mind. That Halloween they put out an album, and the title is the most Limp Bizkit thing possible. "Still Sucks."
[RIFF: the Fred Durst dad look. Or use this:]
There's a version of getting older where you try to look young. And there's the Fred Durst version, where you show up looking like a substitute teacher and let a field full of people chant along anyway. I respect the second one.
And they're not a nostalgia act. They're bigger than they've been in twenty years. "Break Stuff" has passed a billion plays on Spotify, and "Rollin'" joined it in that club in 2025. In September 2025 they put out a song called "Making Love to Morgan Wallen," and it went to number one on Billboard's Hot Hard Rock Songs chart. Their first number one on a Billboard songs chart since 1999.
One straight thing. In October 2025, the band's bass player and co-founder, Sam Rivers, died. He was forty eight. He was the first guy Fred recruited, after seeing him play a bar in Jacksonville. Fred put up an eight minute video for him the next day and said what Sam left them is priceless. And that week, people went back to the music, and "Break Stuff" went to number one on that same hard rock chart, twenty six years after it came out.
And this one I love. Coachella, the festival that built its whole first ad campaign on being the anti Woodstock '99, has never booked Limp Bizkit. And this year Fred floated starting his own festival for the bands Coachella won't invite.
Twenty seven years later, he's still mad at the guys who run festivals.
Honestly? After this story? Fair.

## OUT
That's Woodstock '99. A peace festival on a Superfund site, a wall called the Peace Wall, four dollar water, a song called "Break Stuff," and a song called "Fire" while the field was on fire.
[RIFF: defacingthemusic.com, Guest List, subscribe, socials. Or use this:]
Get on the Guest List at defacingthemusic.com. Water's free. Pizza's real.
I'm Duck. Due to unforeseen circumstances, I'll see you next time.
[THEME SONG]

title: Due To a Possible Rabies Infection
subtitle: Who Let That Guy Bring a Bat?
body:
## COLD OPEN
[CLIP: Cold open: the slaughterhouse, the doves, the freezer]
A sixteen year old in Birmingham, England, gets a promotion at the slaughterhouse. From puke remover to cow killer.
Seventeen years later, he walks into a record company sales convention with doves in his jacket.
A year after that, a family in Des Moines, Iowa, has a dead bat in the freezer. And their seventeen year old has a ticket to a concert.
All of these things are connected. None of them end well for the animals.
## TODAY
Today: a slaughterhouse, a sales convention, a catapult full of calves' livers, a frozen bat, a hospital in Iowa, and the Alamo.
Everybody knows Ozzy bit the head off a bat. Almost nobody knows why. Because it was kind of an accident. And it was set up by about a year of very bad decisions.
And somewhere in this story there's a guy. You think you already know who. You might be right. Stick around anyway.
I'm Duck, and due to a possible rabies infection, this is Defacing the Music.
[THEME SONG, hard stop]
Episode [NUMBER]. Who Let That Guy Bring a Bat?

## THE SLAUGHTERHOUSE KID
Let's start at the beginning, because Ozzy's whole life is a setup for this.
John Michael Osbourne. Born December 1948 in Aston, a working class part of Birmingham, England. Factories, smoke, no money. Leaves school around fifteen and starts bouncing through the worst jobs you can think of.
One of them is a slaughterhouse in Digbeth, in Birmingham. And Ozzy's own version of it is incredible. His first job there was cleaning out the stomachs of dead sheep. He says for the first two or three weeks, he did nothing but throw up. Then, quote, "once I'd proved myself as puke remover, they promoted me to cow killer."
That's a career path. Most people's first promotion is "assistant manager." Ozzy's was "cow killer." And you want to know the craziest part? It's going to matter. Later in this story, a guy who used to gut animals for a living is going to have a tour where he throws animal guts at people. I don't know if anybody connected those dots in 1982. I'm connecting them now.
[RIFF: worst job you ever had, and whether it beats puke remover. Or use this:]
I've had bad jobs. I've never had a job where throwing up was the probation period.
He also did a short stretch in Winson Green prison in Birmingham, for a burglary, because he couldn't pay the fine. And when he gets out, he wants to sing. So he puts up a card in a local music shop. Depending on who tells it, it says "Ozzy Zig Needs Gig" or "Ozzy Zig Requires Gig." And at least one version adds the line that sold it: "Has own PA."
That's how you start Black Sabbath. Not talent. Not a demo. The guy owns speakers.
Tony Iommi, Geezer Butler and Bill Ward answer that card, and by 1968 they're a band. They become Black Sabbath, and they basically invent heavy metal. The sound, the darkness, the whole thing. Every band with a black T-shirt owes them money.
And in April 1979, Black Sabbath fires him.
For partying too hard. In the seventies. Think about how much partying you have to do to get fired from Black Sabbath. That's getting kicked out of a frat for being too loud.
[FILL: Sabbath kept going with Ronnie James Dio, who was great. Ozzy, by his own account, holed up in a hotel and mostly just drank.]
And then the person who saves him is Sharon Arden. Her dad, Don Arden, managed Sabbath. Sharon decides Ozzy can be a solo star. She becomes his manager, later his wife, and she builds a band around him, with a young guitar player from California named Randy Rhoads. Keep him in mind. We'll get back to Randy.

## THE DOVE
[CLIP: The doves at the sales convention]
March 27th, 1981. Los Angeles. Ozzy's first solo record, "Blizzard of Ozz," is coming out in America that same day. It's got "Crazy Train" on it. It's going to be huge. Nobody knows that yet.
His American label is part of CBS, and CBS is having a sales convention. A room full of record company people. These are the people who decide how hard they push your record. And Ozzy's relationship with them is, let's say, rocky. He's the drunk guy who got fired from Sabbath.
So the idea, and most tellings put this on Sharon, is to go in and make nice. Bring some white doves. Release them. Peace. Goodwill. "I'm a changed man."
Stop and think about who signed off on this. You have a client whose last job ended because he couldn't stop drinking. And your plan to win over the suits is: put live birds in his jacket and send him into a room full of strangers.
According to the biographer Mick Wall, Ozzy killed a bottle of brandy in the car on the way there.
So he gets in the room. And he lets one dove go. It flies around. Lovely.
And there's a woman from the PR side talking at him, and she's getting on his nerves. And Ozzy pulls out the next dove. And bites its head off.
His own explanation, later, to Wall: he did it just to shut her up.
In one of his tellings, he spits the head out on the table and she ends up on the floor screaming.
[Pause.]
And then he does another one. That's when they threw him out.
And think about the doves for a second. This was Ozzy's side's idea, so somebody in Ozzy's camp had to actually go get them. Live white doves. That was a task on somebody's to-do list. "Pick up dry cleaning. Doves." And whoever that was did their job perfectly. The doves showed up. The doves were in the jacket. And the plan still ended with a bird missing its head and Ozzy getting walked out of the building.
Now, the story changes depending on when you ask Ozzy. Here's the version he gave Sounds magazine, the British music paper. The bird was already dead. They'd planned to release it, it died beforehand, "so rather than waste it, I bit its head off." Rather than waste it. Like it's leftover pizza. And then the line he loved: "You should have seen their faces." He also said, flat out, "It was not a publicity stunt. I was just out of my fucking face."
And there were photos. Rudy Sarzo, who'd just joined the band as bass player, has described a little series of shots of the PR woman's face as it happens. So this wasn't a rumor. It was documented.
Rudy also has the sequel. He says he met Ozzy that same day, at the Ardens' place, and Ozzy had forgotten there was still another dove in his jacket. He found it. You can guess.
[FILL: And nobody can even agree how many doves there were. Two, or three, depending on who's telling it, plus the one he forgot was in his jacket. But every version ends the same way. Ozzy, a room full of record company people, and a dove with no head.]
So did they drop him? Here's what actually happened. They threw him out. Sharon has said they were escorted out and told not to come back. And the record came out anyway, on that same label, and sold millions. They banned the man from the building and kept selling his album. That's the music business in one sentence.
[TALK: What's the worst thing you've ever seen somebody do trying to impress the boss?]

## WHY NOBODY REMEMBERS THE DOVE
Now, everybody knows about the bat. Almost nobody knows about the dove, and the dove he did on purpose. Why? It was a closed room, nobody went to the hospital, and a bat fits. Ozzy is the Prince of Darkness. A bat is basically merch.
Biting the head off a dove is just weirdly sad.

## THE MEAT
So the record's a hit. Then a second one, "Diary of a Madman." And at the end of 1981 Ozzy goes out on the Diary of a Madman tour, with a stage show built to shock. And part of the show is meat.
Raw meat, thrown into the crowd. Pig intestines. Calves' livers. Ozzy had a catapult on stage, and he'd launch piles of raw meat into the audience, along with plastic rats. Every night.
And it gets better. According to a biography of Sharon by Sue Crawford, Sharon sent ads to the towns Ozzy was playing, encouraging fans to bring their own raw meat to throw at him.
[Pause.]
So it's not just "Ozzy throws meat at you." It's "Ozzy throws meat at you, and also, please, bring meat."
Somebody on that tour had to buy the meat. Every day. In a new city. Walk into a butcher shop in Kansas and go, "Yeah, I'll take whatever you're going to throw away. A lot of it. No, don't wrap it." And remember who's at the front of this tour: a guy who used to kill cows for a living. He's back at work. He just found a way to get paid more for it.
And here's what happens when you throw meat at a crowd. The crowd starts throwing stuff back.
Fans start showing up armed. Rubber snakes. Rubber bats. Rubber everything. And then not rubber. People throw sheep testicles on stage. Somebody throws a live frog. It becomes part of the deal. You go to an Ozzy show, you bring something gross, you throw it at Ozzy, and he does something with it.
Rudy Sarzo saw all of it from the bass spot. He told Yahoo Entertainment the crew used to keep Polaroids of the stuff fans couldn't get past security, including, his words, "the freshly slaughtered head of a cow!" And then this:
"I've had many things thrown onstage. One time in Texas, they threw a gigantic frog. I thought somebody threw a baby onstage, it was so big. I was like, 'What the hell is going on?' I looked out and it's a frog, maybe about a foot and a half."
A foot and a half. That's not a frog. That's a carry-on bag.
[TALK: What's the weirdest thing you've ever seen somebody throw at a stage?]
And word gets around about the dove, too. So now the fans know: this is the guy who bites the heads off things. Bring him something to bite.
So by January 1982, every night, a pile of stuff is landing at his feet. Almost all of it fake.
Almost.

## THE KID
Des Moines, Iowa. Wednesday, January 20th, 1982. Veterans Memorial Auditorium.
And the promoters knew exactly what they were selling. Years later, the Des Moines Register dug up the handbill for this show. Ozzy in a cape and devil horns, under the words "Just when you thought it was safe to go back to a concert." It urges "parental guidance." And it warns, "eating before concert not recommended."
Tickets were eight fifty. In today's money, that's about twenty eight bucks. For that you got Ozzy, a catapult full of livers, and a written warning not to eat first.
And the police in Des Moines have heard about this tour. Before the show, a Des Moines police lieutenant warns Ozzy's manager: if he harms an animal on stage, under Iowa law, he's going to jail. The city knew. The city saw it coming. Just not from the direction it came from.
The lieutenant was Derald Leaming, and here's how he put it to the Des Moines Register: "We had heard about Osbourne sticking birds in his mouth and warned them he would be arrested on the spot if he bit them."
Because there's a seventeen year old high school kid in the crowd named Mark Neal. And Mark has a bat.
Here's how, and this comes from Mark himself, in the Register. About two weeks before the concert, Mark's younger brother came home from school with a bat. He wanted to keep it. As a pet. And the bat, as bats do when you keep them in a house in Iowa in January, did not make it.
[Pause.]
[FILL: Now, one later story in the Register says the bat was already dead when his brother found it. So maybe it never had a chance. Either way, the Neal house now has a dead bat in it.]
So now the Neal family has a dead bat. And a concert coming up. And Mark's friend, Carmen Martin-Kelly, has an idea: don't throw it out. Freeze it.
So they do. The bat goes in the freezer. For about two weeks. In a family freezer. Next to the, I don't know, the Tater Tots. The ice cream. Mom's going in for a bag of peas and there's a bat looking at her.
And they don't keep it a secret, either. Carmen said later, "We were telling everybody before the concert that we were bringing a bat."
And she kept going. Here's more of Carmen, to the Des Moines Register:
"Hell or high water, we were gonna get it in and throw the bat up onstage. We brought a whole bunch of friends who used to sit together in Section 22, so when Mark was headed up towards the stage, I told him to wait a few minutes so I could get up there and tell everybody that Mark's getting ready to throw the bat up onstage."
She warned the section. Section 22 knew what was coming before Ozzy did.
Every one of us knew a kid like Mark in high school. Most of them never got further than a whoopee cushion. Mark went pro.
And here's a detail I love. Mark didn't even buy his ticket. According to the Register, he won it from KGGO, the local rock station. Somewhere in Iowa there's a radio DJ who has no idea he comped the bat.
On the night, Mark seals the bat in a plastic bag and takes it into the show. Some retellings say he hid it in his coat. I can't confirm the coat. But it's Iowa, in January, so I'd bet on the coat.
The Register, years later, says he tucked it into his pocket. Doesn't say which pocket. I'm still betting on the coat.
I can't bring a bottle of water into a concert in 2026. This kid walked into a show with wildlife. In a plastic bag.
[TALK: You're seventeen, you've got a frozen bat and a free ticket. Do you throw it?]

## THE BITE
[CLIP: The bite]
Sometime during the show, Mark throws the bat.
And it lands in front of Rudy Sarzo, the bass player. Rudy says he looked down, saw it, and pointed at it with the headstock of his bass. Kept playing. Mark's own description: "He looked down at it and motioned to Ozzy and, as they say, the rest is history."
So Ozzy walks over. And here's the question I couldn't let go of: why couldn't he tell?
A few reasons. One: he'd had weeks of rubber stuff thrown at him. His brain's been trained. Thing lands, thing is rubber. Two: it had been in a freezer for two weeks. It's not flapping around. It's lying there. Three: Ozzy told the BBC in 2006 that he thought it was one of those Halloween joke bats, because it had some string around its neck. Where the string came from, nobody's ever explained, and I've looked. And four: stage lights, loud, adrenaline, and was he drinking? He doesn't say so in his telling. But this is the guy who did a bottle of brandy on the way to a sales meeting.
So in his memoir, "I Am Ozzy," he says he did what he always did when he got a rubber toy on stage. Chomp.
And then. In his words: "Immediately, though, something felt wrong. Very wrong." His mouth was instantly full of "warm, gloopy liquid, with the worst aftertaste you could ever imagine."
[Pause.]
So, how much did he bite? Did he notice halfway and stop? Not according to anybody who was there. Mark Neal told the Register that he watched Ozzy pick it up, bite its head off, and throw the bat into the audience. So he went all the way through. The head came off. He didn't nibble and check.
What happened to the head after that? Did he spit it out? Swallow it? Hand it to Rudy? Nobody wrote that part down. I went looking. The head's whereabouts are officially unknown.
There's a moment, maybe half a second, where a man's whole brain goes, "Huh. That's not what rubber tastes like." And the rest of his life changes.
And a bat expert from Bat Conservation International told TMZ, after he died, that biting through a bat's neck takes real jaw strength. Muscle, tissue, bone. So whatever else you want to say about him, the man had a strong bite.

## THE HOSPITAL
And here's the thing. He finished the show. Rudy says there was an ambulance waiting for Ozzy when they came off, and Sharon told him, "He bit into a bat."
They take him to Broadlawns Medical Center in Des Moines. Rabies shot. Tetanus shot. And here's how the Des Moines Register started its story two days later, word for word: "Rock Singer Ozzy Osbourne left Des Moines Thursday with a $39,000 haul from a concert at Veterans Memorial Auditorium, a four-day supply of rabies vaccine and a bat taste in his mouth."
Thirty nine thousand dollars and a bat taste in his mouth. That's the most honest summary of a rock and roll night I've ever read in a newspaper.
In today's money, that thirty nine grand is about a hundred and thirty thousand.
The hospital phones blow up. A nurse supervisor there, Pam Culver, got calls from England, from Canada, from all over the US. And people were already saying the whole thing was a publicity stunt. So who steps up to shut that down? Not his manager. Not a publicist. The nurse. Pam told the Register, "If it was a joke or publicity stunt, he sure put himself to a lot of trouble to do it." Which is a very polite Iowa way of saying nobody signs up for five rabies shots for the press.
Picture the Prince of Darkness in a waiting room, filling out a clipboard. "Reason for visit." And he has to write it down. In pen.
Meanwhile, Rudy Sarzo is watching Sharon. Here's Rudy, to Yahoo Entertainment, forty years later:
"Sharon knew immediately that she had an opportunity here. She contacted Michael Jensen Communications, our publicist, and she spun it." He says he watched her get on the phone and say, "Hey, listen, this happened. Let's make a story out of this."
So the nurse is out there telling the world it's not a stunt, for free, and the manager is in the next room calling the publicist. Pam was doing PR for Ozzy and nobody was paying her.
Then the town loses its mind. Mayor Pete Crivaro wants to know whether Ozzy broke an agreement about not using animals in the act. The auditorium makes a new rule: no performer can use, present, or "in any way" make live animals part of a show without management's consent. Which, again, he didn't. The animal was brought by the audience.
And the Register talked to everybody. The auditorium manager, Dave Palmitier, told them Ozzy "did let some doves loose, which he wasn't supposed to do. We found one dead that apparently had been killed in the audience."
So yes. There were doves in Des Moines too. That same night.
And then the promoter, Bruce Kapp, steps in to defend his guy. Here's the defense, word for word: "He did release seven doves to the audience, which he does every night."
Every night. That's the defense.
And he's not done. He tells the paper Ozzy closes his act "by putting raw liver in his mouth and spitting it out, and people think he bit something in two. There's no truth to the report that he bit the head off a chicken in Omaha."
Nobody had asked about Omaha. Now everybody's asking about Omaha.
[TALK: What do you think happened in Omaha?]
Two nights later he plays Milwaukee, and the local Humane Society sends an officer, William Forss, with the power to arrest Ozzy if any animal gets hurt. Forss told the press they'd heard Ozzy planned to "blow up a goat" on stage. Nobody blew up a goat. The show went fine.
And Mark? Mark didn't hide. He was in the Des Moines Register two days after the show, by name. He said, "It really freaked me out." And then he asked the reporter, "I won't get in any trouble for admitting this, will I?"
[FILL: Forty years later, Rolling Stone ran an anniversary piece that said the bat thrower had never come forward. He came forward that week. In the local paper. With a quote.]
And nobody has ever stepped up to say "no, actually, it was me." If it was somebody else, trust me, they'd have said so. This is the most famous throw in rock history. It was Mark Neal.

## THE ALAMO
[CLIP: Ozzy and the Alamo]
And Ozzy is not done. About a month later, the tour's in San Antonio, and Ozzy gets arrested for peeing on the Alamo. Technically a monument on the Alamo plaza, and technically the charge was public intoxication.
And the story goes, from Ozzy's own retellings, that he was wearing one of Sharon's dresses, because she'd hidden his clothes to keep him from going out drinking. He went anyway. In the dress.
Ozzy did not remember the Alamo. But the Alamo sure remembered Ozzy. San Antonio banned him from playing the city for about ten years.

## THE SERIOUS PART
Now I have to slow down.
On March 19th, 1982, a month after San Antonio, the tour is in Florida. The tour bus driver, who was also a pilot, takes a small plane up from the property where they're parked. Randy Rhoads goes up with him, along with the band's makeup artist, Rachel Youngblood. The plane crashes. All three are killed. Randy was twenty five years old.
Randy was the reason those records sounded the way they did. "Crazy Train." "Mr. Crowley." If you play guitar, you know. He took classical lessons on the road. He was just getting started.
[RIFF: what Randy means to you as a guitar player. Take your time. Keep it real, not a bit. If you'd rather keep it short:]
Every guitar player I know has spent at least one afternoon trying to figure out the "Crazy Train" solo. Most of us are still working on it. That's what he left behind.
Ozzy called losing Randy the greatest tragedy of his life. So when we laugh about the bat, and we did, that same tour also had the worst day of his life in it. Two months apart.

## AFTER THE BAT
And somehow, he keeps going. In July 1982, he marries Sharon. Same year as the bat, the Alamo, and Randy. That's a lot of year.
In 1996 the Osbournes start Ozzfest, which runs for years as one of the biggest metal festivals in America.
And then in 2002, MTV puts cameras in their house. "The Osbournes." And the Prince of Darkness, the bat guy, the guy who peed by the Alamo, becomes America's confused TV dad, shuffling around his own house yelling "Sharon!" The first season averaged over five million viewers. At the time, it was the most watched series MTV had ever had. It won an Emmy.
[RIFF: The Osbournes memories. Or use this:]
A whole generation of kids met Ozzy as the mumbling dad on MTV. Their parents knew him as the guy who bit a bat. Both of those are the same man.
And he never ran from the bat. He leaned into it. On the 37th anniversary, in 2019, he sold a plush toy bat. Twelve inches, his logo on the chest, and a Velcro detachable head. Forty bucks. In today's money, that's about fifty. The first batch sold out.
He announced it on Twitter: "Today marks the 37th Anniversary since I bit a head off a fucking bat!"
[FILL: In 2020 he went public with a Parkinson's diagnosis. He spent his last years mostly unable to tour, and still made records.]

## THAT GUY
[CLIP: That Guy verdict]
Okay. Time to name him. That Guy.
The suspects.
Suspect one: Ozzy. The man who bit the thing. And, as we've established, not his first animal.
Suspect two: Mark Neal. The seventeen year old who brought a frozen bat in a plastic bag to a concert, and threw it at a man known for biting the heads off birds. Plus his friend Carmen, who said "freeze it." Every bad idea needs a producer.
Suspect three: the dove. Not the bird's fault, obviously. But the dove story is what got around. That's what told every kid in America, "this is the guy who bites things."
Suspect four: the meat. The catapult, the pig guts, the ads telling fans to bring their own raw meat. That's what taught the crowd to throw stuff back.
And the verdict.
I love Mark. Mark is awesome in the That Guy way. He owned it two days later, in the paper, by name. But Mark was seventeen, and Mark was doing exactly what the show trained everybody to do.
Ozzy bit it. But he thought it was rubber, because the show had taught him to expect rubber.
Here's the thing about the meat. The moment somebody said "you know what this show needs? Guts. Let's throw guts at people, and let's ask them to bring their own," a real dead animal on that stage was just a matter of time.
And that was Ozzy's show. His name on the ticket. His meat in the air. His dove that started the rumor. So That Guy is Ozzy. But the meat did it.
[THAT GUY STING]
[RIFF: your verdict. Kid, Ozzy, or the meat? Or use this:]
If you throw meat at Iowa, eventually Iowa throws something back.

## THE LEGEND
Now, before we go. Ozzy died on July 22nd, 2025. He was seventy six.
Seventeen days before that, he played one last show in his hometown of Birmingham, with the original Black Sabbath back together one more time. He couldn't stand for long anymore, so he sang sitting on a throne. Over forty thousand people in the stadium.
Over a hundred million records sold, between Sabbath and solo. In the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame twice. "Crazy Train" got played live over twelve hundred times. And in August 2026, it passed one billion streams on Spotify.
[RIFF: what Ozzy means to you. Or use this:]
A billion streams. From a guy whose first job review was "good puke remover."
And Ozzy knew exactly how he'd be remembered. He said when he died, the headline would be, "Ozzy Osbourne the bat biter is dead. Bats can now live in peace." And he figured the bats would hear it and go, "Fuck me, thank God he's dead."
And sure, the bat made the obituaries. But so did Prince of Darkness. Godfather of heavy metal.
Not bad for a cow killer from Aston.

## OUT
So that's the story. A slaughterhouse, a sales convention, a catapult full of livers, a bat in an Iowa freezer, a hospital, a monument, and one hell of a life.
[RIFF: defacingthemusic.com, Guest List, subscribe, socials. Or use this:]
Get on the Guest List at defacingthemusic.com. We check coats for bats.
Rest easy, Ozzy.
I'm Duck. Due to unforeseen circumstances, I'll see you next time.
[THEME SONG]

title: Due To Excessive Disco
subtitle: Who Let a DJ Blow Up Center Field?
body:
## COLD OPEN
[CLIP: Cold open: a Thursday night at Comiskey]
July 12th, 1979. Comiskey Park. A Thursday doubleheader nobody was supposed to care about.
Then the whole South Side shows up, and half of them are carrying a record they hate.
There's a wooden crate in center field. There's a radio DJ in an army helmet. There's an owner with an ashtray carved into his wooden leg.

I'm Duck, and due to excessive disco, this is Defacing the Music.
[THEME SONG, hard stop]
Episode [NUMBER]. Who Let a DJ Blow Up Center Field?

## 1979
Okay. Quick context, for anybody who wasn't alive, or was alive and has chosen to forget.
In 1979, disco is everywhere. Saturday Night Fever came out two years earlier and basically turned the whole country into a dance floor with a mirror ball over it. Disco on the radio. Disco on TV. Disco versions of songs that had no business being disco.
And if you were a nineteen year old kid in Chicagoland who'd spent your paper route money on Led Zeppelin records, you felt like the world had moved on without asking you.
That kid had a guy. And that guy was on the radio.

## THE DJ
His name is Steve Dahl. And in early 1978 he comes to Chicago from Detroit radio, where he'd been doing well enough that a Chicago station, WDAI, offers to double his salary to come over and be their rock morning guy.
So he comes. He starts in February 1978. Things are going great.
And then, on Christmas Eve 1978, WDAI switches its format. From rock. To disco.
And they fire him. On Christmas Eve.
[FILL: Everybody who's ever been laid off by email, sit with that for a second. This man got fired on Christmas Eve so a radio station could play "Le Freak." Chic. "Freak out!" That was the number one song in America that week. So, to be fair to the station, they had a point. He still got fired on Christmas Eve.]
So Steve Dahl lands across town at WLUP, The Loop, 97.9 on your dial. And he decides he's going to spend the rest of his life, or at least 1979, making the people who fired him sorry.
