He starts calling his old station "Disco D.I.E." on the air. He mocks disco records every morning. He plays a disco song and then "blows it up" on the air with a sound effect, and his catchphrase for it is "blow 'em up real good," which he swiped from an SCTV sketch.
And he gives his listeners a name. They're not fans. They're an army, at war with disco. He calls them the Insane Coho Lips.
Which needs explaining, because I had no idea either. Dahl's explained it himself. Back then, one of the big street gangs in Chicago was called the Insane Unknowns. And every morning on his way to work, he drove past Burnham Harbor, where the coho salmon fishing boats went out on Lake Michigan. A gang and a fish. Put them together and you get the Insane Coho Lips.
So that's the army. A bunch of Led Zeppelin kids named after a gang and a salmon. Disco never stood a chance.
He does parody songs too. The big one is "Do You Think I'm Disco?", which is Rod Stewart's "Da Ya Think I'm Sexy?" rewritten about a guy whose whole personality is the dance floor. And this is the part that gets me: it comes out as a real single, on a real label, and it actually charts. The B-side is called "Coho Lip Blues." Of course it is.
So that's one half of this story. A guy with a microphone, a grudge, and a few hundred thousand people listening to him every morning.
Now here's the other half.

## THE VEECKS
[CLIP: Bill Veeck's wooden leg ashtray]
The White Sox in 1979 are owned by Bill Veeck. And you have to understand Bill Veeck, because he's one of the most interesting people who ever owned a baseball team, and also because if you understand him, everything that happens next makes sense.
Bill Veeck's dad was president of the Cubs. So he grows up in baseball, here in Chicago, and as a kid he's working at Wrigley Field.
In World War Two he's in the Marines, and in the South Pacific a gun recoils and crushes his leg. Over the years he has surgery after surgery on it, and the number you see over and over is thirty six, and eventually the leg comes off. So he's got a wooden leg.
And Bill Veeck, a heavy smoker, cuts a hole in his wooden leg. And uses it as an ashtray.
That's the guy. That's the owner. That's who's in charge of this building.
And as an owner, Veeck is the king of promotions. Back in 1951, when he owns the St. Louis Browns, he sends a guy named Eddie Gaedel up to bat. Eddie Gaedel is three foot seven. Wears number one eighth on his back. Crouches down. The strike zone is about the size of a cigarette pack. He walks on four pitches.
At Comiskey, Veeck puts in the exploding scoreboard: a White Sox guy hits a home run, and the scoreboard shoots off fireworks and plays sirens. He put names on the back of jerseys, which every team does now. He put the White Sox in shorts.
[RIFF: the White Sox in shorts. Or use this:]
Grown men. Major league ballplayers. Sliding into second base in shorts. I'm a Chicago guy, I'd defend this city in any bar in America, and I've got nothing for the shorts.
[TALK: Eddie Gaedel, the exploding scoreboard, or the shorts. Which Bill Veeck stunt would you have paid to see?]
And here's one more Bill Veeck thing, because it pays off later. You know Harry Caray singing "Take Me Out to the Ball Game" in the seventh inning? That started on the South Side, before he was the Cubs guy. Harry used to sing it in the booth, to himself, and the fans under the booth sang along. And the story goes that Veeck had a microphone hidden in the booth and flipped it on, so one night Harry's voice came booming out over the whole park. Veeck's version of how that happened changed a little every time he told it. But that's the kind of owner he was. If something fun is happening in a corner of the ballpark, turn it up and point everybody at it.
So Bill Veeck believes, all the way down, that a ballgame is a show. And in 1979 the White Sox are not a great team, and people are not exactly lining up to see them, so the show is doing a lot of work. Mike Veeck said it flat out years later: "We were not doing well."
That's Bill's son. Mike Veeck. Who works for the team running promotions.

## THE IDEA
So you've got Steve Dahl at war with disco, on a station that's 97.9 on the dial. And you've got Mike Veeck, looking for a way to fill seats on a Thursday night.
Here's how they find each other. A sales guy at The Loop, Jeff Schwartz, tells Mike that Dahl wants to blow up a pile of disco records. The original plan, the way it's been told, was to do it at a shopping mall. And Mike Veeck hears "a guy wants to blow something up in public" and thinks: not a mall. A ballpark. My ballpark.
And Mike goes to Dahl and makes the pitch himself. Dahl's on board. Dahl's partner on the air, Garry Meier, is in too.
The plan comes together like this. July 12th, a twi-night doubleheader, White Sox and Tigers. Bring a disco record to the gate, and you get in for ninety eight cents. Because The Loop is 97.9. Get it.
Ninety eight cents. In today's money, that's about four bucks and thirty five cents. To get into a major league game.
Your records go in a big crate. Between games, Steve Dahl walks out to center field. And blows them up.
Now, how many people did they think were coming? Here's where it gets good. Dahl said years later the Sox drew "maybe 9,000 people on a good night." The way most accounts tell it, the hope was something like twenty thousand. A big night. A nice bump. And security got staffed for a crowd a lot smaller than what was about to happen, with most of the people working the gates.
[FILL: Accounts disagree on the exact number they were expecting. Every version agrees on one thing: it wasn't this.]
[TALK: you get in for one record you want blown up. Which record are you bringing to the gate?]

## THE CROWD
Okay. So. July 12th.
And it turns out that every single rock kid in Chicagoland, and northwest Indiana, and a good chunk of Wisconsin, heard about this and thought, "Ninety eight cents? To watch a guy blow up disco? I'm in."
The official attendance is 47,795. In a park that held about 44,500.
And that's the official number. The estimates of how many people were really there, inside and outside, go a lot higher. Mike Veeck thought it might have been as many as sixty thousand. One account says there were around twenty thousand more people outside who couldn't get in. Some of them got in anyway. Rusty Staub, who played for the Tigers that night, is quoted telling the New York Times: "People brought ladders. They were climbing in from the outside." That's how the quote gets passed around, anyway. Ladders. To a baseball game.
And the records. The crate fills up fast. So a lot of people don't put their record in the crate. They keep it. They're holding it. In their hands. In the stands. For a whole baseball game.
You can guess.
So game one starts, and the Tribune said it was played "under a constant bombardment of records and firecrackers." They had to stop play more than once.
And the Tigers' Rusty Staub, again, this guy has the best seat for all of it, said the records would come slicing down and stick in the ground. Stick. Like a throwing star. He said he begged his teammates to put on batting helmets. In the field. Defense, in a batting helmet, because the fans are throwing Bee Gees records at your head.
Ron LeFlore, the Tigers center fielder, said a golf ball came out of the stands and bounced between his legs while he was trying to catch a fly ball.
[RIFF: playing outfield while the crowd throws vinyl. Or use this:]
You're a major league outfielder. You've spent your whole life learning to track a fly ball. And now you have to track the fly ball, and the golf ball, and forty copies of "Disco Inferno" coming in sideways like they were thrown by ninjas.
And on top of that: there are firecrackers. There's beer. There is a smell in the air that is not entirely tobacco.
The Tigers manager, Sparky Anderson, had the best line about that part. He told the Tribune, "Beer and baseball go together." And then: "I think those kids were doing things other than beer."
Oh, and there was a baseball game. The Tigers won it, 4 to 1. Least important thing that happened in the building.
[TALK: what's the worst thing you've ever seen thrown at a game or a show?]

## THE BOOM
Between games. Steve Dahl comes out. Through a door in the center field wall, with Garry Meier, and with Lorelei from The Loop. And Dahl is dressed in army fatigues and a helmet. Because it's a war, remember. They circle the field in a Jeep, and the crowd throws firecrackers and beer at them, which in this context is love.
Dahl told Chicago magazine what that lap felt like: "They are throwing beers and cherry bombs at us. And they're the people who like us!"
He gets to center field, gets on the mic, and he tells them, more or less word for word: this is now officially the world's largest anti-disco rally. We took all the disco records you brought tonight, we got them in a giant box, and we're going to blow them up real good.
And then he leads the chant. "Disco sucks." "Disco sucks." Tens of thousands of people.
[RIFF: what that chant sounds like in a ballpark. Or use this:]
I've been at Sox games where the whole park is chanting. It shakes your ribs. Now make it fifty thousand people who've been drinking since four in the afternoon, and the chant is about the Village People.
And then he hits it.
[Pause.]
And it is a real explosion. Not a sound effect this time. The crate blows. It tears a hole in center field. Vinyl goes everywhere, and chunks of the field go with it. There's smoke. There's fire.
And then they come over the walls.

## THE FIELD
[CLIP: The kid who stole second base]
Thousands of people. Some accounts say something like seven thousand. Pour out of the stands and onto the field.
And this is where I went digging, because "fans rushed the field" is not a story. Who? What did they do? So let me give you some of the guys.
There was a teenage vendor working the stands that night named Dave Gaborek. And Dave remembers one long-haired kid who jumps down out of left field, runs across the whole outfield, slides into second base, picks the bag up off the ground, and waves it over his head.
That's it. That's the guy. Slid into second like he'd earned it, and then stole it. Not the base. The actual base.
And he wasn't alone. People ran the bases like they were in the World Series. Sliding into home. Standing on the mound. A future Tribune sportswriter named Paul Sullivan was a kid in that crowd, and he's described it: running around on a major league field, sliding into the bases, standing on the pitcher's mound. He's also said he got off that field early, and that 1968 had something to do with it. The convention riots. Chicago kids remembered what happens when the cops show up to a crowd. Smart kid.
A Chicago radio sports guy named Les Grobstein was there. Before he left the field, he dug up a piece of the turf and took it home. A souvenir. Of grass.
And here's my favorite one. There was a twenty one year old from the South Side in that crowd named Michael Clarke Duncan. Yes. The big guy from The Green Mile. Oscar nominee. And by his own telling, he was in the first hundred or so people onto the field. He slid into third base. And he said he grabbed a bat out of the White Sox dugout on the way.
And then, years later, he admitted that he was actually a big disco fan.
[RIFF: Michael Clarke Duncan at Disco Demolition. Or use this:]
He didn't even hate disco. He just heard there was a riot on the South Side and didn't want to miss it. That's the most Chicago thing I've ever heard. "I don't agree with the cause, but I'm not missing this."
[TALK: the field opens up at a game tonight. Which base are you sliding into, and what are you taking home?]
Then the bigger stuff. Somebody pulled up the bases. All of them. A photographer named Paul Natkin, who was shooting it that night, put it simply: "They pulled all the bases up. They tipped over the batting cage." One account from the crowd says somebody dragged the batting cage out and set it on fire.
Tigers pitcher Jack Morris told the New York Times years later that "all hell broke loose." Fans were tearing up the pitching rubber and digging up the dirt. People were going after home plate.
They're tearing up the grass. They're tearing out seats. They're lighting bonfires in the outfield, with records, and whatever else they can find. And some of them are climbing the poles. Just shimmying up the poles at a major league ballpark, for the view, I guess. Nobody wrote down their names, which is a shame, because I have questions for every one of them.
Dave Gaborek, the vendor, told Chicago magazine: "Kids were climbing foul poles." Foul poles. And then: "I saw a kid marching from third base to home plate with a marijuana leaf sign." Just a parade of one. On a major league field.
[CLIP: The organist and the three nuns]
And up in the stands, the White Sox organist, Nancy Faust, is watching all of this happen. Here's how she told it to Chicago magazine:
"At first I saw little fires breaking out in the outfield. Three nuns were sitting near me. They turned around and asked, 'What is everybody chanting?' In those days, 'Disco sucks' wasn't a nice thing to say. My friend told them, 'They're just going, Let's go, Sox.'"
So the field is on fire, and somebody looks three nuns in the eye and lies to them. At a ballgame. That guy's got bigger problems than disco.
Meanwhile, the White Sox pitcher who was supposed to start game two, Ken Kravec, is out there warming up when this starts. And the way it's been told, he's got shoes and records flying past his head.
Here's Kravec himself, to Chicago magazine:
"The bullpen was right next to the stands. And the wall was only three feet high. The fans were right there. So I began my warm-ups, and every now and then a shoe would fly by me. Then a couple more shoes. And then they started to Frisbee the albums. I mentioned to Ron, 'I don't think it's a good idea for us to be standing here.' So we went out on the field to finish up on the main mound."
Ron is Ron Schueler, the pitching coach. So their plan to get away from the shoes was to walk out into the middle of the field. And Kravec says: "I threw 10 pitches, and the next thing you know, the fans stormed the field."
He goes back to the dugout. Everybody goes back to the dugout. The Tigers are in their dugout. The White Sox are in their dugout. Nobody is going out there.
And the people in charge are trying. The scoreboard flashes "PLEASE RETURN TO YOUR SEATS." Nothing.
Bill Veeck, the man with the wooden leg, goes out there himself, with a microphone, and stands about where home plate used to be, and begs people to go back to the stands, while a bonfire is going in center field. Steve Dahl gets on the mic. And Harry Caray. Remember Harry, the guy Bill Veeck turned into the seventh inning sing-along? Harry gets on the PA too. And there's an account that they played "Take Me Out to the Ball Game" to try to settle everybody down.
It did not settle everybody down.
Mike Veeck, years later, to Chicago magazine: "Harry was a pro. He was the dance band on the Titanic, playing through the disaster."
[RIFF: Harry Caray asking politely. Or use this:]
If Harry Caray can't get you to behave, nobody can. That's a man who could get forty thousand people to sing in the seventh inning. And he couldn't get them off the grass.
And then there's the TV booth. Harry Caray's partner on the White Sox broadcasts was Jimmy Piersall. Former big league outfielder. And not a guy who was easy to shock. This is a man who, when he hit his hundredth career home run, ran the bases backwards. Right order, first, second, third, home. Just running backwards the whole way, facing the wrong direction.
And Jimmy Piersall is on the air, looking down at the field, and he is disgusted. Here's what he told everybody watching at home: "I hope they don't let you people see what's going on here at Comiskey Park. One of the saddest sights I've ever seen in a ballpark in my life."
The man who ran the bases backwards for fun thought this was too much.
And he never let it go. Years later, he was still calling it "the worst promotion in the history of the world."
Finally, the Chicago police come in. In riot gear. And one account says the people still in the stands, the ones who'd just come to see a baseball game, applauded when they showed up.
The field gets cleared. Thirty nine people get arrested, mostly for disorderly conduct. Some accounts say thirty seven. Nobody was seriously hurt, which, when you look at the pictures, is the real miracle of the night.
Although it was close. White Sox pitcher Steve Trout walked out to look at the damage afterward, and here's what he told Chicago magazine:
"People tore the bases apart. Home plate was gone. There was a big spot in center field where the albums had been blown up. There was vinyl everywhere. I walked out to look at center field, and I heard something go by me. It was an album from the upper deck and landed next to my right foot. It was stuck in the ground. I said, 'Holy shit, I could have been killed by the Village People.'"
Killed by the Village People. Put that on the headstone.

## THE FORFEIT
Now. There's supposed to be a second game.
And the White Sox want to play it. Bill Veeck looks at the field, and the field looks like a battlefield, there's a crater in center, and it's still smoking. And he wants to play.
The Tigers manager, Sparky Anderson, says no. He's not putting his guys out there. It's not safe. He wants the game.
The umpires call it off for the night. And the next day the American League president, Lee MacPhail, gives the game to Detroit. A forfeit. 9 to 0.
The White Sox forfeited a home game. Because their own promotion worked too well.
The White Sox manager, Don Kessinger, had this to say: "We have found a lot of ways to lose games this year, but I guess we've added a new wrinkle. It's tough to lose two games when you played only one."
And Bill Veeck did not agree with the forfeit. At all. Here's Bill: "I think the grounds for forfeiting are specious at best. It's true there was some sod missing. Otherwise, nothing was wrong."
Some sod missing. The man is looking at a smoking crater in center field and calling it a divot.
The Sox head groundskeeper, Roger Bossard, said decades later that he still has nightmares about what they did to his field.
And remember the ashtray leg? It comes back. That night, the guys from The Loop are in Bill Veeck's office, because the radio station is going to pay for the damage. Here's Jeff Schwartz, the station's sales manager, to Chicago magazine:
"Les Elias and I were in Bill Veeck's office at two o'clock in the morning waiting to see what the damage results were from the insurance company, because we were going to pay it. Bill goes, 'Gentlemen, I hope you don't mind. It is real late and my leg is killing me.' And in front of us, he unscrews his leg, puts it on the side of his desk, and proceeds to use it as an ashtray. He says, 'I don't know who this guy is, but, boy, does he know how to draw people.' Bill was an entrepreneur. He got it."
Les Elias was the station manager. So that's the insurance meeting. Two in the morning, the field's in pieces, and the owner takes his leg off and ashes in it.
And a Tribune columnist, David Israel, wrote the line that should be on the plaque: "Ten years after Woodstock, there was Veeckstock."
[FILL: As of right now, that's still the last forfeited game in American League history. Nobody in the league has forfeited a game since. The White Sox have one because a guy blew up a crate of Donna Summer records.]
[TALK: you're Sparky Anderson. Do you send your guys back out onto that field for game two?]

## THE OLDER COUSIN
[CLIP: Ten Cent Beer Night]
And here's the thing that makes me crazy. Baseball had already learned this lesson five years earlier. And nobody listened.
June 4th, 1974. Cleveland. The Indians decide to have Ten Cent Beer Night. Ten cents. For a cup of beer. In today's money, that's about sixty five cents. With basically no limit on how many you could buy.
They get 25,134 people, about twice what they expected. There are streakers. There are fans running onto the field all night.
And in the ninth inning, with the game tied, a nineteen year old kid jumps out of the stands, runs up to the Texas Rangers right fielder, Jeff Burroughs, and steals the hat right off his head. Burroughs goes down. And the Rangers manager, Billy Martin, thinks his guy got jumped, and he tells his team, by one player's memory, "Let's go get them, boys!" And the Rangers come out of the dugout carrying bats.
And then the Cleveland players come out with bats too. To save the other team. From their own fans.
The umpire, Nestor Chylak, got hit in the head with part of a stadium seat. He forfeited the game to Texas, and he called the fans "uncontrollable beasts," and said he'd never seen anything like it except in a zoo.
[RIFF: Ten Cent Beer Night vs. Disco Demolition. Or use this:]
So in 1974 baseball found out what happens when you hand a crowd cheap beer. And in 1979 the White Sox said, "Got it. What if we also hand them explosives and a stack of frisbees?"
Disco Demolition is Ten Cent Beer Night's younger brother. Same family. Same forfeit. Worse haircut.

## WHERE ARE THEY NOW
So what happened to everybody?
Start with a kid who was working that night. Vince Lawrence. He was a teenager, working as an usher at Comiskey, and he took the job because he was saving up to buy a synthesizer. He got the synthesizer. And a few years later he co-wrote "On and On," which is one of the first house music records ever made. Here. In Chicago.
So the same night that was supposed to kill dance music, one of the guys who'd help invent the next kind of dance music was standing in the aisle in an usher's uniform.
[FILL: Disco didn't die in center field. It moved a few miles away, got a drum machine, and changed its name to house.]
Steve Dahl's career took off after that night. He was on Chicago radio for decades. He's said he thought disco was probably on its way out anyway, and that the night just sped it up. And in 2016 he put out a whole book about it, "Disco Demolition: The Night Disco Died," full of photos and stories from people who were there.
Bill Veeck took the public heat. He stood in front of the press and took it, so his kid wouldn't have to. He sold the team not long after, and he's in the Hall of Fame now, for everything else he did. Eddie Gaedel, the scoreboard, the shorts. Mostly not this.
And Mike Veeck. The son. The promotions guy.
Mike's career went the opposite way from Dahl's. He was out at the White Sox before the next season. And he's always believed he got blackballed. Nobody in the majors wanted the guy who forfeited a ballgame.
And it got bad. He's talked about it himself. Drinking. A divorce. His dad dying. One profile says he lost his savings betting on jai alai, which is the most 1980s Florida sentence I've ever read.
Twenty years. That's how long it took before a major league team hired him again, the Tampa Bay Devil Rays, in 1999.
But here's the thing. He never stopped doing promotions. He just did them in the minor leagues, where nobody could stop him. He and a group that included Bill Murray, yes, that Bill Murray, from Wilmette, bought a minor league team in 1990. And he ended up running the St. Paul Saints, which he co-owns with Murray and others.
And he got weirder. In Charleston, South Carolina, his team held "Nobody Night." They padlocked the gates and made the fans wait in the parking lot until the fifth inning so they could set the record for the lowest attendance in baseball history. Official attendance: zero. He also announced a Vasectomy Night for Father's Day. That one got cancelled within hours.
And in 2001, when he was working for the Marlins, on the anniversary of Disco Demolition, they finally got him to apologize. To disco. He stood at home plate and delivered an apology to KC, of KC and the Sunshine Band. And he ended it with: "I'm sorry from the bottom of my leisure suit."
There's a whole Netflix documentary about him now, "The Saint of Second Chances." And he's said that Disco Demolition made him great at what he does.

## THAT GUY
[CLIP: That Guy verdict]
Okay. Time to name him. That Guy.
The suspects.
Suspect one: Steve Dahl. The man in the helmet. Who got fired on Christmas Eve, turned his whole radio show into a war, told his army to show up, and pressed the button.
Suspect two: Bill Veeck. The owner. Who spent thirty years teaching baseball fans that anything can happen at the ballpark, and then got surprised when anything happened at the ballpark.
Suspect three: Mike Veeck. The son. Who heard "this guy wants to blow up records at a mall" and said, "What if it was in center field, between games, in front of every rock kid in three states, for less than a dollar?"
And the verdict.
Steve Dahl did exactly what Steve Dahl said he was going to do. He said it on the air, every morning, for months. And his plan was a shopping mall. A parking lot full of rock kids and a pile of records. That's a story the local news does for thirty seconds and everybody forgets by Monday.
Mike Veeck is the one who heard that and said no. Not a mall. My ballpark. He went to Dahl himself and asked him to bring it to Comiskey. It was his promotion: ninety eight cents, between two games of a doubleheader, with a crate of explosives in center field and the security standing at the gates. He's the one who allowed it, and he's the one who asked for it.
So That Guy is Mike Veeck.
[THAT GUY STING]
His dad's on the hook a little. Mike learned it all from Bill. But Bill didn't make the call that night. Mike did.
And Mike agrees. Here he is in Chicago magazine: "My old man said it best: 'It was a promotion that worked too well.' Then my dad went out and took the public berating for me. I'm the one who triggered it."
And Mike paid for it. Twenty years out of the majors. Then he went to the minor leagues and kept doing promotions like this, just with smaller crowds and no explosives.
[RIFF: your verdict. Dahl, Bill, or Mike? Or use this:]
Dahl lit the fuse. But Mike Veeck sold fifty thousand tickets to the fuse for ninety eight cents each.

## OUT
So that's Disco Demolition Night. A guy fired on Christmas Eve, a crate full of records, a kid stealing second base with his hands, a future movie star sliding into third, Harry Caray asking nicely, and the White Sox losing a game nobody ever played.
And every time I hear "Le Freak" at a wedding now, I think about a guy in a helmet in center field. Disco's still playing. The crater's gone.
[RIFF: defacingthemusic.com, Guest List, subscribe, socials. Or use this:]
Get on the Guest List at defacingthemusic.com. Admission's free. You don't even have to bring a record.
Next time, another night that should've been canceled, and wasn't.
I'm Duck. Due to unforeseen circumstances, I'll see you next time.

title: Due To a Septic Tank Over the River
subtitle: Who Let the Bus Driver Find the Bridge?
body:
## COLD OPEN
[CLIP: Cold open: the boat under the Kinzie Street bridge]
August 2004. A sunny Sunday afternoon in Chicago. The good kind of day, the kind we get maybe eleven of a year.
An open-top tour boat is gliding down the river. A hundred-some people on the deck, sunglasses on, cameras out, a guide pointing at buildings.
Overhead, a big shiny tour bus rolls onto an old bridge with a deck you can see the sky through.
Nobody on that boat is looking up.
## TODAY
Today: a jam band from Virginia, a two-night stand in Wisconsin, a very nice hotel on the Magnificent Mile, a switch behind the driver's seat, and one of the worst boat rides in the history of the Great Lakes region.
This one happened right here in Chicago. And nobody here has forgotten it, because we don't let anybody forget anything.
And somewhere in this story, there's a guy. There always is. This time, I promise you, you'll know him when you see him.
I'm Duck, and due to a septic tank over the river, this is Defacing the Music.
[THEME SONG, hard stop]
Episode [NUMBER]. Who Let the Bus Driver Find the Bridge?

## THE BAND
Quick context, for anybody who was not in a college dorm between about 1994 and 2004.
The Dave Matthews Band is from Charlottesville, Virginia. Dave Matthews himself grew up partly in South Africa, and he settled in Charlottesville in the mid eighties. And around 1990 he's tending bar at a place called Miller's, and he's writing songs, and he starts putting a band together with some local guys. Some of them are jazz guys. A saxophone. A violin. A drummer who can actually play.
Their first public show, in the spring of 1991, is at the city's Earth Day festival. Earth Day. File that one away, because this story is going to circle back and find it.
[FILL: I didn't plant that. That's just the real date on the real flyer. This band's first gig was a party for the planet.]
And the thing about the Dave Matthews Band is they become huge mostly by touring. Playing everywhere, letting fans tape the shows, building a following one frat house at a time. By 2000 they were the top-grossing touring band in the country. Something like sixty eight million dollars in ticket sales that one year.
[RIFF: your personal Dave Matthews feelings. Or use this:]
I'm a guitar player. I'll say this much. Whatever you think of the songs, those guys can play. And every guitar player of my generation has been in a room where somebody picks up an acoustic and starts "Crash Into Me," and you just have to let it happen. It's like weather.
So by 2004, this is a big operation. A real band, with a real crew, and a fleet of tour buses. Five drivers, according to the paperwork the state filed later. And on that fleet, the band members had their own buses. The violin player, Boyd Tinsley, had a bus. And that bus had a driver.
His name is Stefan Wohl. A Texas guy, from a little town outside San Antonio called Selma. Forty two years old.

## THE BUS
Here's something about tour buses, because a lot of you have never had the honor.
A tour bus is a house on wheels. Bunks, a lounge, a little kitchen. And a bathroom.
And that bathroom goes somewhere. It goes into a tank under the bus. In the RV world they call it the blackwater tank. Black. As opposed to gray, which is your sink and your shower. Black is the other stuff.
And that tank needs to be emptied. And there are places you do that. Dump stations. Campgrounds. Specific facilities with specific pipes. It is a whole procedure. Every driver knows it.
[FILL: Ask anybody who's ridden on a band bus. The first rule they tell you, before where to sleep, before where the beer is, is about the toilet. Bus guys are very serious about the toilet.]
And according to the lawsuit the state of Illinois filed later, on this bus, emptying the tank was a matter of flicking a switch. A toggle. Behind the driver's seat.
Not a lever you trip with your knee. Not a button next to the radio. A switch you have to reach back for.

## THE WEEKEND
So, August 2004. The band is playing a two-night stand at Alpine Valley. That's up in East Troy, Wisconsin, about ninety minutes from the city, a big outdoor amphitheater out by a ski hill. If you grew up around here, you've been to Alpine Valley, and you've sat in traffic leaving Alpine Valley for longer than the show.
And between shows, the band's not sleeping in East Troy. They've got rooms at the Peninsula. On Superior Street, just off Michigan Avenue. A very nice hotel. The kind of place where the doorman's coat costs more than my car.
[FILL: That's the right move, honestly. You play the ski hill, then you sleep in a real bed on the Magnificent Mile. That's the life.]
So on Sunday, August 8th, with the second Alpine Valley show still to play that night, Stefan Wohl is driving Boyd Tinsley's bus into downtown Chicago. Alone. Nobody from the band is on it. He's headed for the Peninsula. One report of the state's complaint says he was coming from a lot on the west side of the river to pick somebody up at the hotel.
And his route takes him over the Kinzie Street bridge.

## THE RIVER
Now let me tell you about the Chicago River, for out-of-towners, because this matters.
The Chicago River is ours. We are weird about it. In 1900 this city reversed the direction the river flows. Turned it around. Made it run backwards, away from the lake, because we were dumping so much sewage into it that it was getting into our drinking water.
So the river has a history with this exact problem. I want that on the record.
And then for a hundred years, the city worked on cleaning it up. And by 2004, the river's a showpiece. Every St. Patrick's Day we dye it green and thousands of people in plastic hats stand on the bridges and cheer for a river changing color.
And in summer, one of the big things to do, for tourists and locals, is the architecture boat tour. You sit on an open deck, a guide points out the buildings, and you go "ooh" at the Wrigley Building. It's honestly great. If you've never done it, do it. Maybe check the bridges first.
[RIFF: the architecture boat tour. Or use this:]
You sit there with a cold drink, a guide talks about Mies van der Rohe, and for about ninety minutes you feel very cultured. Nobody tells you to look up. Nobody's ever needed to.
That Sunday, the boat is called Chicago's Little Lady. It's running the one o'clock Chicago Architecture Foundation tour. Open top. More than a hundred people on it. Sources say anywhere from a hundred to a hundred and twenty.
One of them is a guy named Tracy Dangott. He's there with his wife at the time and two friends. And they've picked their seats on the open deck. Which, on a beautiful day, is where you sit. You'd be an idiot to sit inside.
And the boat is heading under the Kinzie Street bridge.

## THE BRIDGE
The Kinzie Street bridge crosses the North Branch of the river, not far from where it meets the main branch. It's a movable bridge, and the deck is open steel grating. Metal mesh. When you drive over it your tires hum. And if you're standing under it, you can see daylight through it.
Which means, if something liquid comes down on top of it, it doesn't stay on top of it.
So. The boat goes under. The bus goes over. Later, police would put out a still from a security camera with a time stamp on it: a black and silver bus on the Kinzie Street bridge at 1:18 in the afternoon.
And somewhere up there, Stefan Wohl flicks the switch.

## THE DROP
[CLIP: That's not water, buddy]
The figure everybody uses is about eight hundred pounds of human waste. One other report put it at eighty to a hundred gallons. I'm not going to argue about the units. It is a lot. It is the entire tank.
And it comes through the grate in a sheet.
There was a Chicago Tribune reporter on that boat. And the passengers described a downpour of foul-smelling, brownish-yellow slurry. That's from the reporting. I didn't come up with "slurry." I wouldn't have. One report said about two thirds of the people on board got soaked. It ruined people's clothes. Several people got sick.
[RIFF: the sound of it. Or use this:]
I keep thinking about the half second before anybody understands what it is. It's sunny. There's no cloud. And something wet is falling on you. Your brain says rain. Your brain tries really hard to say rain.
And then, according to Chicago magazine, which did an oral history of this, years later, the guide on the boat tries to keep it together. The guide tells everybody that it appears some water has hit the deck.
[Pause.]
And a man from the back of the boat says: "That's not water, buddy."
[FILL: That's the most Chicago sentence ever spoken. No panic. No screaming. Just a guy correcting the record. I would like that man to be our mayor.]
And then, according to people on board, the screaming started.
Tracy Dangott's group was sitting in the part of the boat that got it the worst. And here's his detail, the one that tells you who he is. When the boat got back to the dock near Michigan Avenue, he took his motorcycle helmet and washed it out with a hose.
His motorcycle helmet. A thing with one big opening, designed to catch whatever comes at your head.
[FILL: I don't need to say anything else about that. You already pictured it. I'm sorry.]
The boat gets back to the dock. The crew cleans it with disinfectant. And everybody gets a refund on their ticket, which was twenty five bucks.
Twenty five dollars. For that. I'd want a little more than my twenty five back. I'd want the boat.
And Dangott, twenty years later, told the Sun-Times it was a few years before he could take it a little less seriously. Which is fair. And he's been back on the architecture tour since. Which is the bravest thing in this whole story.

## WHOSE BUS
[CLIP: The wrong driver gets his own tank inspected]
So now Chicago is very upset, and Chicago wants to know whose bus.
A witness gave police a license plate. An Oregon plate. And it comes back to a bus that drives for the Dave Matthews Band. A 2003 Monaco coach. The driver is a guy named Jerry Fitzpatrick, who'd been driving Dave Matthews himself around for about three years.
Wrong guy. But he doesn't know he's going to be cleared yet. He just knows his plate is the one the cops have.
So Jerry Fitzpatrick says, my bus was parked in front of the Peninsula the whole time. And then he does something I love. He's down in Effingham, Illinois, and he finds a local cop, Sergeant Paul Gardner of the Effingham Police Department, and asks him to come look inside his septic tank.
And the sergeant does it. And then gets on Jerry's cell phone, with a Tribune reporter, and reports that the tank is nearly full.
And Sergeant Gardner said, quote, "One of the strangest requests I've ever had, that's for sure."
[RIFF: the Effingham tank inspection. Or use this:]
I like to imagine that sergeant's day. He's minding his own business. A tour bus guy walks up. "Officer, I need you to look in my toilet tank and then talk to a newspaper." And he says yes. That's public service. Nobody gave that man a medal and somebody should.
And that's the alibi. A full tank. Jerry Fitzpatrick's tank was full because Jerry Fitzpatrick did not empty it on a boat. Honestly that's airtight. That's better than most alibis on Dateline.

## THE DENIAL
So it's not Jerry. But it's still pointing at the band, because the band was in town with a fleet of buses, staying a few blocks away.
And here's where the band makes its decisions, and they're not great ones.
The band's publicist puts out a statement. Management had looked into it, and all of their buses were parked at the time.
All of them. Parked. Nothing to see here.
Then the band puts a letter on its website, to the people of Chicago. They say they've suspended the driver while they figure it out, and that he's still denying he was involved. And they say they'll make amends if it turns out it was their bus.
And then they go one further. The band members offer to give DNA samples. To prove it wasn't theirs.
[Pause.]
DNA. From the boat. They were going to let science check the boat.
[FILL: Picture the lab tech who gets that assignment. Picture the paperwork. "Sample source: deck, Chicago's Little Lady."]
The state's investigators said, thanks, we'll manage without the DNA. Which, I think, was the right call for everybody.
And Stefan Wohl? He'd talked to investigators soon after. And the prosecutor later said Wohl admitted driving the bus over the river that day, but, quote, "he denied having discharged any waste over the bridge."
So he tells them yes, I was on the bridge. Yes, at that time. In that bus. With that switch. But nothing came out.
[FILL: I understand the instinct. Somebody walks up and says, "Hey, did you dump eight hundred pounds of shit on a boat full of tourists?" You're gonna say no. That's just reflex.]
And you can see how the band got there. Their guy tells them he didn't do it. They believe their guy. They tell the city. That's the chain. Every step of it is a person deciding to trust the person below them, and the person at the bottom is the one with his hand on the switch.

## THE CAMERAS
[CLIP: Busted by the East Bank Club cameras]
But here's the thing about the Kinzie Street bridge. Right there by the river, there is a very big, very fancy health club called the East Bank Club. It's where half the city's lawyers and politicians go to sweat.
And the East Bank Club had security cameras.
And Lisa Madigan's investigators and Chicago police detectives went through tapes from businesses around there. And they found a bus. On the bridge. At 1:18. And it was Boyd Tinsley's bus. With one guy in it.
The camera didn't catch the actual soaking. It didn't have to. It caught the right bus on the right bridge at the right minute.
[RIFF: the East Bank Club. Or use this:]
Of all the buildings on that river. The bus picked the one with a better security system than most banks. You could've done this under any bridge in Chicago. You found the one being watched by the gym where the judges work out.

## THE CHARGES
And now it gets official.
The state attorney general, Lisa Madigan, sues. The band and the driver. Water pollution and public nuisance. The city gets in on it too.
And in January 2005, the Cook County State's Attorney charges Stefan Wohl with misdemeanors. Reckless conduct, and discharging contaminants to cause water pollution. He turns himself in and gets out on a thousand dollar bond.
And here's the line that matters for our purposes. Before they charged him, prosecutors didn't just watch the tape. They talked to engineers. About the bus. About the tank. About the switch. And the prosecutor, a guy named Robert Egan, said: "We were satisfied with what they told us that it could not have been an accident."
Could not have been an accident. That's the engineers. Not me.
In March he pleads guilty. He gets eighteen months of probation, a hundred and fifty hours of community service, and a ten thousand dollar fine. The maximum. And the fine goes to Friends of the Chicago River, which is a group whose entire job is protecting the river.
So the guy who dumped the tank paid the river people. I like that. That's the closest thing to justice this story has.
His lawyer, every time a reporter called, did not call back. Not when he was charged. Not after the plea. And as far as I could find, Stefan Wohl never told anybody, in public, why.
And the band fires him.
[FILL: I'd love to know what he puts on the next job application. "Reason for leaving previous position."]

## WHY THERE
[CLIP: Why would you dump it there?]
So let's do the thing this show is for. How did this get made? Who decided this was a good idea?
Here's everything that's on the record. He was alone. He was on his way to the hotel. The switch was behind his seat, and engineers told prosecutors it couldn't happen by accident. He told investigators nothing came out. Then the tape. Then the plea.
And here's what's not on the record: the why. Nobody ever said. Not him, not his lawyer, not the band.
So I'm going to give you the options, and I want to be clear these are me guessing, not facts.
Option one: he thought the bridge was a road. He's not from here. Maybe he thinks he's over a storm drain somewhere, flicks it, and has no idea there's a river under the grate.
Option two: he knew there was water down there, and figured water's water. Eight hundred pounds into a river that size, who's gonna notice? Answer: a hundred people and a Tribune reporter.
Option three: he's about to park outside the nicest hotel on the Magnificent Mile and pick somebody up, and he does not want to be the guy with a full tank parked in front of the Peninsula. So it's now or never.
[RIFF: which option you buy. Or use this:]
I'm a guitar player, not a bus driver. But I have been in a van that needed a decision made quick. And I can tell you every bad decision on tour starts with the same sentence. "Nobody's gonna know."
And nobody would have known, except for the grate, the boat, the reporter, the guy with the helmet, and the gym.

## THE BAND PAYS
And the band. Once the tape made it clear it was their bus, they own it.
They put out a statement saying the whole thing was awful, and it went against so many of the principles they hold dear. Environmentalism. Accountability. And, mostly, principles of humanity.
[Pause.]
Principles of humanity. I don't think I've ever seen those words used about a bus toilet before or since.
They donated fifty thousand dollars to the Chicago Park District, and fifty thousand to Friends of the Chicago River. And in April 2005 they settled with the state for two hundred thousand dollars, about a month before they came back to play Chicago. They didn't have to admit guilt. And as part of the deal they had to follow written procedures for emptying the bus tanks, and keep a written log of every single tank dump. Until 2010.
[RIFF: the bus toilet logbook. Or use this:]
Somewhere there's a binder. For five years, every time a Dave Matthews Band bus emptied its tank, somebody had to write it down. Date, time, location. For the Illinois Attorney General. That's a real job somebody had on that tour. And I hope they put it on a resume.
There were also personal injury lawsuits from people on the boat, separate from all that.

## EARTH DAY
And here's the part that gets me.
Go back to the first gig. Earth Day. 1991.
The Dave Matthews Band has always been one of the most environmentally serious big bands in the world. And in 2004, the same year as the bus, they launch something called BamaGreen. A program to make their tours greener. Biodiesel in the trucks and buses. Cutting plastic bottles at shows. Over the next fifteen years it cut a huge amount of carbon.
And in 2019, the United Nations Environment Programme names the band a Goodwill Ambassador.
The United Nations. Fifteen years after Chicago.
[FILL: I'm going to assume nobody at the UN brought up the boat. I'm going to assume it came up in the meeting and somebody said, "We've all agreed not to bring up the boat."]
And Dave himself, in an interview in 2009, said he'd keep apologizing for it as long as he had to. And in 2024 the band went into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
So they're fine. They're in the Hall. They're UN ambassadors. They did the work.
And every August 8th, the Chicago news runs the anniversary story anyway. Every year. Because this is Chicago. We don't forget. We still talk about the Bartman ball and that was a foul ball.

## THAT GUY
[CLIP: That Guy verdict]
Okay. Time to name him. That Guy.
The suspects.
Suspect one: the Dave Matthews Band. Their name's on the bus. They said all the buses were parked. They offered up their DNA, God help us. They paid the settlement. And they'll be answering for it at every Chicago show until the sun burns out.
Suspect two: the Kinzie Street bridge. Open steel grating over a river full of tour boats. If you designed a bridge specifically so this could happen, it would look exactly like the Kinzie Street bridge.
Suspect three: Jerry Fitzpatrick. Kidding. Jerry's the hero. Jerry got a cop to look in his tank. Jerry is cleared forever.
Suspect four: Stefan Wohl. The man who was alone on that bus, on that bridge, with that switch behind his seat.
[Pause.]
And the verdict.
This one's easy. One bus, one driver, one hand on one switch. It's Stefan Wohl. He pleaded guilty. Nobody else was on the bus.
[THAT GUY STING]
Dave Matthews was not on the bus. Boyd Tinsley was not on the bus. The band didn't build the bridge, and the bridge didn't flick the switch. The bridge has been sitting there minding its own business for about a hundred years.
And the band's mistake was believing their guy and saying "it wasn't us" before anybody checked the tape. Then offering DNA. That's bad. That's a lesson. But they paid for it. They paid for it in cash, and they'll pay for it in jokes forever.
So That Guy is Stefan Wohl. Go back to what the engineers said: it could not have been an accident. Somebody reached back and decided. And I'll even give him the "awesome" part, because the rule is the rule. Of all the bridges, in all the cities, on all the tours in America, he found the one bridge with holes in it, over the one river where we already reversed the flow once because of this exact problem, at the one moment a boat full of tourists was underneath, next to the one gym with cameras on it.
[RIFF: your verdict. Do you let the band off? Or use this:]
I don't know if that's a guy with terrible luck or a guy with incredible aim. Either way, he's That Guy.

## OUT
So that's the Dave Matthews Band bus. Earth Day band, two nights at Alpine Valley, a nice hotel, a switch behind the seat, a cop in Effingham looking in the wrong tank, and a hundred people on a boat getting the worst architecture tour in history.
And somewhere, there's still a man who was on that deck, telling everybody at the bar, "That's not water, buddy." And he's right. He was always right.
[RIFF: defacingthemusic.com, Guest List, subscribe, socials. Or use this:]
Get on the Guest List at defacingthemusic.com. It's safe. It doesn't go over any bridges.
Next time, another one. Another band, another night, another guy.
I'm Duck. Due to unforeseen circumstances, I'll see you next time.

title: Due To a Cheese Sandwich
subtitle: Who Sold Them Paradise?
body:
## COLD OPEN
[CLIP: Cold open: the styrofoam box]
April 2017. Great Exuma, the Bahamas. A Thursday night.
A guy who paid thousands of dollars for the most exclusive music festival on Earth is standing on a gravel lot, holding a styrofoam box.
He was promised supermodels. Gourmet food. A private island that used to belong to Pablo Escobar.
He opens the box.
And by the next morning, the whole planet knows exactly what's inside it.
## TODAY
Today: a twenty-five-year-old founder from New York, a rapper from the early 2000s, a plain orange square that sold out a festival, a truckload of water stuck at customs, a field of disaster relief tents, and the most famous sandwich of the twenty-first century.
Also, the festival put out an official statement that starts with the words "Due to unforeseen." I didn't make that up. They named the show for me.
And somewhere in this story, there's a guy. There always is. This time he's not hard to find. But keep an eye out anyway, because he brought friends.
I'm Duck, and due to a cheese sandwich, this is Defacing the Music.
[THEME SONG, hard stop]
Episode [NUMBER]. Who Sold Them Paradise?

## WHO IS BILLY
Before we get to the island, you have to meet Billy.
William McFarland. Born December 1991, in New York. And from early on, Billy is a "founder." Not of anything in particular. Just a founder. As a lifestyle.
In 2013, in his early twenties, he starts a company called Magnises. It's the whole story in miniature.
Magnises is an invitation-only club for young professionals, built around a charge card. You join, you get the card, and the card gets you into exclusive events. The pitch is basically, "You are the kind of person who gets into things."
[FILL: I'm from Chicagoland. Our exclusive club is the back room of a bar where the owner's cousin plays darts. Nobody pays a membership fee. You just have to know Gary.]
He raises about a million and a half from investors for it. File that away. He's selling the feeling of being on the list. That's his instrument. Some people play guitar. Billy plays "you're invited."
Next he starts Fyre Media. And Fyre Media's big idea is an app for booking talent. You want a famous rapper at your party, you open the app, you book him. Like ordering a pizza, if the pizza had a manager.
To get people to notice the app, he decides to throw a festival.
To advertise an app. On an island. In a few months.

## WHO IS JA RULE
And Billy has a partner. Ja Rule.
For anybody who wasn't around in 2001, I need to explain how big Ja Rule was. Real name Jeffrey Atkins. He was on the Jennifer Lopez "I'm Real" remix, which went to number one. Then "Always on Time" with Ashanti, which also went to number one. He had that gravel voice where every song sounded like a guy whispering to you from a fire escape.
And then he got into a feud with 50 Cent. If you were around, you know how that went. It got so bad that in 2003 Ja Rule sat down with Minister Louis Farrakhan, who wanted to step in before somebody got hurt.
So by 2016, Ja's not on the radio much. But he's famous. Famous enough to open doors. And Billy is very good at walking through doors other people open.
[RIFF: a buddy pitching you a business idea at a bar. Or use this:]
Every musician has a guy who wants to "partner up." He's got a vision, he's got a buddy with a boat, he's got a cousin with a PA. And the move, every single time, is to go home. Ja Rule did not go home.

## THE ORANGE SQUARE
Now here's the part where Billy is a genius. And I mean that. For about two weeks, Billy McFarland is a genius.
December 2016. Fyre puts out a promo video, shot in the Bahamas. Supermodels on the beach and out on the water. Bella Hadid. Emily Ratajkowski. Hailey Baldwin, who's now Hailey Bieber.
[CLIP: 1.2 million for the vibe and an orange square]
According to later reporting, between November 2016 and February 2017, Billy's company paid one modeling agency, IMG, about one point two million dollars.
For the vibe. One point two million dollars for the vibe.
Then the move that changed marketing. A wave of models and influencers all post the same picture on Instagram, at the same time. And it's not a picture of anything. It's a plain orange square. Just orange. With a link.
[Pause.]
That's the ad. A color.
And it works. Kendall Jenner posts about it, and she was reportedly paid at least a quarter million dollars for it. Years later she agreed to pay ninety thousand dollars to settle a claim over that post in the Fyre bankruptcy case.
[FILL: A lot of those posts didn't say "this is an ad." There are federal rules about that.]
Tickets go on sale. Depending on the source, they run from around fifteen hundred bucks to twelve grand, with packages reported as high as a quarter million. The lineup goes up: Blink-182, Major Lazer, Migos, Pusha T, Tyga, Disclosure, dozens more.
And people buy. Of course they buy. They just watched Bella Hadid on a boat.

## THE ISLAND
Okay. The promo video says this is happening on a private island once owned by Pablo Escobar.
It was not owned by Pablo Escobar.
The island in the video is Norman's Cay. And Norman's Cay does have a drug history. It was tied to Carlos Lehder, a Medellín cartel guy who worked with Escobar. So Billy didn't make up an island with a cocaine past. He just picked the wrong drug lord. Right cartel, wrong employee.
And then they lose the island. The organizers get kicked off Norman's Cay, and the most repeated version is that the Escobar line in the ads didn't help. Whatever the exact reason, the island's gone, and there are about four months left to find somewhere else to throw the greatest party in the world.
So it moves to Great Exuma. Not a private island. A big island with people living on it. And the site, when guests finally see it, gets described as an unfinished gravel lot.
[RIFF: "private island" versus "gravel lot." Or use this:]
It's like getting booked to play a stadium, and you show up and it's the parking lot of a Menards, and the promoter goes, "Well, it's outdoors. Like a stadium."

## THE WARNING SIGNS
It's easy to laugh at rich kids who wanted to party with supermodels. And we will. But most of the warning signs were behind the curtain.
In early April, the Wall Street Journal reported that the organizers had missed a series of deadlines to make advance payments to the performers.
If you've ever played for money, you know what that means. If the promoter can't pay the band, the promoter can't pay anybody.
And Billy's raising money the whole time. Later, in court, he admitted he defrauded eighty investors and faked documents to get more money for this thing. So the money that should be building bathrooms is coming from people being lied to about how much money there is.
Then, the day before it starts, Blink-182 pulls out. Their statement said they weren't confident they'd have what they needed to give fans the kind of show they always give.
That's a polite way of saying, "We looked at it."
Blink-182 is not a fussy band. And they looked at it and went, "Nope."

## THE WATER
[CLIP: Andy King and the Evian at customs]
Here's a side story I love, and it goes in the "this is how he tells it" pile, because it comes from one guy, on camera, in the Netflix documentary.
His name is Andy King. Veteran event producer. Brought in to help pull this thing off.
Andy says the festival had a huge shipment of Evian water stuck at Bahamian customs. Four eighteen-wheelers, he says. And customs wanted about a hundred seventy-five thousand dollars in cash to release it.
And Billy, according to Andy, asked Andy to go take care of it. Personally. With the customs official. With his mouth.
[Pause.]
And Andy says he was ready. He was going to take one for the team.
Then, in his telling, the official couldn't have been nicer, nothing like that was needed, and the water got released.
[RIFF: Andy King, crew guy above and beyond. Or use this:]
I've worked with great production guys. Guys who'll run cable through a thunderstorm. Not one of them ever offered that. Andy King is the most committed crew guy in the history of live music, and he didn't even have to do it.
And then Evian put out special bottles with him. That's the world now. You almost do a thing for water, and the water company gives you a campaign.

## ARRIVAL
Thursday, April 27th, 2017. Guests start flying in from Miami.
They land, they get on buses, and they pull up to the site. And it's tents. Not glamping tents with a rug and a chandelier. The tents you see on the news after a hurricane. Disaster relief tents. Rows of them. A skeleton staff. Nothing finished.
[FILL: That weekend, people online were calling it "the Hunger Games for rich people." Which is mean. And correct.]
These are people used to a guy with a clipboard who fixes things. And they're walking around a gravel lot, in the dark, looking for him.
[Pause.]
The guy with the clipboard is also looking for the guy with the clipboard.

## THE SANDWICH
And then, dinner. The very first night. Thursday.
A guy named Trevor DeHaas takes a picture of what he got. The styrofoam box. Two pieces of bread. Two slices of cheese. Little salad. He tweets it out, basically saying, this is the dinner they gave us, and this whole thing is a disaster.
And it goes everywhere. Every news site. Every late show. Forget the orange square. The sandwich is the brand now.
Now, in fairness to the cheese. Some people who were there have said not everybody got the sandwich. One attendee remembered a hot meal, chicken and pasta and a salad. Some reports say the sandwiches mostly went to staff.
That's not the defense you think it is. "Not everybody got the sad sandwich" is not going on the poster.
[RIFF: review the sandwich like a food critic. Or use this:]
That's not a meal. That's what you make at two in the morning when the bread's a little stale and you've given up. It's a sandwich that's sorry. It's a sandwich that knows.
And the epilogue. In 2021, Trevor DeHaas sold that tweet as an NFT, to help pay for dialysis and a kidney transplant. So after all that, the sandwich finally did some good for somebody.

## GETTING OFF THE ISLAND
By Friday, it's over before it starts.
Fyre puts out a statement, and I swear the universe wrote this for me. It said that "due to unforeseen and extenuating circumstances," Fyre Festival had been "fully postponed."
[Pause.]
Unforeseen. The Wall Street Journal saw it. Blink-182 saw it from another country. It was very, very foreseen.
Now everybody has to leave at once. Some guests tweeted that they were locked inside the airport terminal while they waited, without food or water. That's their account from the time, so hold it as that.
The Bahamas Ministry of Tourism puts out its own statement. It says it's extremely disappointed. And it makes a point of saying it was not an official sponsor of Fyre Festival.
[FILL: That's a government going, "Hi. We don't know him."]
The ministry sent a team of more than thirty people to help get everyone home. By Saturday most of the guests were gone, a lot of them flown back to Miami.
And Ja Rule tweets an apology. He says it was not a scam, it was not his fault, and he's taking responsibility.
Not my fault, and I take responsibility. Same tweet. That's a guy who rear-ends you, gets out, and goes, "I'm so sorry. Also, you hit me."

## THE FALLOUT
[CLIP: Fyre sold on eBay]
Billy McFarland got arrested by federal agents on June 30th, 2017, and charged with wire fraud.
And then, while out on bail, he ran another scheme. Selling fake tickets to exclusive events.
While on bail. For a fake exclusive event. He sold more fake exclusive events.
In March 2018 he pleaded guilty. That October he was sentenced to six years in federal prison and ordered to forfeit twenty-six million dollars. He got out early, in 2022. As of 2025, reports say he still owed roughly that whole twenty-six million.
Ja Rule got named in a hundred-million-dollar class action. In 2019 a judge dismissed him from it, saying there wasn't enough to show he committed fraud. He was never criminally charged. And in a recorded staff meeting that the New York Times reported on, he summed it up himself: "False advertising, maybe, not fraud."
In January 2019, two documentaries come out four days apart. Hulu drops "Fyre Fraud" with no warning. Then Netflix drops "Fyre." And they go to war. The Hulu side points out that the Netflix film was made with Jerry Media, the company that did Fyre's social media marketing in the first place. The Netflix director says Billy told him Hulu offered Billy two hundred fifty grand for an interview. Hulu's director called that number a lie. Nobody's settled who's right.
So even the movies about the scam had a scam argument.
And Billy announced a Fyre Festival 2. In April 2025 it got postponed indefinitely. Then he sold the Fyre brand on eBay, for about two hundred forty-five thousand dollars.
[Pause.]
The most exclusive brand in the world. Sold on the same website where you buy a used carburetor.

## THE SERIOUS PART
Okay. I need to slow down, because the people who got hurt worst by Fyre weren't the ones with the expensive tickets.
That site was built by Bahamian workers. Locals who hauled, built, cooked and cleaned for weeks. And a lot of them were never paid.
One of them was Maryann Rolle. She ran a restaurant on Exuma and catered for the festival. When the money never came, she used about fifty thousand dollars of her own savings to pay the people who'd worked for her.
After the Netflix documentary told her story in 2019, a fundraiser for her blew way past its goal, well over a hundred thousand dollars. Ja Rule apologized to her publicly. Good. But she never should have needed any of it.
[RIFF: the crew gets paid last. Keep it straight. Or use this:]
Anybody who's worked a gig knows the crew gets paid last. At Fyre, a lot of the crew never got paid at all. And they were the only people on that island who actually did their jobs.

## THAT GUY
[CLIP: That Guy verdict]
Okay. Time to name him. That Guy.
The suspects.
Suspect one: Ja Rule. The famous face. The guy whose name made it feel real. A judge says he wasn't on the hook for fraud, and he'll tell you he got played too. But he co-founded it, and he tweeted "not my fault." That's a suspect.
Suspect two: the orange square. The models, the agency, the influencers who got paid six figures to post a color without saying it was an ad. That's a crowd of suspects, and a lot of them were on a boat.
Suspect three: Billy McFarland. The founder. The guy who sells you the feeling of being on the list.
[Pause.]
And the verdict.
It's Billy. I know the show's more fun when it's the stagehand. But he lied to investors, he admitted it in court, and then he did it again on bail. You don't get to be a side character in your own fraud.
[THAT GUY STING]
Now the "that guy is usually awesome" part, and I'm saying this carefully. Take the crimes out, and you have to take the crimes out, and the orange square was brilliant. One color. No product. Sold out a festival. The man understood exactly how badly people want to be invited. He just never built the party.
[RIFF: your verdict. Billy, or everybody who wanted to be on that boat? Or use this:]
Billy's guilty. But a lot of people looked at a plain orange square and went, "Yes. Take my money." And that square is still out there. Waiting for the next guy.

## OUT
So that's it. A charge card club, an app nobody remembers, a rapper, a color, the wrong drug lord's island, four trucks of water, a gravel lot, and a sandwich that had to carry the whole thing on its back.
They promised paradise, and the only thing that showed up on time was the cheese.
[RIFF: defacingthemusic.com, Guest List, subscribe, socials. Or use this:]
Get on the Guest List at defacingthemusic.com. It's free, there's no orange square, and nobody gets a sandwich. Next time, another one.
I'm Duck. Due to unforeseen circumstances, I'll see you next time.

title: Due To a Skipping Track
subtitle: Who Let the Tape Run?
body:
## COLD OPEN
[CLIP: Cold open: the track skips]
July 1989. An amusement park in Connecticut. A summer night, and MTV is filming.
The hottest pop act in America is on stage. Two guys with long braids and the best dance moves in the business, and the crowd is screaming every word of their big hit.
And then the song hiccups.
"Girl, you know it's..." "Girl, you know it's..." "Girl, you know it's..."
Over and over.
And the two guys on stage just stand there.
## TODAY
Today: a German producer with a secret, two dancers with a dream, three number one singles, a Grammy, a backing track with a mind of its own, a press conference where everybody finally sang, and the only Grammy ever taken back.
Also, refunds. America got refunds. For feelings.
And somewhere in this story, there's a guy. There always is. And I'll warn you now, it's not who the jokes were about.
I'm Duck, and due to a skipping track, this is Defacing the Music.
[THEME SONG, hard stop]
Episode [NUMBER]. Who Let the Tape Run?

## WHO IS FRANK FARIAN
[CLIP: Frank Farian already did this with Boney M]
To understand Milli Vanilli, you have to start with a guy who isn't in Milli Vanilli.
Frank Farian. German record producer. And in the seventies, Frank Farian builds a group called Boney M. You know Boney M even if you think you don't. "Rasputin." "Daddy Cool." Every wedding DJ in Europe still owes this man a fruit basket.
Boney M had a guy named Bobby Farrell. Great dancer. Tall, skinny, all knees and elbows, the face of the group on TV. And here's the thing. On the records, the deep male voice wasn't Bobby. It was Frank. Farian sang the male parts in the studio, and Bobby performed them on camera.
And this was not a big secret in the business. People knew.
[FILL: So Frank had already run this play once. It worked. It worked for years. When something works, you don't stop. That's how you end up with a fourth Fast and Furious.]
So file that away. Frank Farian has a template. A great voice in the studio, and a great-looking performer in front of the camera. And he does not see a problem with that.

## WHO ARE ROB AND FAB
Now let's meet the guys in front of the camera.
Rob Pilatus. His mother was a German dancer, his father an African American serviceman. And Rob spent his first four years in an orphanage in Bavaria, in Oberammergau, before a family in Munich adopted him. Growing up Black in Germany in the sixties and seventies, he said he got bullied, called names, made to feel like he didn't belong.
Fab Morvan. Fabrice. From Paris. Moved to Germany at eighteen.
And the two of them meet in the Munich club scene. The stories differ on exactly where. One version is a dance class at a club. Another says they first crossed paths in Los Angeles and reconnected in Munich. But everybody agrees on what they were. Dancers. Models. Two young guys who looked like stars before anybody knew their names.
And they want to be a group. They want to sing.
[RIFF: being twenty-something and knowing you're going to be famous. Or use this:]
Everybody in music has been that guy. You're twenty-two, you've got the hair, you've got the outfit, you've got the moves, and you know, you just know, that somebody important is going to walk through that door. And for most of us, nobody does. For Rob and Fab, somebody did.

## THE DEAL
That somebody is Frank Farian.
Around 1988, Farian has a batch of songs recorded. Studio singers. Good ones. A rapper named Charles Shaw, a singer named Brad Howell, another singer named John Davis, plus others. What Farian wants is a face. Somebody who looks like the music sounds.
So he signs Rob and Fab.
And here's a detail that matters later. By their own account, they signed without taking any legal advice. Two young guys, a famous producer, a stack of paper. Sign here.
And at some point, it becomes clear. They're not going to be singing on the record. They're going to be the record.
Now, where'd the name come from? The story goes that it came from a trip to Turkey, where they saw a slogan that sounded like "Milli Vanilli." I can't nail down the details, so that one goes in the "the story goes" pile. Which, honestly, is the right pile for this whole band.
[FILL: It's a great name, though. You can't say "Milli Vanilli" angry. Try it. You can't. It comes out like a kid's game.]

## AMERICA
The record comes out in Europe first. Then it crosses over to America on Arista Records, under the title "Girl You Know It's True."
And it explodes.
"Girl You Know It's True" goes to number two on the Billboard Hot 100. Then "Baby Don't Forget My Number" goes to number one. "Girl I'm Gonna Miss You," number one. "Blame It on the Rain," number one. Every single from that album made the top five.
By January 1990, the album is certified six times platinum. Six million copies in America.
And the videos are everywhere. The braids. The outfits. The dancing. Rob and Fab are on MTV every hour. They are the look of 1989.
[RIFF: what 1989 looked like. Or use this:]
If you were alive in 1989, you saw those two guys more than you saw your own family. Somebody in your house had a cassette. Somebody's older sister had the poster. Your gym teacher played it during the dodgeball unit.

## THE SKIP
So now they're huge. And when you're huge, you tour. Which, if you don't sing, is a problem.
July 21st, 1989. They're on MTV's Club MTV tour, playing Lake Compounce, an amusement park in Bristol, Connecticut.
And they're doing what pop acts did a lot back then, honestly. Dancing hard and performing to a track.
And then the track skips.
The line "Girl, you know it's" starts looping. Over and over. Stuck. Like a CD in a car going over a pothole, except the pothole never ends.
And Rob and Fab are standing up there with microphones in their hands, in front of a crowd that was singing every word along with them about ten seconds ago.
[Pause.]
Rob described it to MTV later. He said he couldn't keep repeating it, fifteen times, so he panicked, stopped, and went off stage.
And here's the side character. MTV's "Downtown" Julie Brown, the VJ, who's hosting this tour. According to her, she chased Rob off stage and talked him into going back out to finish the show.
[FILL: That's the "according to her" pile. It's her story from a TV special years later. I believe it, I just can't prove it.]
And the wild part? That night didn't end Milli Vanilli. The show went on. The records kept selling. The truth didn't fully come out for more than a year.
But Rob knew. He said later that he knew right then and there, it was the beginning of the end.
[RIFF: a gear failure on stage, the moment your stomach drops. Or use this:]
Every musician has had the moment. The amp cuts out. The click track goes. Something fails, and for one second, the whole room can see exactly how the trick works. For most of us, that's a bad night. For Rob, it was the trick.

## THE MOUTH
Now, here's where it gets hard to watch.
Because after the skip, Rob and Fab didn't get quieter. They got louder.
[CLIP: More talented than Paul McCartney]
In an interview with Time magazine, Rob, twenty-four at the time, said this, and I'm quoting Time: "Musically, we are more talented than any Bob Dylan. Musically, we are more talented than Paul McCartney."
[Pause.]
And then he said Mick Jagger's lines are not clear.
[RIFF: a guy who didn't sing on his own record dissing Paul McCartney. Or use this:]
That's a guy who didn't sing on his own album telling a national magazine that he's better than Paul McCartney. Paul McCartney wrote "Yesterday." Rob didn't sing "Blame It on the Rain." I need the scoreboard on this one.
But think about it from where Rob's sitting. Kid from an orphanage, bullied, finally the most famous guy in the room. Holding a secret that could take it all away. Some people get quiet when they're scared. Some people start yelling about Bob Dylan.

## THE GRAMMY
February 21st, 1990. The Grammys. Milli Vanilli wins Best New Artist.
They go up. They take the trophy. They thank people.
Best New Artist. For two guys who, as the whole world would find out, were not the artist.
And some people already had questions. Because back in December 1989, one of those studio guys, Charles Shaw, the rapper, told Newsday that he was one of the real voices on the album, and that the guys on the cover were impostors.
And then he took it back.
Now, the widely repeated version is that Farian paid Shaw a hundred fifty thousand dollars to retract it. That number gets repeated everywhere, usually with an "allegedly" next to it, and I've never seen hard proof. So it goes in the "reportedly" pile.
[FILL: A guy tells the newspaper the truth, takes it back, and the lie keeps going for almost another year. That's how big the money was.]

## THE CONFESSION
So what finally breaks it?
The usual version goes like this. Rob and Fab want to sing on the next album. For real. With their own voices. And Frank Farian isn't having it.
In November 1990, Farian goes public. He admits that Rob and Fab didn't sing on the record.
And then the whole world turns on Rob and Fab. Not on the producer. Not on the label. On the two guys with the braids.
Within days, the Grammy organization takes the award back. Best New Artist, revoked. And to this day, it's the only time the Grammys have ever done that. One time. Ever. Thousands of awards, and these are the guys.
[FILL: Reportedly, the duo had already said they'd give it back on their own. And they asked that it go to the singers who actually sang on the album. That didn't happen.]
Then Rob and Fab do a press conference in Los Angeles. More than two hundred reporters show up. And at one point, the two of them sing. Live. A cappella. A few bars of "Girl You Know It's True."
[Pause.]
The first time a lot of people ever heard their real voices was the day they got caught.
[RIFF: the press conference. Two guys singing for a room full of reporters who came to watch them die. Or use this:]
Imagine having to audition for the whole world, on the worst day of your life, in a room full of people who already decided you're a punchline.

## THE REFUNDS
[CLIP: America sued for refunds]
And then America did the most American thing possible. America sued.
Class action lawsuits. People wanted their money back. For an album they listened to, liked, and danced to, for over a year.
The settlement came out of a court in Chicago, our town, and an estimated ten million buyers were eligible. And the numbers in the settlement, as reported, were about a buck back for a single, two for a cassette or record, three for a CD.
[Pause.]
And you got to keep the album.
[FILL: So the song still sounds exactly the same. You just know who's singing it now. And for that, three dollars.]
Arista dropped them and pulled the album out of print. One of the biggest-selling records of its time, just gone from the catalog.
[RIFF: what's the album you'd want a refund for. Or use this:]
I've bought records that made me feel lied to. Not one of them ever sent me three dollars.

## WHAT HAPPENED NEXT
Fab kept going. He kept singing. Live, with his own voice, for decades. He ended up with the rights to the Milli Vanilli name. In 2023 there was a documentary, "Milli Vanilli," on Paramount Plus, that let the two of them tell their side.
And then, and I love this, Fab wrote a memoir called "You Know It's True." He read the audiobook himself. And for the 2026 Grammys, that audiobook got nominated.
[Pause.]
Thirty-five years after they took the Grammy away, the Grammys nominated Fab Morvan for reading his own words, out loud, in his own voice.
He lost. To the Dalai Lama.
[FILL: That's fine. You can lose to the Dalai Lama. Nobody's mad at you for losing to the Dalai Lama.]
And Frank Farian? He kept right on making hits. In the nineties he was behind acts like La Bouche and No Mercy. Frank Farian died in January 2024 at his home in Miami. He was eighty-two.

## THE SERIOUS PART
Rob Pilatus died in April 1998, in a hotel near Frankfurt, from an accidental overdose of alcohol and prescription drugs. He was in his early thirties.
[Pause.]
[RIFF: a few words for Rob. Keep it straight. Or use this:]
He was a kid who wanted to sing, and when he finally got to, nobody was listening anymore.

## THAT GUY
[CLIP: That Guy verdict]
Okay. Time to name him. That Guy.
The suspects.
Suspect one: Rob and Fab. They knew. They took the deal, took the stage, took the Grammy, and Rob told Time he was better than Paul McCartney. They're not innocent.
Suspect two: the record business. Arista, the label, pushing a record to six million people. MTV, putting them in every living room. And the Grammys, who handed them the award and then took it back like none of them had ever heard of a studio singer. That's three different companies, and every one of them made money.
Suspect three: Frank Farian. The guy who'd already done this with Boney M. The guy who had the singers and the dancers, put them together, and kept the secret until the dancers wanted to sing.
And the verdict.
Frank Farian. Rob and Fab carried the blame for thirty years, but Farian built the machine, and he'd built it before. And when it came out, two young guys who signed without a lawyer took the hit, while the guy with the plan went on making records.
[THAT GUY STING]
The "that guy is usually awesome" part: the songs were good. They still are. "Blame It on the Rain" comes on, you know every word. Farian knew how to make a hit. He just didn't think the people singing it mattered.
Now, to be fair, this is disputed. Plenty of people will tell you Rob and Fab were grown men who knew exactly what they signed up for. And that's not wrong.
[RIFF: your verdict. Farian, the duo, or the whole business? Or use this:]
Rob and Fab lip-synced. Fine. Frank Farian lip-synced an entire group, twice, and nobody took his trophies away.

## OUT
So that's it. A producer with a template, two dancers who wanted to sing, three number ones, a skipping track in Connecticut, a revoked Grammy, and a three-dollar refund.
And thirty-five years later, the guy who never got to sing on his own record got a Grammy nomination for using his own voice. Took the long way.
Girl, you know it's... true.
[RIFF: defacingthemusic.com, Guest List, subscribe, socials. Or use this:]
Get on the Guest List at defacingthemusic.com. Every word on this show is me. No backing track. Next time, another one.
I'm Duck. Due to unforeseen circumstances, I'll see you next time.

title: Due To Language
