subtitle: Who Dared the Sex Pistols?
body:
## COLD OPEN
[CLIP: Cold open: say something outrageous]
December 1st, 1976. London. Teatime.
Families are sitting down in front of the telly for a cozy local news show. Something to have on while the kettle boils.
On screen, a fifty-something host in a suit is leaning toward a young guitar player, and he's egging him on.
Go on. You've got five seconds. Say something outrageous.
It's live. There's no delay.
And the kid is thinking about it.
## TODAY
Today: a geologist who became a TV host, a clothing shop on the King's Road, a guitar player who stole his gear from David Bowie, a singer who auditioned to a jukebox, Freddie Mercury's teeth, and a couple of minutes of television that made a whole country lose its mind.
Also a lorry driver and his telly. We'll get there. That one comes with an asterisk.
And somewhere in this story, there's a guy. There always is. And this time, the guy might be the one asking the questions.
I'm Duck, and due to language, this is Defacing the Music.
[THEME SONG, hard stop]
Episode [NUMBER]. Who Dared the Sex Pistols?

## WHO IS BILL GRUNDY
First I need you to meet the host. Because he's not who you'd think.
Bill Grundy. Born in Manchester in 1923. Son of a factory owner. Studied geology at the University of Manchester.
Geology. Rocks. That's the start of this story. A rock guy.
When Granada Television launches up north, Grundy gets on the air reading the news, while he's still working as a geologist. And he turns out to be good at it. Sharp. Quick. A little prickly. The kind of TV guy who's smarter than the show he's on and makes sure you notice.
And here's the detail that blew my mind. October 1962, on a Granada show called People and Places, Bill Grundy introduces a young band from Liverpool on their first ever TV appearance.
The Beatles.
[Pause.]
Same Bill Grundy. The guy who introduced the Beatles to television is the same guy who introduced the Sex Pistols to television. He's both bookends. He's the opening act and the closing act of an entire era of British music, and he probably didn't like either of them very much.
[RIFF: Bill Grundy, the accidental bookends of British rock. Or use this:]
That's like being the doctor who delivers a baby, and then twenty years later you're the cop who arrests him. You were there for both. You should've seen it coming.
By 1976, Grundy is presenting Today, a teatime news magazine show from Thames Television. And this is important for later. Today wasn't national. It was only seen in the Thames region. London and the area around it. A local show.
Which, for what's about to happen, doesn't matter at all.

## THE SHOP
Now, the Sex Pistols.
The Sex Pistols basically start in a clothing store. A shop on the King's Road in London called Sex, run by Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood. Clothes built to upset people. Stuff you could not wear to your aunt's house.
And Malcolm McLaren is our first side character. Because McLaren isn't a musician. He's a guy with ideas, a shop, and a very good sense of what makes people angry.
Two of his customers are a couple of kids, Steve Jones and Paul Cook. They want to start a band. And from around 1974, McLaren starts advising them.
[CLIP: Steve Jones steals Bowie's gear]
Now let me tell you about Steve Jones. Because Steve Jones, by his own admission, was a thief. Not a little thief.
In July 1973, David Bowie plays two nights at the Hammersmith Odeon. The last shows he ever did as Ziggy Stardust. Big moment in rock history. And Steve Jones, eighteen, sneaks into the venue and steals gear. Cymbals. An amp head. Microphones. And, he says, Bowie's own microphone, with lipstick on it.
[RIFF: stealing from Bowie. Or use this:]
He's said he loved Bowie and he couldn't help it. He was a kleptomaniac. That's the most rock and roll thing I've ever heard. "I love you so much, I'm taking your microphone."
Now, the details of how he got in change depending on who's telling it. Steve says he hid up in the rafters. Paul Cook says they'd just go around the back. Pick your favorite. Either way, part of the early Sex Pistols setup was hot Bowie gear.

## JOHNNY
They need a singer.
And in 1975, a kid walks into the shop. John Lydon. Born in London to Irish parents. Grew up in a council flat in Finsbury Park, North London.
And when Lydon was seven, he got meningitis. Spent about a year in hospital, in and out of a coma. He's said it messed with his memory, and he's called it the first step that put him on the road to Rotten.
So that's the guy. And according to the most repeated version, McLaren notices him because he's wearing a T-shirt that says "I Hate Pink Floyd."
[Pause.]
Not "I love" anything. "I hate Pink Floyd." That's the résumé. That's the cover letter.
And the audition. August 1975. In the shop. No band. No rehearsal room. They put Alice Cooper's "I'm Eighteen" on the shop's jukebox, and Lydon sings along to it. Flails around. Sneers. And that's it. He's in.
[FILL: Lydon tells it like he was the one who put the song on. Others say the band talked him into it. Either way, the audition was a jukebox. Somebody should frame that jukebox.]
Steve Jones gives him the name Johnny Rotten. Because of his teeth.
That's how bands work. You don't pick your nickname. Your guitar player picks it, and it's always about your worst feature.
With Glen Matlock on bass, they play their first gig in November 1975, at an art college in London. And for the next year, they build up a following. A crowd of fans start showing up to every show. Kids from the suburbs, dressed like the shop. One bunch gets called the Bromley Contingent. Keep an eye on them. They're about to be on TV.

## THE BOOKING
October 1976. The Sex Pistols sign with EMI. Huge label. The company behind the Beatles' records. And the reported advance is forty thousand pounds.
They put out their first single, "Anarchy in the U.K." They're about to start a tour, the Anarchy Tour.
[CLIP: Freddie Mercury's teeth]
And now we need to talk about Freddie Mercury's teeth.
Queen is on EMI too. And Queen is booked on Today, with Bill Grundy, on December 1st. And at the last minute, Queen cancels, because Freddie Mercury needs emergency dental work.
The story goes that Freddie hadn't been to a dentist in about fifteen years, and the only appointment he could get was the same time as the show. I can't prove the fifteen years. But the dental emergency is in every account.
[FILL: If Freddie flosses, punk might show up a little later. Think about that next time you skip it.]
So EMI needs to fill the slot, and they send their new band. The Sex Pistols. And along with the band come a few of their fans from the Bromley Contingent, including a young woman who'll soon be famous herself, Siouxsie Sioux.
And here's the setup. A live teatime show. A host who's been on TV for twenty years and has nothing to prove. And four guys and a few of their fans, in a TV studio, about to go live.

## THE INTERVIEW
So I'm going to walk you through this. And fair warning up front: there are a bunch of transcripts of this interview floating around, and they don't match word for word. So I'm going to quote the bits that every version agrees on, and paraphrase the rest.
Grundy introduces them, and right away he's needling them. In one widely reported line, he says they're as drunk as he is. Later, he insisted he was sober.
Then he goes after the money. He brings up that they got forty thousand pounds from a record company. Isn't that against their whole anti-materialism thing?
And Glen Matlock says, "the more the merrier."
And then, depending on the transcript, Steve Jones says something like, they've already spent it. With a swear in the middle.
That's the first one. It kind of slides by.
Then Grundy brings up Beethoven and Mozart, and Johnny Rotten mutters a rude word under his breath. Grundy catches it. And instead of moving on, like any host in the history of television would, he asks Johnny to say it again.
[Pause.]
He asks him to say it again. On live teatime television.
And Johnny does.
Then Grundy turns to the fans standing behind the band. Siouxsie tells him she's always wanted to meet him. And Grundy flirts back, something like, did you really, we'll meet afterwards, shall we?
And that is when Steve Jones wakes up. He calls Grundy a dirty old man.
And Grundy, instead of shutting it down, eggs him on. "Go on, you've got another five seconds. Say something outrageous."
[Pause.]
And Steve Jones calls him a "dirty bastard."
Grundy says go on, again.
"You dirty fucker."
And then the line that I think about more than the swearing: "What a fucking rotter."
[RIFF: "What a fucking rotter." The most British insult ever said on TV. Or use this:]
"Rotter." That's a word from an old movie. That's what a guy in a top hat calls another guy in a top hat who cheated at cards. Steve Jones drops two F-bombs and then reaches all the way back to 1910.
And Grundy wraps it up. Closes the show. Roll credits. The band is bouncing around in the background. The whole thing was a couple of minutes.

## THE PAPERS
And the next morning, the papers go nuclear.
The Daily Mirror's front page, December 2nd: "The Filth and the Fury!"
The Daily Express: "Fury at Filthy TV Chat."
The Daily Telegraph: "4-Letter Words Rock TV."
And the show wasn't even national. Most of the country never saw it. And now the whole country is reading about it over breakfast. That's how the Sex Pistols went national. Not on TV. In the papers, about TV.
Now the lorry driver. And this is the asterisk I promised.
[CLIP: The lorry driver kicks in his telly]
The papers reported that a forty-seven-year-old lorry driver, watching at home with his eight-year-old son, got so furious about the language that he kicked in the screen of his brand new TV. He's quoted as saying it blew up and knocked him backwards.
That's how the papers told it. It's been repeated in pretty much every history of punk since. But it comes from tabloid coverage during a tabloid frenzy, and even his name gets told different ways in different retellings. So I'm putting it in the "the papers reported" pile.
[RIFF: the lorry driver. Or use this:]
Think about this guy for a second. He's so angry about bad language in front of his kid, that he, in front of his kid, kicks a TV until it explodes. That's not a lesson in manners. That's a new kind of language. His son learned more words that night from Dad than from the Sex Pistols.

## THE FALLOUT
So what happened to everybody?
Bill Grundy got suspended for two weeks. The reporting says Thames called it a gross error of judgement. And it's generally agreed it wrecked his career. Today itself ended the following year.
[FILL: Twenty years of solid TV, the Beatles' first TV intro, and he's remembered for two minutes of daring a punk band to swear. That's show business. You can do a thousand good gigs and they'll remember the one where your pants split.]
The Sex Pistols' Anarchy Tour started falling apart. Local councils and venues banned the shows. Sources disagree on how many dates actually happened, but most of the tour got cancelled.
In January 1977, EMI dropped them. Their statement said it felt it couldn't promote the band's records, given the bad publicity.
Then in March 1977, they signed with A&M Records. On a table set up outside Buckingham Palace. At seven in the morning.
[Pause.]
That deal lasted six days.
So in about six months, the Sex Pistols got signed and dropped by two of the biggest labels in the world. And it only made them bigger. Glen Matlock was out of the band in early 1977, and Sid Vicious came in on bass, despite, by most accounts, not really knowing how to play it yet. And then they put out "God Save the Queen" in the middle of the Queen's Silver Jubilee, because of course they did.
And that Grundy clip? It's been called the most requested clip in British TV history. In 2000, a documentary about the band took its title straight off the Mirror's front page: "The Filth and the Fury."
Bill Grundy died in 1993, in Stockport, at sixty-nine. And the first line of his obituary was never going to be the Beatles.

## THAT GUY
[CLIP: That Guy verdict]
Okay. Time to name him. That Guy.
The suspects.
Suspect one: Steve Jones. The guy who actually said it. Stole gear from Bowie, swore on live TV, called a grown man a rotter. He's guilty of everything he's ever been accused of, mostly by himself.
Suspect two: Freddie Mercury's teeth. And, fine, EMI, who sent a punk band to a teatime show as a substitute for Queen, like those are the same thing. Somebody at EMI looked at a list of their bands, saw a gap where Queen used to be, and went, "Those lads. They'll be fine."
Suspect three: Bill Grundy. The host. The one with twenty years of experience.
[Pause.]
And the verdict.
It's Bill Grundy. He asked Johnny to repeat the rude word. He flirted with a fan on air. And then, with the kid already swearing at him, he said, "Go on. Say something outrageous." He didn't just let it happen. He asked for it. Twice.
[THAT GUY STING]
Now, this one is disputed. Some people say Grundy was set up, that he was the old guard getting ambushed by kids who wanted a headline. And there are people who've argued Grundy deserved better than being remembered for this. That's fair.
But here's the "that guy is usually awesome" part. Bill Grundy introduced the Beatles to TV, and then he introduced the Sex Pistols to the whole country. Not on purpose. But he did it. That's a career.
[RIFF: your verdict. Grundy, Jones, or Freddie's dentist? Or use this:]
You can't dare a punk band to say something outrageous and then act surprised when they do. That's like handing Keith Moon a match.

## OUT
So that's it. A geologist, a clothing shop, Bowie's stolen microphone, a jukebox audition, Freddie Mercury's teeth, and two minutes of live television that made a country choke on its tea.
He told them to say something outrageous, and for once in their lives, the Sex Pistols did exactly what they were told.
[RIFF: defacingthemusic.com, Guest List, subscribe, socials. Or use this:]
Get on the Guest List at defacingthemusic.com. Go on. You've got five seconds. Next time, another one.
I'm Duck. Due to unforeseen circumstances, I'll see you next time.

title: Due To Great Balls of Firearms
subtitle: Who Let Jerry Lee Back to Graceland?
body:
## COLD OPEN
Memphis. November 1976. Three in the morning.
A brand new Lincoln idles at the gates of Graceland. The ones with the music notes on them.
On the seat, champagne the driver doesn't even like. On his knee, a tiny silver pistol.
Upstairs, the King of Rock and Roll has some very specific instructions.
And the guy in the Lincoln? He's already been turned away from this gate once. Since then, he's flipped a Rolls-Royce.
## TODAY
Today: a piano bought with a mortgage, a Bible school with a strict policy on boogie-woogie, a bass player who came over to drop off a record and got shot, a Rolls-Royce upside down in a Tennessee suburb, a bar owner who hands a drunk man a gun, a bottle of champagne versus a car window, and Elvis, home, upstairs, not coming down.
Two legends from the same little record label in Memphis, twenty years after they sang hymns around the same piano. And one of them is at the gate.
And somewhere in this story, there's a guy. There always is. This time you'll think he's easy to spot. You're mostly right.
I'm Duck, and due to great balls of firearms, this is Defacing the Music.
[THEME SONG, hard stop]
Episode [NUMBER]. Who Let Jerry Lee Back to Graceland?

## YOU KNOW THIS GUY
[CLIP: You know this song, you just didn't know it was him]
Okay, quick question before we start. Do you know who Jerry Lee Lewis is?
Because a lot of people know the name and that's it. They couldn't pick him out of a lineup. And honestly, he's been in a couple lineups.
So let me fix that. You know this song. "Goodness gracious, great balls of fire." That's him. That's Jerry Lee.
And this one. "Whole Lotta Shakin' Goin' On." Also him. That's his first big hit. It comes out on Sun Records in April 1957, and it goes to number three on the pop chart and number one on both the country and the R&B charts. All three. At the same time.
[FILL: You know how hard that is? I can't get one family group chat to agree on a restaurant.]
Now, the look. Picture a skinny kid from Louisiana with this big wavy blond hair, slicked up on top, and by the second verse it's hanging down in his face like a curtain. He doesn't sit at the piano. He stands. He kicks the bench across the stage. He pounds the keys with the heel of his shoe. Sometimes he plays with his feet. Sometimes his elbows. Sometimes, reportedly, his ass. He plays the piano like it owes him money.
And the moment that makes him: July 28th, 1957, his first time on national TV, The Steve Allen Show. He does "Whole Lotta Shakin'," he kicks the bench away, and according to an NPR piece, Steve Allen, the host, picks up the bench and throws it back across the stage. Live. And after that, the song is everywhere.
His nickname is The Killer. Where that came from depends on who you ask. One version, which his own camp told when he died, is a fight at school back in Ferriday, where young Jerry Lee tried to choke a grown man with the man's own necktie. Another version is that he just called everybody "Killer" as a kid, and it came back around. Either one works for me.
And if you're my age, you might've seen the movie. "Great Balls of Fire!" 1989. Dennis Quaid plays Jerry Lee, and Winona Ryder plays his wife. And here's a fun one: Jerry Lee didn't trust anybody else to sound like Jerry Lee, so he went back in the studio and re-recorded his own old hits for the soundtrack. In his fifties. The closing credits say the piano and vocals are performed by "The Killer himself."
So that's who's at the gate. Now let's go find out how he got there.

## FERRIDAY
Jerry Lee Lewis is born September 29th, 1935, in Ferriday, Louisiana. Small town. Poor family. Deep Assembly of God, which is a church where people get the Holy Spirit and it shows.
And the kid is obsessed with the piano. So his father, Elmo, mortgages the family home for three hundred dollars and buys him a used upright piano.
Mortgages the house. For a piano. For a kid.
[FILL: My parents wouldn't buy me a second guitar cable. Elmo Lewis put the house on the line. And honestly? Good bet. That piano paid off.]
And here's a weird true fact about Ferriday. Jerry Lee grows up with two cousins. One is Mickey Gilley, who becomes a country star. And the other is Jimmy Swaggart, who becomes one of the biggest TV preachers in America.
So out of one family, in one tiny town, you get a rock and roll wild man, a country singer, and a televangelist. And all three of them play the piano. That's not a family, that's a church picnic talent show that got out of hand.
[RIFF: the cousins. Or use this:]
I picture Thanksgiving at that house. One cousin's playing honky tonk, one's preaching about the devil, and Jerry Lee's at the piano doing both at the same time.

## THE BIBLE SCHOOL
[CLIP: Expelled from Bible school for boogie-woogie]
So his mother has a plan for him, and the plan is church. Sometime in the early fifties she gets him enrolled at the Southwest Bible Institute in Waxahachie, Texas. The idea is he'll sing and play gospel, and only gospel.
He lasts about three months.
Because at the school, they have him play at an assembly. A hymn. "My God Is Real."
And Jerry Lee plays it boogie-woogie.
In front of the faculty. At Bible school.
And that was it. The way the story usually gets told, he was done there that same night, and the dean expelled him the next morning.
[FILL: Think about how good you have to be at piano to get thrown out of Bible school for it. That's a review. That's a five star review from God's own HR department.]
And the school's still there, by the way. In 2024 it changed its name to Nelson University. I don't know if they've let anybody play boogie-woogie at an assembly since. I'm guessing they keep an eye on it.
That's the whole Jerry Lee Lewis story in one scene. Gospel on the inside, boogie-woogie on the outside, and he can't keep either one of them quiet.

## SUN
In 1956, Jerry Lee goes to Memphis. To Sun Records. Sam Phillips' label. The little studio on Union Avenue where Elvis got started.
He gets work there as a session piano player.
And on December 4th, 1956, he's playing piano on a Carl Perkins session when Elvis Presley walks in. Elvis is already the biggest star in the world. He'd left Sun for RCA, but he dropped by to say hi.
And they start jamming. Gospel songs, country songs, whatever. Johnny Cash shows up. And somebody leaves the tape running.
The next day the Memphis Press-Scimitar runs a story and calls them the Million Dollar Quartet. Elvis, Johnny Cash, Carl Perkins, and the new kid on piano.
So that's the first time Jerry Lee and Elvis are in a room together. Friends. Jamming. Singing hymns around a piano at the studio where both of them got their start.
Keep that picture in your pocket. Twenty years later, one of them's going to be at the gate.
[RIFF: the Million Dollar Quartet. Or use this:]
Four guys around a piano, no plan, just playing the songs they grew up on. Every musician has had that night. It's the best night there is. Most of us didn't have Elvis on harmony.

## FOLLOW THAT
And then the hits happen, and Jerry Lee becomes The Killer for real.
And here's my favorite Jerry Lee legend. This one goes straight in the "legend goes" pile.
The story goes that at a big package show, Jerry Lee was furious that Chuck Berry was closing instead of him. So at the end of his set, he poured gasoline on his piano, set it on fire, walked off, and said something like, "Follow that."
Is it true? It gets told everywhere. The details move around. Nobody can agree on the city, the year changes depending on who's telling it, and nobody has a picture of a burning piano.
But it's such a Jerry Lee move that I have to tell it. Even if it never happened, everybody who knew him believed it could have.
[FILL: If it didn't happen, somebody made up the greatest exit line in rock and roll and gave it away for free.]

## 1958
And then 1958.
Jerry Lee goes to England on tour. At the airport, a reporter asks the girl he's traveling with who she is.
And she says she's his wife.
Her name is Myra Gale Brown. She's his cousin. First cousin once removed. And she's thirteen years old.
[Pause.]
The tour is canceled after three shows. Back home, the radio drops him. His price goes from big money to bar money more or less overnight. Rock and roll's next big thing turns into the guy nobody will book.
There's no joke in this part, and I'm not going to try to find one.
He spends the next decade clawing back, and he does it through country music in the late sixties. And by the seventies he's a big country star again. Still The Killer. Still drinking. Still carrying guns. And that's where we pick him up.

## 1976
1976 is a very bad year for Jerry Lee Lewis.
September 29th, 1976. His forty first birthday. Now, you'll see some write-ups say it was the day before his birthday. The date most of them give is September 29th, and that is his birthday, so I'm going with on his birthday. Happy birthday, Jerry Lee.
He's at home in Collierville, outside Memphis. And at about 1:35 in the afternoon, his bass player, Norman "Butch" Owens, thirty one years old, comes by the house. Why? To drop off a copy of the new album. It's called "Country Class."
And Jerry Lee has a .357 Magnum.
Now, here's where the versions split. Jerry Lee told the officers that the two of them were messing around with the gun and he didn't know it was loaded. Butch Owens, in the lawsuit he filed the next year, said Jerry Lee pulled the gun and shot at a Coca-Cola bottle that was about three feet away from him.
Either way, he hits Butch Owens. In the chest.
Owens survived. He spent about a month in the hospital. He sued Jerry Lee for four hundred thousand dollars. And Jerry Lee got charged with, and I love how small this sounds, firing a gun inside the city limits.
[FILL: You know how bass players already feel overlooked. This was the one time everybody was looking at the bass player, and it's because the piano player shot him.]
So, let's just note where we are. The man shot his own bass player in September. On his birthday. While the guy was delivering the album. And two months later, nobody has taken the guns away.

## ELVIS
So where's Elvis in November 1976?
Elvis is forty one too. Same age as Jerry Lee, about nine months older. And Elvis is not doing great. His health is bad. He's spending a lot of time inside Graceland, behind the gates, with his people around him.
His longtime girlfriend Linda Thompson is on her way out of his life around then. And according to Ginger Alden's own account, she met Elvis on November 19th. A few days before all this.
So Elvis is up there in the mansion, brand new relationship. And down at the gate, Jerry Lee Lewis is about to happen to him.

## THE OTHER GUY WHO CAME OVER THE WALL
[CLIP: Springsteen climbs the Graceland wall]
And here's something I didn't know until I started digging. Jerry Lee is not the only rock star who showed up at Graceland uninvited in 1976. He's not even the first one that year.
April 1976. Bruce Springsteen plays a show in Memphis. And afterward, around three in the morning, he and Steve Van Zandt take a cab to Graceland. Because Bruce wants to meet Elvis.
And Bruce climbs over the wall. Runs up the driveway toward the house. There's a light on upstairs. He's going to knock on the door.
And security stops him and walks him back out. And they tell him Elvis isn't even home. Depending on who's telling it, Elvis is in Lake Tahoe or Las Vegas. Bruce asks the guard to tell Elvis that he came by.
So that's the good version. The polite version. A young guy who just wants to say thank you, gets turned around, goes home.
Seven months later, the Graceland gate guys get the other version.
[RIFF: showing up at your hero's house at three in the morning. Or use this:]
Same time of night, same gate, same year. One guy brought Steve Van Zandt. The other guy brought a derringer. That's the whole difference between a cute story and a police report.

## THE FIRST VISIT
Okay. Here's the clock, because this is where it gets nuts, and it all happens in about a day.
Early in the morning, November 22nd, 1976. Jerry Lee pulls up to Graceland in his Rolls-Royce. A Silver Shadow. He wants to see Elvis.
And the guard tells him Elvis is asleep. And he's turned away. And that time, he leaves.
Then, around 9:30 that morning, in Collierville, at the corner of Peterson Lake Road and Powell Road, he takes a curve and flips the Rolls-Royce. Upside down.
According to Rick Bragg's book, his wife at the time, Jaren, was in the car with him.
He gets cited for driving while intoxicated, reckless driving, and driving without a license. And here's the part that kills me. The breathalyzer reportedly barely registered. One account says he flat out passed it.
[Pause.]
So a reasonable person, at this point in the day, goes home. A reasonable person has had a sign from God. Two signs. One was a gate, and one was a Rolls-Royce with its wheels in the air.
[RIFF: the upside down Rolls-Royce. Or use this:]
You know what it takes to flip a Rolls-Royce? Those things weigh about as much as a church. You have to really commit to that corner.
Jerry Lee does not go home.

## THE VAPORS
That night, less than twelve hours after the wreck, Jerry Lee is out holding court at a place called the Vapors. One of his favorite clubs in Memphis.
And at some point that night, the man who owns the club gives Jerry Lee Lewis a gun.
[Pause.]
I want to slow down on that. The man is drunk. He has shot his own bass player within the last two months. He has wrecked a Rolls-Royce that morning. And somebody looks at him and thinks, you know what this guy needs? A pistol.
It's a .38 derringer. Tiny thing. Jerry Lee told Rick Bragg, decades later, the club owner "give it to me." A .38 derringer. There's another version, from one of Elvis's bodyguards, that says it was a gift from a sheriff in Mississippi. Either way, somebody in a position of authority, a bar owner or a lawman, handed The Killer a loaded gun on the worst week of his life.
And why does he leave the Vapors and go back to Graceland?
Jerry Lee's answer, for the rest of his life, was simple. Elvis called him. He said Elvis called the club and invited him to come over. His sister, Linda Gail Lewis, told it the same way, and added that Elvis was feeling low that night and wanted somebody to talk to.
Nobody from Elvis's side ever confirmed that call. Nobody ever flat out denied it either. So that one goes in the "story goes" pile, and it stays there.
Around 2:30 in the morning, he leaves the Vapors.

## THE GATE
And now we're at the cold open. November 23rd. A little before three a.m.
He comes back to Graceland. Different car. Since the Rolls is upside down, it's a brand new white Lincoln Continental. One version says he bumped the gate with it when he pulled up. That's one account, so I'm not swearing to it.
And the guard on duty is family. Most accounts say it's Elvis's cousin, Harold Loyd. You'll see it spelled a couple of different ways. And the guard has already been told: don't let this guy in. Who gave that order, nobody has ever really pinned down. Could've been Elvis. Could've been his dad. Could've been the guys who'd seen Jerry Lee drunk before. Or it could just be what you do when the same drunk guy shows up twice in one day.
So the guard calls up to the house. And in Loyd's retelling, Elvis gets on the line and wants to know what the hell is going on down there. And Loyd says Jerry Lee is "sittin' in his car down here outside the gate, wavin' a derringer pistol and raisin' hell." And demanding to come up and see Elvis.
And Elvis's answer, according to the guard's version: call the police. And when they get there, tell them to "lock his butt up and throw the goddamn key away."
Now. That's the guard's version of a phone call, told later, by the guard. Elvis's uncle Vester, who also worked the gate, said Elvis told everybody to ignore it. And Jerry Lee's fan club president insisted the guard never even told Elvis he was there. So you've got three versions of what Elvis said, and one of them is that he said nothing.
[FILL: And the legend goes Elvis watched the whole thing on a closed circuit security monitor in the house. It's been reported. I've never seen anybody prove it. But I want it to be true so bad. Elvis in a robe, eating something, watching Jerry Lee Lewis on a little black and white TV like it's a Western.]

## THE COPS
Either way, the police come. Patrolman B.J. Kirkpatrick pulls up and finds Jerry Lee sitting in the Lincoln.
And the gun is right there. A chrome-plated, over-and-under .38 derringer. Two barrels, one on top of the other. And it's not on the dashboard and it's not on the floor. It's balanced on his knee. Cocked and fully loaded.
There's another officer's memory, from a piece years later, that Jerry Lee had tried to hide it, wedged between his knee and the car door, and when they opened the door, the gun fell out onto the floorboard.
[Pause.]
Which, honestly, is the most Jerry Lee hiding spot possible. "Officer, I have hidden the gun. In the door. Of the car. That you're about to open."
They arrest him at 3:07 in the morning. Carrying a pistol and public drunkenness. And while he's in custody, he complains to the cops that the local press hates him. Which, in fairness, was about to get a lot worse.
He posts a two hundred and fifty dollar bond and he's out about three hours later. So he got to Graceland around three, and was back on the street by breakfast. Twice in one day, Memphis just kind of let him go.

## THE CHAMPAGNE
[CLIP: Champagne bottle vs. car window]
And now, the champagne.
Jerry Lee has been drinking champagne all night. And he went on record about this later, he was drinking a lot of champagne, he doesn't even like champagne, and it made him a little wild.
A little.
So at some point he finishes a bottle. And he goes to toss the empty out the car window.
Except the window is closed.
And the bottle goes right through the glass. And Jerry Lee cuts his face. According to the arresting officer, that's how the window got broken: an empty champagne bottle, thrown through a closed window, from the inside.
Which window? Every account I found just says "the window." I'd love to tell you it was the driver's side. Nobody wrote that down, so I'm not going to make it up.
[FILL: I want everybody to appreciate that the most violent thing that happened at the gates of Graceland that night was Jerry Lee Lewis versus his own car window. And the window lost, but so did Jerry Lee.]
[RIFF: drinking something you don't even like. Or use this:]
That's the part that gets me. He doesn't like champagne. He's drinking it anyway. Bottles of it. That's not a party, that's a man punishing himself with bubbles.

## COURT
Now, you'd think, gun, Graceland, three in the morning, this is it, he's done.
Nope.
The case gets continued six times. Six. And finally it goes to trial on May 3rd, 1977, in Memphis City Court.
And Jerry Lee takes the stand. And he says he'd been on medication. He'd forgotten the pistol was even in the car. He was never screaming. And he was at Graceland because Elvis called him.
And the judge, Albert Boyd, gives what might be the most Memphis ruling of all time. He says Jerry Lee was not "in control of himself at the time, but transporting a pistol doesn't mean he had intentions of going armed."
[Pause.]
Acquitted.
So, legally, in the eyes of the State of Tennessee, Jerry Lee Lewis was just a very drunk man transporting a cocked derringer on his knee to his friend's house.
[RIFF: the judge's ruling. Or use this:]
"He was not in control of himself, but he didn't intend to go armed." He was armed! It was on his knee! It was cocked! I don't know what else the gun had to do. Introduce itself?

## WHAT JERRY LEE SAID LATER
And Jerry Lee told his side for the rest of his life.
Elvis called him. The gun was a gift from a club owner. He'd forgotten it was there, it slid off the dash. He never waved it at anybody. And he never, ever meant to shoot Elvis.
Then, in his seventies, he sat down with the writer Rick Bragg for two summers of interviews for his authorized biography, "Jerry Lee Lewis: His Own Story," which came out in 2014. And when he gets to Graceland, you can still hear it bugging him.
He told Bragg he thought Elvis told the cops to lock him up. He said the idea that Elvis would be scared of him, as well as they knew each other, was ridiculous. And he said this about Elvis. "He was a coward. He hurt me. That did."
And he never saw Elvis again after that night.
Because nine months later, on August 16th, 1977, Elvis died. At Graceland. He was forty two.
So the last time those two guys were anywhere near each other, one was upstairs, and the other one was in a police car with a cut on his face. Twenty years after they sang hymns around a piano at Sun.

## WHERE ARE THEY NOW
Jerry Lee Lewis kept playing. He kept drinking for a long time. He kept carrying guns. And he went into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in its very first class, in 1986. Right alongside Elvis.
And he lived a long time. A long, long time. He got into the Country Music Hall of Fame in October 2022. His doctor told him not to travel, so Kris Kristofferson and Hank Williams Jr. showed up for him. Twelve days later, on October 28th, he died. He was eighty seven.
[FILL: Jerry Lee outlived Elvis by forty five years. Nobody in 1976 would've taken that bet. Including his doctors. Including Jerry Lee.]
Butch Owens, the bass player, recovered after a month in the hospital, and he took Jerry Lee to court. I couldn't find out how that lawsuit ended, so I'm not going to guess.
Myra Gale Brown grew up, got out, remarried, and told her own story in a book. And that book is what the Dennis Quaid movie was based on. So the movie about Jerry Lee is her version, not his.
Graceland is a museum now. The music gates are still there. You can walk right up to them.

## THE SERIOUS PART
Real quick, and straight.
Nobody got hurt at the Graceland gate that night except Jerry Lee and his window. But this story has real people in it who got hurt.
Butch Owens came over to drop off a record and took a bullet in the chest from his own bandleader. He survived, he took him to court, and he deserved a lot better.
And Myra Gale Brown was thirteen years old. A kid. She was not a scandal. She was a kid, and the adults around her failed her.
Those two are not the joke. They never are on this show.

## LEGEND OR FACT
Quick round, because this story has more versions than a Jerry Lee live album.
He set his piano on fire and told Chuck Berry "follow that." Legend. Great one. Never pinned down.
Elvis called him and invited him over. His story, his sister's story, never confirmed, never denied.
He was waving the gun around. That's the guard. Jerry Lee said it slid off the dash.
The gun was cocked and loaded. Fact, according to the police.
Elvis said "lock his butt up and throw the goddamn key away." That's the guard's retelling. Elvis's uncle says it was "ignore it."
Elvis watched it all on a security monitor. Legend.
He flipped the Rolls the same day. Fact. Peterson Lake Road and Powell, 9:30 in the morning.
Champagne bottle through a closed window. Fact. It's in the officer's report. And it's still my favorite part.

## THAT GUY
[CLIP: That Guy verdict]
Okay. Time to name him. That Guy.
The suspects.
Suspect one: the champagne. Jerry Lee's words, not mine. He didn't like it, and it made him wild. I'm putting the bottle on the list.
Suspect two: the guy who owned the Vapors. Or the sheriff, depending on the version. Somebody looked at a man who'd shot his bass player and flipped a Rolls in the same couple of months and said, "Here, take this little gun." That guy is in the running. That guy is very much in the running.
Suspect three: Elvis. Maybe he called. Maybe he said "come over." And then when Jerry Lee came over, he stayed upstairs and let his cousin and the Memphis police deal with it. If Jerry Lee's story is true, the King started this.
Suspect four: Jerry Lee Lewis. A man who shot his bass player in September, flipped a Rolls-Royce in the morning, and came back to the same gate that night with a cocked derringer on his knee.
And the verdict.
The Elvis thing is disputed. Nobody can prove that phone call happened. And even if it did, "come hang out" is not "bring a cocked derringer."
The bar owner gets an honorable mention. Big one. That's a How Did This Get Made decision if I've ever heard one.
And the champagne can't drive.
So it's Jerry Lee. It's obviously Jerry Lee. It has never been more obviously one guy on this show.
[THAT GUY STING]
But here's the part I mean. This is a man who got thrown out of Bible school for playing too good. Whose dad mortgaged the house for a piano. Who sat at that piano with Elvis, and Cash, and Perkins, as the new kid. And twenty years later, he wasn't trying to kill anybody. He was drunk at three in the morning, banging on his old friend's gate, because he wanted to hang out. And his old friend wouldn't come down.
[RIFF: your verdict. Is Elvis on the hook at all? Or use this:]
Everybody has a friend who shows up at three in the morning. Most of us just don't have a gate. Or a cousin with a phone. Elvis had both.

## OUT
So that's Jerry Lee at Graceland. A piano and a mortgage, boogie-woogie at Bible school, a birthday with a .357, an upside down Rolls-Royce, a bar owner with a spare derringer, a champagne bottle versus a window, a judge who said it was fine, and Elvis, upstairs, not coming down.
And the gates are still there. You can go see them. You can even get in now. It costs a lot more than it did for Jerry Lee, and they really prefer you don't bring the derringer.
[RIFF: defacingthemusic.com, Guest List, subscribe, socials. Or use this:]
Get on the Guest List at defacingthemusic.com. No gate. No guard. Leave the champagne in the car.
I'm Duck. Due to unforeseen circumstances, I'll see you next time.

title: Due To a Flare Gun Indoors
subtitle: Who Brought a Flare Gun to a Zappa Show?
body:
## COLD OPEN
[CLIP: Cold open: a flare gun at a Zappa show]
December 1971. Montreux, Switzerland. A casino on Lake Geneva, with the Alps sitting behind it like a postcard.
Frank Zappa's band is on stage, deep into a long, weird synthesizer solo.
Somebody in the crowd raises a flare gun. Points it at the ceiling. And pulls the trigger.
Indoors.
And across the water, a British rock band that came to town to make a record is about to have a very different week than the one they planned.
## TODAY
Today: a Swiss casino, a flare gun, a band losing every piece of gear it owned, a festival boss running into a burning building, a truck borrowed from the Rolling Stones, the Swiss police banging on a door in the middle of the night, and the riff. You know the riff.
And somewhere in this story, there's a guy. There always is. This time he had a flare gun. Keep an eye out for him.
I'm Duck, and due to a flare gun indoors, this is Defacing the Music.
[THEME SONG, hard stop]
Episode [NUMBER]. Who Brought a Flare Gun to a Zappa Show?

## MONTREUX
Okay. Montreux. Let me set the table.
Montreux is a little resort town on Lake Geneva. Old hotels. Mountains. Rich people in nice coats walking slowly. The loudest sound on a Tuesday is a spoon hitting a teacup.
And in the middle of it is the Casino. Now, "casino" makes you think Vegas, slot machines, a guy named Sal. This was more of an entertainment complex. It opened in 1881 as the Kursaal: a casino, a restaurant, a winter garden, a theatre. And for ninety years, every time somebody had an idea, they bolted another room onto it. A terrace. A dance hall called the Lido. A swimming pool in the fifties. And in 1969, a new concert hall called the Hourglass, le Sablier.
And for a few years it had been home to something that put this quiet little town on the map.
The Montreux Jazz Festival.

## FUNKY CLAUDE
And that festival was the work of one guy. Claude Nobs.
Claude Nobs was born in 1936. He did not start out in music. He trained as a cook. Then he took a job at the Montreux tourism office. Which is maybe the least rock and roll job in the history of Europe.
But Claude had taste and he had nerve. He started putting on concerts in the mid sixties, while still at the tourist office, and in 1967 he launched the Montreux Jazz Festival. It turned into one of the biggest music festivals in the world, and Claude ran it for decades.
[RIFF: Claude Nobs, the tourist office guy who built a world famous festival. Or use this:]
Every town has a Claude. The guy at the chamber of commerce who says, "What if we got a band?" Most of the time you get a cover band at the sidewalk sale. Once in a while you get Montreux.

## FRANK
Now. Frank Zappa. The mustache.
Zappa was born in Baltimore in 1940. His dad was a chemist who worked in the defense industry. And here's the detail I can't get over. The way Frank told it, he learned to make gunpowder when he was about six. He kept experimenting with explosives until he was around fifteen.
So that's the kid who made gunpowder in his bedroom. Keep him in mind when somebody else brings the fire to his show.
The family moved west, to California, and Frank ended up in music. Not normal music. His first album with the Mothers of Invention, "Freak Out!", came out in 1966. Doo-wop, satire, noise, jokes, orchestra stuff. Zappa was a composer who happened to have a rock band.
And by 1971, his band had a lineup that I personally find hilarious. Because two of the lead singers were Mark Volman and Howard Kaylan. If those names don't ring a bell: they were from The Turtles.
"Happy Together." "Imagine me and you, I do." That Turtles.
So the guys who sang the sweetest, sunniest pop song of 1967 are now in Frank Zappa's band, going by Flo and Eddie, doing filthy comedy rock. And they still sang "Happy Together" in the Zappa shows. It's on the Fillmore East live album from that year.
So that's the band that rolls into Montreux in December of 1971. Zappa, Flo and Eddie, and a keyboard player named Don Preston, with a Minimoog synthesizer, which in 1971 was still a pretty exotic thing to bring on tour.

## THE ROOM
Before anything catches fire, let's look at the room. Because this is the part of the story where people make decisions, and nobody thinks they're making decisions.
The Hourglass hall had a ceiling made of wood. One account says it had "tropical island" decorations. Other people remember curtains, papier-mache Christmas decorations, and rattan. Nobody fully agrees on the rattan. A fire engineering study looked at the photos fifty years later and couldn't spot any. What everybody agrees on is that the fire started up there, and that up there was the kind of thing that burns.
Up on the wall was the hall's big emblem, an hourglass. A hydraulic clock. Full of liquid. And when the Swiss held a tribunal about the fire the next year, one claim was that it held forty five hundred liters of paraffin. The casino's lawyer said no, no, it was only three thousand liters of mineral oil.
[FILL: "Only three thousand liters of mineral oil" is the most lawyer sentence I have ever read. That's your defense? It was the other flammable liquid?]
Outside, the building was covered in scaffolding, because it was being renovated.
Inside, somebody had taken out the chairs. So the crowd sat on the floor. One fan who was there, Alain Rieder, said standing concerts weren't the fashion yet, so everybody just sat down on the ground.
How many people? The papers said about two thousand. Zappa said twenty five hundred to three thousand kids, packed in, "well over capacity." One later account said as many as four thousand.
There were security people, volunteers from the tourist office, and four firefighters on duty for the show.
And according to Zappa, writing in his book years later, there was one more decision. A lot more kids were outside trying to get in. So, he said, the organizers had "cleverly chained the doors shut."
[RIFF: chaining the doors because of gate crashers. Or use this:]
Every club owner in history has had the same thought. "If I lock that door, nobody sneaks in." Which is true. It is also true that nobody gets out. It's the same door. It works both ways. That's how doors work.
Now, to be fair to the casino, an eyewitness said the security staff and the young hotel and casino workers got all the emergency exits open fast. So it's Zappa's word against that. But Zappa said it more than once. In a French TV interview, he said people got to an exit and it was locked, and they had to bang it down.

## THE SHOW
The show was on Saturday, December 4th, in the afternoon. A matinee. It started around two. Which feels wrong for a fire story, but here we are.
By most accounts it's a good show. A packed house. And they get into "King Kong," a long instrumental the Mothers liked to stretch out, and Don Preston takes a synthesizer solo.
And somewhere around a quarter after four, somebody in the audience fires something up at the ceiling.
And the ceiling, I'm sorry to tell you, was the kind that catches fire.

## THE GUY WITH THE GUN
[CLIP: Nobody knows who fired the flare]
So who was it? This is where I went digging, and here's what's actually out there.
The common version, the one in the song, is a flare gun. One of the guys in Deep Purple said someone behind them shot off a flare that went up into the rafters. Ian Gillan has said he saw two of them. And Claude Nobs said later that Gillan told him the guy was standing right next to him and fired before anybody could stop him.
A woman who was there told a Lausanne paper two days later that a young man near her fired a small pistol at the start of the concert, and then fired it again later, and that's the one that lit the ceiling.
So he warmed up. He did a test shot. At the start of the show. And nobody took it away from him.
[FILL: That's the part that kills me. Shot one, nobody does anything. Shot two, the building's gone. There was a whole Zappa set in between where somebody could've said, "Hey man, what's in the jacket?"]
But not everybody saw a flare. Zappa himself, in one telling, called it more like a bottle rocket or a Roman candle. A guy named Peter Schneider, who wrote about being one of the last ones out, thought it was a kid throwing lit matches up at the low ceiling. And one Lausanne paper reported witnesses who saw it start in an electric lamp hanging near the ceiling, which would mean a short circuit and no gun at all.
The fire engineers who studied it fifty years later landed on this: the consensus is some kind of firework or flare. Not proven. Consensus.
And the man himself? The Swiss police named a suspect. He took off right after, they put out a search, and they never found him. The rumor is he went to South America. He was never caught, never charged, never tried, and never told his side. His name is out there online. I'm not saying it, because nobody ever proved it.
So "the guy with the flare gun" is a real guy. We just don't get to meet him.

## IT'S PART OF THE SHOW
And for a second, nobody panics. Because it's a Zappa show. Weird stuff happens at a Zappa show. Smoke and fire might just be the bit.
Alain Rieder said that at first the fire was tiny, and he figured they'd put it out and the concert would keep going.
And Peter Schneider, the guy who was one of the last ones out, wrote this, and I love him for his honesty. He looked behind him, saw a big ball of flame, and, quote, "Because I was very stoned it looked beautiful." He thought the fire was part of the show.
[RIFF: being too high to notice the building is on fire. Or use this:]
Every one of us has been at a show where something went wrong and we thought it was on purpose. An amp blows, you think it's a sound effect. The drummer falls off the riser, you think it's choreography. This guy watched the ceiling catch fire and thought, "Wow. Production values."
And this next part is legendary, but the details shift depending on who's telling it. The story goes that somebody on stage made a joke. "Fire! Arthur Brown in person!"
[FILL: For the young people: Arthur Brown's big hit in 1968 was a song called "Fire," and he performed wearing a helmet that was on fire. Great joke, if you were alive in 1968.]
Who said it? Some accounts say Zappa, some say Mark Volman, some say Howard Kaylan. And Rieder has said the idea of Zappa laughing it off is nonsense. So it goes in the "the story goes" pile.
Meanwhile, people tried to put it out. Zappa said in that French interview that a guy ran up with a fire extinguisher, and when he used it, fire came out of the ceiling and part of the roof fell down. One of the four firefighters on duty tried a hose reel and couldn't get it going.
And Claude grabbed a hose too. And here's the detail one person who was around tells: the water barely went two meters up. Because the pressure in that line had been turned down. So the coffee machine wouldn't explode.
[Pause.]
The story goes. I can't prove the coffee machine. But somebody, at some point, made a call about that coffee machine, and it was not a fire safety call.

## EVERYBODY OUT
Here is where Frank Zappa becomes the responsible adult.
And we don't have to guess much about what he said, because the show was taped. Zappa later put the recording out himself, on an official bootleg set called Beat the Boots, and you can hear him telling people to stay calm. The line that gets quoted is: "Fire! If you'd kindly move calmly toward the exit, ladies and gentlemen. Calmly."
Ladies and gentlemen. The building is on fire and he says "if you'd kindly."
And the room didn't have great ways out. So people went for the windows. Behind the curtains on each side of the stage there were floor to ceiling windows. People ripped the curtains open. Zappa said one of his roadies picked up an equipment case and smashed the big window. Claude Nobs, years later, told it as Zappa smashing it with his guitar, which Zappa never claimed. And Schneider says what got him out was a firefighter breaking a window with an axe.
So depending on who you ask, the window got broken by a roadie, a firefighter, or the guitar that Frank Zappa did not use. My money's on the guy with the equipment case. Roadies break things for a living.
And then people jumped. About ten feet, give or take, into the grass. Rieder said he hung off a ledge and let himself drop.
And one witness said that before jumping, they went back for their belongings. Which were exactly where they'd left them. In the burning building.
[FILL: Somewhere out there is a person who walked back into a burning casino for a bag, and I respect the priorities.]
And the no-chairs thing, the thing that sounds like a bad decision? Schneider thinks it helped. No rows to climb over, broad daylight, and, his words, nearly everybody was so stoned that the fear didn't kick in, so they walked out in a more or less orderly way.
The tourist office said everybody was out in three and a half minutes. Claude said about five. The fire department got the alarm at 4:22, and the first trucks pulled up three and a half minutes later, right as the last of the crowd came out the front door.
And Zappa said his roadies were the last ones out, and an explosion from the heating system blew them out the door.
And here's the thing I have to say clearly. Nobody died. Zappa said three people went to the hospital, one of them a roadie caught in that blast. For a fire that took down an entire building with a crowd inside, that is about as lucky as it gets.
[RIFF: the calm voice in an emergency. Or use this:]
Every band has the one member who's good in a crisis. The guy who, when the van catches fire on the interstate, is already on the shoulder with the extinguisher while the drummer films it. That day, that guy was Frank Zappa.

## CLAUDE RUNS IN
[CLIP: Funky Claude runs into the fire]
And Claude Nobs. The chef. The tourist office guy.
While the place is burning, Claude is going back in. The festival's own history, and his obituaries, credit him with pulling out several young people who had hidden inside the casino, because they thought they'd be safe from the fire in there.
One of the guys who went in with him, Michel Ferla, explained the search plan. "We crawled through the burning building on all fours. At that time a lot of marijuana was smoked. We wanted to be sure that no one had fallen asleep."
That's the most Swiss rescue in history. Calm. Thorough. And checking under every couch for a sleeping hippie.
That is why he's in the song. "Funky Claude was running in and out." That line is about a real man running into a real burning building to drag out kids who'd made a terrible decision about where to hide.
I want that on his headstone. Not "Founder of the Jazz Festival." "Ran Into The Fire."

## THE BUILDING GOES
About eighty firefighters came in from all over the area. And the fire just ate the place. The Hourglass, then the rest of the building. The scaffolding outside burned like torches. Somebody said the whole thing looked like a giant torch, with black smoke you could see from miles away.
And here's my favorite detail from the firefighters. One of their senior guys said the water system ran dry after two hours. So they started pumping water straight out of the lake.
They put the fire out with Lake Geneva.
They saved a garage next door. They did not save the theatre. The estimate at the time was twelve to fifteen million Swiss francs in damage.
And everything the Mothers brought on that tour was inside. All their gear. Gone.

## DEEP PURPLE
Deep Purple. British hard rock band, and in 1971 they're right in the classic lineup. Ian Gillan singing. Ritchie Blackmore on guitar. Jon Lord on the organ. Roger Glover on bass. Ian Paice on drums.
And they're in Montreux on purpose. Here's how that decision got made. They were supposed to be touring America at the end of 1971. Then Ian Gillan got sick, and the dates fell through. So now they've got a hole in the calendar and a record to make. One account adds they wanted somewhere unusual, and somewhere outside Britain's taxes.
They'd booked the casino to record their next album, in the off season, after the casino's last show of the year. That last show was Zappa.
And they didn't book a regular studio. They booked a truck.
The Rolling Stones Mobile. A recording studio in a truck, owned by the Rolling Stones. You park it outside a building, run cables in, and now the building is a studio. That truck is on a lot of great records from that era, including parts of Led Zeppelin's fourth album.
[CLIP: Smoke on the Water gets its title]
So the plan is: Zappa plays the last show, everybody goes home, the casino goes quiet for winter, and Deep Purple moves in and makes a record with the Stones' truck parked outside.
And Deep Purple had passes to the show. Roger Glover has told the story: they got to their hotel rooms and there was a fruit basket, a bottle of Swiss wine, and a pass to see Zappa at the casino. Ian Gillan has said he was in the audience when the flare went up.
[Pause.]
So the welcome gift was a ticket to watch your recording studio burn down.
And the story goes, from French-language press and retold by Claude himself, that Gillan got out fine and then went back inside the burning building. For his girlfriend's jacket. Claude called it typical of him.
[FILL: Gentlemen. If your girlfriend's jacket is in a burning casino, it's a gift to the casino now. Buy her a new jacket.]
The smoke drifted out over Lake Geneva. Smoke. On the water.
And yeah. That's the title. It was sitting right there.
Roger Glover gets credit for the title, and there are two versions of how. In one, he woke up from a dream a few days later with the phrase in his head. In another, he wrote it down right away. Either way, it's Roger's.

## THE PAVILION
So now Deep Purple has a truck, a booking, and no building.
And Claude Nobs, who has just had the worst day of his professional life, starts finding them somewhere else to record. Because that's the kind of guy he is.
First stop: a local hall called the Pavilion. They set up, and they start jamming. And out of that jam comes a riff.
Ritchie Blackmore. Four notes. Well. You know.
[RIFF: the riff. If you've ever picked up a guitar, you've played it. Or use this:]
If you have ever picked up a guitar, you know this riff. You learned it before you knew what a chord was. You learned it on one string. Every guitar teacher in America has heard it ten thousand times and would like it to stop.
Blackmore has explained it a few ways. He's said it's built in fourths, that old, kind of medieval sounding interval. He's also said in an interview that it's Beethoven's Fifth, turned around. Plenty of musicians say it doesn't sound like that at all. So Beethoven goes in the "the story goes" pile.
And then the neighbors complain.
[CLIP: Roadies hold the door against the Swiss police]
It's the middle of the night in a quiet Swiss town, and a hard rock band is blasting away in a public hall. The band has told this one many times: the police showed up and started pounding on the door, and the road crew held the door shut so they could finish the take.
So the backing track for the most famous riff in rock history got finished while roadies physically held the door against the Swiss police.
[FILL: Second time that week a door in Montreux got held shut on purpose. This time, at least, nobody needed to get out.]

## THE GRAND HOTEL
Then they moved again, to the Grand Hotel, which was empty for the winter. And this is another decision that sounds insane and worked.
They parked the Stones truck at the main entrance and set up the band at the end of a corridor off the lobby, where the hallway made a T. To kill the echo in a big empty hotel, they hauled in mattresses. Ian Paice said about a hundred of them, lining the hallway.
So the band that just lost its studio to a fire is now recording in a hotel hallway made of beds.
And the truck was outside, so every time they wanted to hear a take, somebody had to walk out through the hotel, out the front, into the truck. It was such a pain that, by one account, they mostly stopped listening to playbacks. They just played it and trusted it.
[RIFF: recording without playbacks. Or use this:]
That's the scariest way to make a record. No playback. You play it, you nod at each other, you go, "Yeah, that felt good," and you move on. Every band I've ever been around would argue about that for an hour. Deep Purple just went, "Fine. Next."
Gillan wrote the lyrics, and they're basically a news report of the week: the fire, Funky Claude, the Grand Hotel, and the man of the hour, who the song calls "some stupid with a flare gun." That's his official review.

## THE HIT
The album was "Machine Head." It came out in March 1972. And here's the funny part. Nobody in the band thought "Smoke on the Water" was the single. Gillan has said it was just another riff to them. One retelling of the sessions says it only made the album as filler.
It became a single in the States in 1973, and it went to number four on the Billboard chart.
And it never left. Every garage, every guitar store, every talent show. All because some guy brought a flare gun to a Zappa matinee.
And the casino? Rebuilt. It reopened in 1975, with a recording studio inside called Mountain Studios. In 1979, Queen bought it. Freddie Mercury ended up making records in the building that replaced the one that burned, and today there's a statue of Freddie on the lakefront.

## THE SERIOUS PART
Now I need to slow down for a minute, because Zappa's week was not done.
The fire took everything the Mothers had brought. And they kept going anyway. They rented equipment and got to London, and six days later, on December 10th, 1971, they're playing the Rainbow Theatre.
And during the show, a man in the audience named Trevor Howell gets on stage and shoves Zappa off it. Into the orchestra pit. Onto concrete. Accounts put the fall at somewhere between ten and fifteen feet.
Zappa was badly hurt. A broken leg, a head injury, injuries to his back and neck. He was in the hospital for weeks, and he spent a long stretch of the next year in a wheelchair, off the road. Zappa wrote later that the band thought he was dead. He also said the injury to his throat dropped his voice for good.
Howell got a year in jail. And his reason depends on which report you read. One version, the one Zappa repeated, is that it was about his girlfriend and Zappa. Another contemporary report says he just didn't think the concert was good value for the money. So the motive goes in the "the story goes" pile. Either way, there are a lot of ways to complain about a ticket price, and this is the worst one.
That doesn't get a joke. That lineup of the Mothers was basically done. A guy who had just calmly walked a couple thousand people out of a burning building got thrown off a stage six days later.

## THAT GUY
[CLIP: That Guy verdict]
Okay. Time to name him. That Guy.
The suspects.
Suspect one: the guy with the flare gun. Fired once at the start of the show, according to one witness, and nobody stopped him. Fired again, and the ceiling went. Swiss police named a suspect, he ran, and they never caught him. So he stays "the guy."
Suspect two: the people who ran the building. A wooden ceiling, a giant hourglass full of either paraffin or "only" mineral oil, a room Zappa said was way over capacity, doors Zappa said were chained against gate crashers, and a fire hose that, the story goes, got turned down for a coffee machine. Every one of those is a decision somebody made on a normal day without thinking about the bad day.
Suspect three: Frank Zappa. Kidding. Partly. The man made gunpowder at six and his show was the one that caught fire. That's either cosmic justice or a coincidence and I'm calling it a coincidence.
[Pause.]
And the verdict.
It's the flare gun guy. The building made it worse, and I'm not letting the coffee machine off the hook. But buildings full of wood and bad choices sit there for ninety years without burning down. What they need is one guy in a crowd of a couple thousand people who thinks, "You know what this King Kong solo needs?" And then does it twice.
[THAT GUY STING]
And to be straight with you: we don't know his name for sure, we don't know exactly what he fired, and we never heard his side. What we know is what he did.
But here's the "that guy is usually awesome" part. And I hate it. Without that guy, there is no "Smoke on the Water." No fire, no song. Every kid who ever learned that riff on one string owes a little piece of it to the worst decision anybody made in Switzerland that year.
[RIFF: your verdict. Do you thank him or not? Or use this:]
He burned down a casino and accidentally wrote the first lesson in every guitar book. I'm not thanking him. But I'm not not thanking him.

## OUT
So that's it. One Swiss casino. One flare gun, maybe two shots. A Zappa band that lost all its gear and then had a week that got worse. A chef from the tourist office crawling through a fire looking for sleeping hippies. Firemen pumping Lake Geneva. Roadies holding a door against the police. A hallway full of mattresses. And four notes every guitar player on Earth can play.
And the lesson, if there is one: if the casino is on fire, do not hide in the casino. Claude will come get you, but don't make Claude do that.
[RIFF: one last thought, maybe play the riff, or tell people your first riff. Or use this:]
Next time you hear some kid in a guitar store playing that riff on one string, don't roll your eyes. That kid is doing history.
Next time, another night that went sideways. There's always another one.
[RIFF: defacingthemusic.com, Guest List, subscribe, socials. Or use this:]
Get on the Guest List at defacingthemusic.com. No flare guns. We check.
I'm Duck. Due to unforeseen circumstances, I'll see you next time.

title: Due To Pyro and a Sore Throat
subtitle: Who Stood James Hetfield on the Flamethrower?
body:
## COLD OPEN
[CLIP: Cold open: James walks to the wrong spot]
August 8th, 1992. Montreal. Olympic Stadium.
Two of the biggest bands on the planet on one bill. Metallica is up first, and they're cooking.
They go into "Fade to Black." The slow one.
And James Hetfield walks toward a spot on the stage where, at that exact second, there is not supposed to be a person.
And that's only the first thing that goes wrong in this building tonight.
## TODAY
Today: the loudest tour of 1992, a stadium that took thirty years to pay off, a pyro guy who got called a traitor, a guitar tech who keeps getting promoted the worst possible way, and a riot in a city that did nothing to deserve it.
Two bands. One night. Zero full sets.
And somewhere in this story, there's a guy. A few people are going to get blamed tonight, some of them by their own managers. Only one of them gets the sting.
I'm Duck, and due to pyro and a sore throat, this is Defacing the Music.
[THEME SONG, hard stop]
Episode [NUMBER]. Who Stood James Hetfield on the Flamethrower?

## 1992
Okay. Context. Because if you were not alive and holding a cassette in 1992, you need to understand how big these two bands were.
In August 1991, Metallica put out the self-titled record. Everybody calls it the Black Album. "Enter Sandman." "Nothing Else Matters." Your mom knew "Enter Sandman." That's how big.
A month later, Guns N' Roses put out "Use Your Illusion I" and "Use Your Illusion II." Two albums. Same day. Because one wasn't enough for Axl.
So in 1992, somebody has the idea: put them together. One stadium tour. Metallica and Guns N' Roses, co-headlining. The biggest metal band in the world and the biggest rock band in the world, every night, for the price of one ticket.
[RIFF: what that ticket meant if you were sixteen in 1992. Or use this:]
If you were sixteen in 1992 and you got a ticket to this, you were the most important person in your high school for about a week. You wore the shirt to school. You wore it until your mom made you take it off.

## WHOSE IDEA WAS THIS
So who's the somebody? Who had the idea?
By the account in Louder, the music magazine, the idea of hitting stadiums with Guns came from Lars Ulrich. Metallica's drummer. The business brain of the band.
May 12th, 1992. A club in Hollywood called the Gaslight. Lars and Slash sit down at a press conference and announce it. And Lars says, quote, "I've always wanted to play with Guns N' Roses since we met them in 1987."
That's sweet. That's a guy who's a fan. And that's a guy who has never had to wait for Axl Rose.
Then somebody has to figure out who goes on last. And this is the decision the whole night hangs on. Guns N' Roses were adamant that they close every show. And Metallica? By most accounts, Metallica happily went along with it. Fine. You close. We'll go on first, play hard, and be at the bar.
[FILL: Axl wanted Nirvana to open. Kurt Cobain said no. So Faith No More got the slot. Even the opening act was a whole thing.]
Now, here's why that decision matters. Metallica showed up on time. Every night. Played. Went home. Guns N' Roses had a habit of going on late. Like, late. Accounts from the tour describe fans waiting two or three hours after Metallica finished before Guns came out.
And they didn't ease into it, either. Opening night, July 17th, RFK Stadium in Washington, D.C. The break between bands was supposed to run about two hours. It took three. Night one. That's the first data point. Everybody on that tour knew, from the very first night, that the band going on last was the band that couldn't be counted on to go on.
[FILL: If you've ever been in a band with a guy who's always late to practice, multiply him by a stadium.]

## JAMES
Let me tell you about James Hetfield. Because the guy we're about to set on fire had a hell of a road to get here.
James grew up in Southern California. His parents were Christian Scientists. And if you don't know, that's a faith that leans hard on prayer instead of doctors.
When James was sixteen, his mother died of cancer. She had refused medical treatment because of her beliefs.
He wrote about it later. The song "The God That Failed," on the Black Album, comes out of that. He's said it's less about blaming God and more about the fact that his mom's faith didn't save her.
I'm not going to make a joke there, and I'm telling you this for a reason: this is a guy who grew up in a house where you didn't go to the doctor. Keep that in your head for the hospital part.
A couple years later, in 1981, he answers an ad. A kid named Lars Ulrich, a Danish kid whose dad was a pro tennis player, is looking for people to start a band. Lars plays drums. Sort of. That's Metallica.
And here's a little piece of foreshadowing. In 1986, Metallica's opening for Ozzy Osbourne, and James breaks his wrist. Skateboarding. Can't play guitar. So the band hands his rhythm guitar parts to their guitar tech, a guy named John Marshall, and James just sings.
File John Marshall away. He's the guy who keeps getting the call.
[FILL: Imagine your whole job is tuning another guy's guitars, and every few years, the universe goes, "Hey. Get out there."]

## AXL
And then there's Axl.
Axl Rose was born William Bruce Rose Jr., in Lafayette, Indiana. A Midwestern kid. Not far from here, honestly. A couple hours down the road from Chicago. And in the early eighties he heads out to Los Angeles with his buddy Izzy Stradlin, and a few years later they're Guns N' Roses, and "Appetite for Destruction" is selling more copies than God.
[CLIP: Axl walks off and gets arrested at JFK]
And Axl, by 1992, has a reputation. For being brilliant. And for walking off.
Here's the big one. July 2nd, 1991. Riverport Amphitheatre, outside St. Louis. In the middle of "Rocket Queen," Axl spots a fan with a camera. Accounts differ on the exact order of events, but Axl goes after the guy, ends up in the crowd, and then the band leaves the stage.
And St. Louis riots. Dozens of people hurt. Damage in the hundreds of thousands. A judge issues a warrant for Axl for inciting a riot.
And here's my favorite part. A year later, July 1992, Axl flies back into New York. And they arrest him at the airport. At JFK. That same summer. Five days before the tour with Metallica even starts.
He ended up with probation and a fifty thousand dollar donation to local charities.
[RIFF: getting arrested at the airport. Or use this:]
You know how your worst fear at the airport is that they lose your bag? Axl's was a little different. Axl got off the plane and his bag was fine. Axl was what got lost.
So that's who's closing this show. A singer who had already walked off one stage and watched a city riot. A year earlier. And everybody who signed off on the billing knew it, because it was in every newspaper in America.

## THE BIG OWE
[CLIP: The Big Owe, paid for with cigarettes]
Now, the venue. Montreal's Olympic Stadium.
It was built for the 1976 Summer Olympics. And Montreal locals have a nickname for it. Officially it's "the Big O."
Unofficially? "The Big Owe."
Because the thing cost so much money that Quebec didn't finish paying it off until 2006. Thirty years. And a big chunk of it was paid by a special tax on tobacco. Quebec basically paid for its stadium with cigarettes.
[FILL: The final bill, with interest and repairs, comes out to about one point six billion Canadian dollars. They were still paying it off when the iPod came out.]
And here's the kicker, at least according to the stadium history folks. In 2006, Quebec brought in an indoor smoking ban. Which cut into the tobacco tax. Which slowed down paying off the stadium. So Montreal's health got better, and its stadium payments got worse.
In 1992 it's also where the Montreal Expos play baseball. Put a pin in the Expos. They come back in this story in a very specific way.
That's the room. A concrete UFO that the whole province chipped in for, one pack of smokes at a time. And by the end of the night, people are going to be throwing parts of it.
And the guy putting on the show in Montreal is a local legend. Donald Tarlton. In the business he was Donald K. Donald, and when he died, the concert trade press called him the ultimate Canadian impresario. And he went into this one, by his own account years later, nervous. He told the Montreal Gazette, quote, "People had told me to be careful. So I was not looking for aggravation at all, whatsoever."
He was not going to get his wish.

## PYRO PETE
Before we get to the fire, you need to meet the fire guy. Or, actually, the fire guy who wasn't there.
[CLIP: Lars calls the pyro guy a traitor]
There's a pyro tech named Pete Cappadocia. Goes by Pyro Pete. He'd done pyrotechnics for both bands before this tour. Metallica and Guns. So when the two bands team up, Pete's the obvious guy to do both.
And Lars catches wind of this. And Lars, according to Pete on a podcast called Appetite for Distortion years later, says, more or less, "I don't want you shooting Guns N' Roses. I only want you shooting us."
So Pete has to pick one. And Guns offered him the better deal. He goes with Guns.
And Pete says Lars had one of his people confirm how much Guns was paying him, and then Lars called him back, cursed him out, and called him a traitor.
[RIFF: getting cursed out by Lars Ulrich over a paycheck. Or use this:]
Imagine getting a voicemail from Lars Ulrich calling you a traitor. Over your job. You're not in the band. You blow stuff up for a living. And the drummer of the biggest metal band on Earth is taking it personally that you went where the money was. Which, honestly, is a very Lars thing to take personally.
So Metallica's pyro that summer is run by somebody else. Pete describes him as Metallica's own guy, a guy who'd shot their pyro in Europe. I couldn't find his name in anything. And I'm not going to go digging for it, and you'll see why.

## FADE TO BLACK
So. August 8th, 1992. Faith No More opens. Metallica comes on. And the show's going great.
And Metallica has a big production. Lots of pyro. And when they get to "Fade to Black," there's a pyro cue at the front of the stage.
And here's a little detail. "Fade to Black" opens with that clean, pretty guitar part, so James is wearing a double-neck guitar for it. A big ESP double-neck. Two guitars bolted together. That guitar is going to come up again in about a minute.
James walks into the cue.
[Pause.]
Now. How. This is the part where the stories don't all line up, and I'm going to give you all of them, because I don't get to pick.
James's own version: he was confused about where he was supposed to stand. He walked forward. Walked back. And the guy running the pyro didn't see that he'd walked back out into that spot.
Pyro Pete, the guy who was working for Guns that night, has told it this way: the stage monitors had been moved, and a piece of the pyro had been moved, and James walked to his spot. And by one write-up of that interview, he took about an extra half step and put his arm right over the cue just as it went.
There's also a version that the pyro had gotten bigger. Far Out Magazine says the crew had increased the charges and put them at the front of the stage and out on the wings. And one account says James got told about the new stuff on the wings, but nobody told him the old stuff out front was still there too. That's one account. I can't nail it down past that.
And the general summary you'll see everywhere is "a miscommunication with the pyro crew."
[FILL: Honestly, all of those can be true at the same time. That's what makes it scary. Nobody has to screw up very much.]
And the flame went up. Accounts describe it as around twelve feet. And it caught James on the left side. His arm. His hand.
And that double-neck? James wrote about it in his guitar book, "Messengers," years later. The guitar took some of the flame. It shielded him from the worst of it. The neck is unpainted wood, so you can still see where it got scorched. He kept it.
[RIFF: the half step. Every musician knows the stage mark. Or use this:]
Every musician who's ever played a real stage knows the tape on the floor. You hit your mark. And most nights, if you miss it by half a step, the worst that happens is you're out of the light. On this night, half a step was the difference between a great show and a burn unit.

## THE NUTS
So James gets off stage. And he's in a lot of pain. And this next part is his own story, so it's his to tell, and he tells it a little bit proud.
He's backstage, waiting for a ride to the hospital. And somebody, a security guy by most tellings, bumps right into his burned hand.
And James says, quote, "I just lost it. I screamed and punched him right in the nuts."
[RIFF: the worst possible moment to bump into James Hetfield. Or use this:]
There is a list of people you do not bump into. And at the top of that list, permanently, is the guy from Metallica whose arm was on fire a few minutes ago. Whatever else that security guy did in his career, nobody remembers it. They remember this.
Then he's off to Montreal General Hospital. A hospital spokesperson confirmed he got treated there, and that he checked out during the night. The guy from the house with no doctors, getting patched up and walking out before sunrise.
And back at the stadium, Lars, Kirk Hammett and Jason Newsted went out and told the crowd they couldn't keep going. Metallica's done for the night.

## THE WAIT
So now there's a giant hole in the night. And everybody's looking at Guns N' Roses to fill it.
